domains.summary: NYC geography is very uneven. In October 2019, 16 of the city's 263 taxi zones produced half of all yellow-cab pickups and 89% came from the 55-zone Manhattan core. App (HVFHV) pickups needed 60 zones for half and were 59.5% outer-borough (June 2021). So the same map rewards different positioning for a taxi, an app driver and a robotaxi. The biggest geographic profit drivers are where demand concentrates and where drop-offs strand the driver: Brooklyn and the Bronx receive about four yellow drop-offs per pickup, and the share of core trips heading to outer boroughs rises from 1.4% at 8am to 17.7% at 4am. Airports were 7.9% of yellow trips but 22.2% of driver revenue, yet holding-lot waits have been reported at 2-3 hours, and Newark is drop-off-only for NYC cars. Rules tied to places matter as much as roads: the green-taxi hail exclusion zone, the Congestion Relief Zone (Manhattan at or below 60th St; $0.75 per taxi trip, $1.50 per HVFHV trip), the 96th St surcharge line, inbound-only Hudson tolls ($16.79 peak), airport fees and out-of-town pay rates. The user's idea of comparing road density with foot traffic becomes a 'pickup-ability' index (stoppable curb vs pedestrians), built from NYC DOT pedestrian counts, Pedestrian Mobility Plan street classes and MTA hourly subway ridership. Robotaxi geography in NYC is hypothetical: Waymo's test permits (Manhattan south of 112th St and Downtown Brooklyn, no passengers) expired on 31 March 2026, so the geofence is a benchmark setting. The dossier has 70 variables in 10 sub-boxes (19 high, 32 medium, 19 low impact; 39 core). Many headline numbers are my own computations on TLC trip records (GitHub copies, because the TLC host is blocked). Official fee and rule pages could be read only through search snippets, and the shared web-search budget ran out before some items were verified; those are tagged [U].
key_corrections: How it was checked: the web-search budget was already used up and the official hosts were blocked, with no proxies used. The check rests on re-running every own-computed TLC figure, a verbatim GitHub copy of the Rules of the City of New York and Admin Code (current to 13 Aug 2026), and GitHub copies of official pages tagged [S]. Counts are per variable: corrected beats uncertain, uncertain beats verified.

R01-006: green cabs also may not start base-dispatched (pre-arranged) trips in Manhattan south of E 96th / W 110th, and an e-hail counts as a hail. 'E-hail still allowed' was wrong (35 RCNY 51-03, 82-13; tag upgraded from [S] to [P*]).

R01-054: the $2.50 HVFHV airport fee is already on Jan 2023 records, on pickups and drop-offs, so 'since Apr 2023' was wrong. The April 2023 change was the yellow access fee rising from $1.25 to $1.75. The $20 Newark taxi surcharge is in force (35 RCNY 58-26(c)(3)), not a proposal. A $2.00 access fee for 2026 is uncertain.

R01-021 / R01-056 / R01-059: on taxi trips to EWR, Westchester and Nassau the passenger pays tolls both ways, so the taxi's empty-return toll is reimbursed. Taxis may refuse these trips after 8 h of operation. R01-059 impact cut from high to medium.

R01-026: HVFHV Jan 2023 records give a pickup-minus-on-scene median of 0.8 min, with 90% under about 2 min (Uber). Lyft leaves on_scene_datetime empty in 99.9% of trips. The '0.5-5 min [U]' range was replaced and impact cut from medium to low.

R01-011 / R01-032 / R01-041: 34 RCNY 4-11(b) bars non-taxis from cruising to look for passengers, and 4-11(a) lets a waiting taxi stand only at a stand. The anti-idling limits (3 min, 1 min near schools) are confirmed in Admin Code 24-163.

R01-019 / R01-020: Brooklyn and Queens share a land border, so bridges and tunnels are not the only links between boroughs. The Henry Hudson Bridge is tolled and the Staten Island-NJ crossings were missing. Trip records confirm the $6.94 MTA car toll from Aug 2023. R01-019 impact cut from high to medium.

R01-004: the lowest-ratio zone is Windsor Terrace (0.08), not Washington Heights North (0.09). JFK's 3.81 drops to 3.53 under a lighter cleaning filter. All other own-computed figures were reproduced exactly.

Smaller fixes: the 14th St busway runs 3rd-9th Ave, not 3rd-8th (R01-028). The 200 ft bus-lane rule is about right turns (R01-027). Some avenues are two-way (R01-013). The 25 mph base limit is fixed by law (R01-015). R01-070 refusal rules also cover Westchester, Nassau and Newark (P*). The taxi 'returning home' rule was added to R01-062. R01-001 impact cut from high to medium.

Marked uncertain: 2026 MTA car toll, PANYNJ toll-by-plate, later CRZ phases, the 113 relief-stand count, Schaller's '11 vs 8 min', JFK hold-lot wait times, Pedestrian Mobility Plan class shares, the paraphrased findings of Buchholz, Frechette et al. and Yazici et al., and the 2026 HVFHV pay values (these match the indexed rule).
interactions: R01 x R02 (time): land-use mix sets each zone's daily profile; night outward drift (core-to-outer-borough share 1.4% at 8am vs 17.7% at 4am) and airport and hub pulses are time-specific, so zone attributes should be zone x hour tables.

R01 x R03 (events): venues (R01-047), hubs (R01-049) and bridges (R01-019) are where events strike; subway outages near busy stations (R01-036) shift demand to cars; with/without event info should be tested on these fixed POIs.
R01 x R04 (weather): rain raises hail demand most on high-pedestrian streets (R01-034) and slows curb pickups (R01-026); low-lying highways can flood [U]; grade affects EV range [U].
R01 x R05 (riders): population, jobs and transit access drive demand; neighbourhood income moves card use and tips (25.9% vs 19.3% tip/fare); robotaxi walk distance (R01-033) drives cancellations.

R01 x R06 (competition and matching): concentration (R01-003) and imbalance (R01-004) set crowding in hot zones; Frechette, Lizzeri and Salz (2019) find increasing returns to scale in matching and that platform competition reduces effective density [S]; Buchholz (2022) shows competition spreads taxis away from the densest pedestrian areas [S]; airport queue length (R01-052) depends on competitor supply.
R01 x R07 (fares and rules): R01 owns the polygons and triggers (CRZ, 96th St line, airports, EWR, out-of-town, hail exclusion); R07 owns the amounts.
R01 x R08 (vehicle and energy): charger and fuel locations (R01-064, R01-065), grade (R01-018), deadhead distance and tolls on empty returns (R01-021, R01-059).

R01 x R09 (driver and decisions): repositioning (R01-011), airport queue (R01-053), cruising route (R01-041) and go-home (R01-061, R01-062) are geographic decisions; Haggag, McManus and Paci (2017) show productivity gains from neighbourhood-specific experience [S], which supports the 10-days-then-day-11 learning evaluation.
R01 x R10 (traffic and routing): road hierarchy, one-way grid, turn bans and chokepoints (R01-012 to R01-019) form the graph that R10 loads with congestion; CRZ speed effects belong in R10.
R01 x R11 (fleet): zone adjacency and travel-time skim (R01-010), depots (R01-063) and the robotaxi geofence (R01-008) are the fleet rebalancing substrate.
R01 x R12 (benchmark settings): spatial resolution (R01-009), whether historic heatmaps and PU/DO ratios count as public info, and the replay period (2019 vs 2025+ with the CRZ) are harness settings.

open_questions: Replay period: pre-pandemic 2019 (stable, no Congestion Relief Zone) or 2025+ (CRZ live, current taxi/app mix, cbd_congestion_fee field)? This changes zone shares and speeds.
Spatial resolution for version 1: taxi-zone level with random intra-zone points, or an OSM road graph from the start? Curb, hail-visibility and pickup-ability variables need the graph.

Robotaxi city: NYC has no robotaxi passenger service (Waymo test permits expired 31 Mar 2026). Use a hypothetical NYC geofence, or a second city with real service (San Francisco, Phoenix) where public trip data are scarcer?
Is HVFHV on_scene_datetime populated well enough to fit per-zone rider-driver rendezvous time (R01-026)? I could not read the data dictionary.
Can NYC TLC app drivers legally accept pickups in NJ, Westchester or Nassau (for example after an EWR drop-off)? This sets how harsh the empty return is.
Current amounts not verified: MTA car E-ZPass toll after 4 Jan 2026; Newark taxi surcharge; speed-camera operating hours; yellow-cab double-meter rule beyond the city line.
Is there a public source for TLC driver residence by ZIP or borough? Without one, 'take me home' scenarios rest on a design guess.
Should pre-mid-2016 yellow records with exact coordinates [U] be used to calibrate street-level hail rates (R01-040), given that demand has shifted since?
Should the agent get historic zone heatmaps and PU/DO ratios as 'public information'? They are public data, but providing them changes what the benchmark measures (learning vs reading a map).

Generalisation: for other cities, replace TLC zones, service-zone classes and NYC-specific polygons with local equivalents; keep the R01 schema generic (zones, rule-trigger polygons, POI layers, crossing edges).

domains.summary: Time is the key that every other profile in the simulator is looked up by. On an ordinary weekday, NYC app-ride demand swings 7.7-fold (4,900 trips/h at 3 am to 37,700 at 6 pm, HVFHV Jan 2023) and yellow-taxi demand 27-fold, so the agent's most valuable decision is when to work and where to be each hour. Busy is not the same as profitable: the 4-6 pm rush is the slowest traffic (12 mph) and pays the least per engaged hour ($50), while the 4-5 am airport-heavy hours pay the most ($62-64) but leave more idle time, so the simulator must model speed, trip mix and driver supply, not only trip counts. Day of week, season and holidays reshape the curve. App rides peak on Saturday and yellow taxis on Thursday. Hybrid work leaves the yellow morning peak about 11% lower on Mondays and 19% lower on Fridays than on Tuesday to Thursday. Months vary about ±7% (app) and ±15% (taxi). Legal holidays cut taxi trips to 45-90% of normal while traffic runs 20-45% faster. Dated public pulses are worth a lot: New Year's night doubles demand and pays about 60% more per engaged hour; Broadway let-outs triple Times Square pickups within 15 minutes; JFK arrivals peak at 9-11 pm and airport departures at 4-6 am. Time rules (the $1 overnight and $2.50 weekday rush taxi surcharges, switched off on holidays, and the $5 JFK rush surcharge) are confirmed in the data itself. Several popular intuitions are small in the aggregate data: no 4 am bar-closing spike, only about a 12% lunch bump, no measurable darkness effect after DST, and a 3-5% Ramadan iftar dip. These stay in as low-impact variables for realism. The data has time traps (naive timestamps on DST nights, a 2-month release lag, a 2025 regime shift with yellow trips up 19%). I recommend a 168-slot hour-of-week × day-type × month design, replaying real dates, a 4-5 am day boundary, and calendar awareness as its own experiment arm. Evidence comes mainly from my own analysis of 60M real TLC trips, from GitHub LFS copies verified by SHA-256 against a catalog of the original files. nyc.gov, mta.info and similar hosts were blocked and the shared web-search budget ran out after 4 searches, so regulations and studies are tagged [S] or [U]. Scripts and CSV outputs are in /home/user/benchmark/research/research_notes/RoboTaxi Bench variables/R02_time_patterns_data/.
key_corrections: New data trap found: TLC's own yellow 2023 file (SHA-256 matches the catalog) is missing about 95% of trips from about 13:00 on 21 Sep to 24 Sep 2023 (4,633-5,732 trips/day vs about 105,000). The Sep 2023 monthly index (0.90) and Sep Friday/Thursday ratio (0.90) are artefacts of this gap. Added to R02-065 and flagged in R02-027, R02-028 and §2.4.

R02-059 lockouts: 35 RCNY 59D-22(c), effective 1 Aug 2025 [P*], requires 72 hours' notice before an HVFHV restricts a driver's access on a day, and at least 16 hours of access once the driver logs on (restarting after 8 h off), with a $500 fine. Hour-by-hour lockouts apply only to 2023-24 replays.

R02-045 lease caps replaced with rule values from 35 RCNY 58-21 [P*]: $105 day shift; night $115 Sun-Tue, $120 Wed, $129 Thu-Sat; weekly $630/$737; hybrid +$3; late return up to $25/h. Shift clock times are not in the rule.
R02-060 confirmed from 35 RCNY 80-14(f) [P*]: 10 h passenger time per 24 h with an 8-hour reset, and 60 h per Monday-Sunday week.

R02-036 and §2.3: the '348 trips on a normal Monday' baseline for yellow at 1 am on 1 Jan 2024 could not be reproduced. The other non-holiday Mondays had 425-533, so the night was about 14-17x normal, not 21x.
R02-009 and summary: the lunch bump is mostly the late-morning ramp, since pickups at 13:30 (700/15 min) equal noon (696). The lunch-specific bump is under 5%.
Summary and R02-067: theatre let-outs roughly double zone 230 pickups within 30 min (2-3x a dark Monday), not 'triple within 15 min'. Pickups stay raised for 45-60 min, not 15-30.
R02-026: the Sunday-evening airport signal is in volume (about 1,780 vs 1,170-1,460 airport pickups/h), not share. Weekday 23-01h shares (5.5-8.2%) match Sunday's.

R02-013 (bar-closing taper) and R02-039 (Ramadan iftar) were downgraded from medium to low, consistent with the dossier's own summary. The Ramadan dip re-computes at 2.4-4.2%, not 3-5%. Impact totals are now high 23, medium 30, low 16.
R02-061: NYC AV testing requires an operator in the driver's seat (34 RCNY 4-17(d)(4)) [P*], and Waymo's test permit expired on 31 Mar 2026 [S], so NYC robotaxi hours are a counterfactual setting.

R02-052: PATH and the LIRR run all night, so they have no 'last train'; only Metro-North has an overnight gap [U]. R02-051: MLB games average about 2 h 40 min since the 2023 pitch clock, not about 3 h [U].

Smaller fixes: R02-010 (12.3 mph and $49.7-49.9 are 16-17h; 18h is $52.4), R02-020 (14-15% tip incidence is weekend only; yellow uplift is 16-19h), R02-025 (yellow's busiest night is Thursday), R02-029 (fastest month depends on hour), R02-033 (HVFHV 2025 667k), R02-034 (holiday speeds +14-45%), R02-041 (recess -3 to -12%; Sept jump confounded with office return), R02-047 (LGA 11-28/h overnight, 502-764/h daytime).

Upgraded to [P*] from rule text: R02-037, R02-054 and R02-055 (35 RCNY 58-26: $1 night 8 pm-6 am; $2.50 and JFK $5 rush 4-8 pm weekdays, not on legal holidays; fare change eff. 18 Dec 2022). Data checks also show no night surcharge on JFK flat fares, the holiday exemption also applying on MLK, Presidents' and Memorial Day, and the airport fee rising from $1.25 to $1.75 in April 2023.

Verified by independent DuckDB re-computation: all §2.1 hourly HVFHV values, day-of-week counts, holiday ratios (within ±0.04 under a different exclusion list), NYE ratios, pay and waits, nightlife, theatre, airport and shift-change tables, DST counts, monthly indices, sun times, and Uber-only on-scene times. Not verifiable here (DNS-blocked, search budget exhausted): CRZ amounts and hours, Con Ed TOU, NY 4 am closing, Kastle, DNAinfo 2011, CPUC hours, MTA headways, TLC lag.
interactions: R01 Geography: hotspots move with the clock (Midtown/FiDi in the morning, nightlife zones 22-03h, JFK 21-23h, airport-bound residential trips 04-06h), so each zone needs its own hour-of-week profile, not one city curve scaled.

R03 Events: R03 owns event sizes, while R02 supplies timing: end-time distributions (R02-051), theatre let-outs (R02-050), the fixed annual calendar (R02-053) and NYE (R02-036). The with/without event-info arm should be crossed with the with/without calendar-info arm (R02-005) so that knowing 'it's Saturday night' is not credited as event knowledge.

R04 Weather: weather effects depend on the hour (rain at 6 pm hits a market already short of cars; rain at 3 am an empty one), and season sets the weather mix (snow Dec-Mar, heat Jul-Aug); sun times (R02-063) feed lighting and the visualiser.

R05 Riders: trip purpose changes by hour (commute, airport, leisure, late-night safety), and with it price sensitivity, tipping (R02-020) and destination; night transit gaps (R02-052) push riders to cars.

R06 Competing supply: supply by hour is the hidden half of hourly profit. Waits by hour (R02-019) are the main public calibration target. Supply has its own time patterns: the taxi shift change (R02-044), the Ramadan iftar dip (R02-039), seasonal and holiday absences (R02-032), and drivers chasing NYE-type surges.

R07 Fares and rules: time bands include taxi overnight and rush surcharges (R02-054/055) and their holiday exemptions (R02-037), CRZ toll bands (R02-056), NYC platform log-in limits (R02-059) and hours-of-service caps (R02-060); utilization-based minimum pay leads platforms to ration hours by time of day [U].
R08 Vehicle and energy: time-of-use electricity (R02-057) and fleet charging windows (R02-062) belong in demand troughs; cold months cut EV range; fuel prices have weekly and seasonal cycles.

R09 Driver: working-hours choice (R02-004), break timing incl. the lunch the user mentioned (R02-021) and go-home timing (R02-022) interact with fatigue and circadian rhythm; 'take me home' is a time decision.

R10 Traffic: speed by hour, season, school term and holiday (R02-016, R02-029, R02-041, R02-034) sets how many trips fit in an hour; holidays run 20-45% faster and the September school start runs 20% slower in the morning.

R11 Fleet: fleet decisions are timing decisions: stagger shifts and charging into troughs, pre-position for predictable pulses (let-outs, airport banks, NYE), and respect robotaxi operating-hour windows (R02-061).

R12 Benchmark: date selection (R02-003), day-type strata (R02-002), day boundary (R02-068), tick length (R02-067), DST handling (R02-064/065) and date contamination (R02-066) decide comparability; for 'learn on 10 days, test on day 11', day 11's type must be matched or deliberately different, and the choice reported.

open_questions: Hourly driver supply is not in public trip data (driver IDs removed), so true hourly earnings including idle time cannot be computed. Calibrate a supply model to match wait times by hour, use TLC monthly driver counts and utilization reports, or use the 2013 FOIL hashed-medallion data to reconstruct taxi shifts.
Ramadan and other supply-side observances need HVFHV months with on-scene times (Mar-Apr 2023-2025) to separate a supply dip (longer waits) from a demand dip; only HVFHV Jan 2023 was available here.

Current 2026 values of the time rules need primary checks: taxi surcharges, the airport fee ($1.75 since Apr 2023 per data), CRZ toll level and scheduled increases, Uber/Lyft NYC log-in limits, the TLC fatigue rule and lease caps.
Replay real dates (realistic, auditable, but models may recall famous dates) or synthetic typical days (contamination-safe but less real)? Possibly both, labelled.
For the 'learn on 10 days, test on day 11' protocol, should day 11 match the training day types or be a deliberate out-of-distribution day (holiday, DST day, event day)?
Robotaxi time patterns: no public hourly robotaxi demand for NYC; do robotaxi riders have a different hourly mix (novelty, perceived night safety, no tipping)? CPUC data may help.
Bar-closing and lunch effects are small citywide; are they large enough at venue or block level to model in v1?
Which calibration year? 2025-26 data reflect congestion pricing and a +19% yellow rebound; should a pre-2025 regime be offered as a robustness test?
Average lunch time and length (the user's placeholder): ATUS distributions were not reachable; the ride-data bump centres at 11:30-12:00, which fits a noon lunch but is unverified.

domains.summary: Events and disruptions produce a driver's best and worst hours, and they are where public information can give a model a real edge. To size real New York events, I used 41.3M yellow taxi trips (all of 2023 plus January 2024), 18.5M Uber/Lyft (HVFHV) trips from January 2023 and the Retrosheet 2023 baseball game logs. During the US Open, taxi pickups at Flushing Meadows ran at 15 times their normal level. Broadway's 8pm let-out almost doubles Times Square pickups compared with a dark Monday. On New Year's night, app fare per mile was 1.8 times a normal Sunday's and driver pay per engaged hour was about 60% higher. Closures cut the other way: the New Year's Eve frozen zone took Times Square pickups to zero from 5pm, UNGA week cut Midtown East pickups by 41%, parades cut pickups along the route by 34-46%, and trips there ran 12-22% slower. After-event surge is real but short. On the busiest nights at MSG/Penn and Times Square, fare per mile rose 25-42% and waits roughly doubled, then fell back within about an hour, so the agent's key skill is timing under end-time uncertainty (2023 MLB games: 162 min, sd 20). Yellow taxis carry only a few trips per 10,000 attendees at outer-borough venues and almost none at MetLife, so app trip data are needed to set event mode shares; that is the biggest gap left. The dossier also gives a protocol for the with/without event-information test: four information levels, paired seeds, a guard against models remembering famous real events, counterfactual event injection, and a flag for a real TLC data gap (Sep 21-24 2023) that would look like an event. Most venue, regulation and robotaxi facts are tagged [U], because nyc.gov, MTA, NYC Open Data and news sites were blocked and the shared web-search budget was used up. Scripts and outputs are in R03_events_data/ next to the dossier.
key_corrections: R03-044 / R03-046 / key-numbers table: the Sep 29 2023 flash-flood baseline included Fri Sep 22, a TLC data-gap day with 4% of normal records. Against the 4 other Fridays, yellow trips were +18% at 8am (not +46%) and +10-21% from 06:00 to 10:00, but 11-28% lower from 11:00 to 17:00. Daily trips fell 12% (not +9%). Fare per trip was +31-40% and fare per engaged hour flat (-1%), so R03-044's impact moves from high to medium.

Baseball (R03-002, 004, 011, 012, 016): two Yankee night games fell in the Sep 21-24 data gap. interactions: R01 Geography: venues map to taxi zones and road nodes (R03-002); closures edit the road graph; licence borders limit pickups at out-of-city events (R03-010).

domains.summary:
Weather affects profit per hour in three ways that pull against each other. It raises demand (rain, cold, heat, smoke, transit failures). It slows traffic and raises crash risk (rain, snow, ice, floods). And it changes supply: yellow taxis are capped, app supply responds through surge, and robotaxis may pause.

We joined public TLC trip records to NOAA Central Park weather, and the pattern is clear. On wet days in January 2023, Uber completed trips rose about 6% and Lyft about 4%, while yellow-taxi trips did not change. Uber pickup waits rose about 9% (22-40% in the evening peak), but curb dwell did not change. Across 2023, rain and cold shifted the mix toward trips under one mile (+0.5 to +2.5 points) and left tip rates unchanged.

Extreme days dominate the tails. The 29 Sep 2023 flash flood (5.48 in) lifted yellow trips 46-63% in the morning peak while Manhattan speeds fell about 30%. A secondary analysis of NYC DOT sensors finds speeds 5-9% lower in rain but up to 49% lower in heavy snow.

Temperature is the second big lever for electric cars and robotaxis: range is about 41% lower at 20°F with the heater on, and charging is slower in the cold. For robotaxis, the weather operating envelope can remove supply entirely: Aurora reported that weather limited its driverless trucks in Texas about 40% of the time in 2025.

The benchmark therefore needs three things:
- hourly weather, because daily data dilute the effect (+6% per wet day here, against about +25% per rainy hour reported by Brodeur and Nield);
- a choice between replaying historical weather and generating it;
- an information setting (none, current conditions, public forecast, oracle) that mirrors the team's with/without-events test.

Evidence caveat: NOAA, NWS, Open-Meteo, NBER, IZA and fueleconomy.gov were unreachable, and the shared web-search budget was used up before this domain started. The figures therefore rest on our own TLC analysis [P], GitHub copies of NOAA data and documentation [P*], secondary GitHub notebooks [S] and background knowledge [U].

Output: 61 variables in 9 sub-boxes (15 high, 30 medium, 16 low impact; 14 core, 33 extended, 14 stretch). Overlaps with R03, R08, R11 and R12 are labelled as cross-links. The analysis scripts and small outputs are saved in /home/user/benchmark/research/research_notes/RoboTaxi Bench variables/R04_weather_environment_data/.
key_corrections: Method: re-ran all 8 R04 analysis scripts on the saved TLC and NOAA inputs. Every [P] number and every [P*] climate statistic reproduced. Sun times were recomputed with an independent NOAA solar-position implementation and agree within 1-2 minutes.

Limits: no new web searches were possible (shared budget exhausted). NOAA, NWS, IEM, Open-Meteo, IZA, NBER, ag.ny.gov, fueleconomy.gov, NYC Open Data and Wikipedia did not resolve. Only GitHub copies could be re-read, and no proxies or mirrors were used.

R04-041 crash multiplier: the notebook shows rainy-hour crash rates of -1% to +5% at 08:00-17:00, about +10% at 00:00, 07:00 and 18:00, and +20% to +34% at most night hours, not '10-35% higher' at every hour. Impact lowered from medium to low.
R04-011 surge response: impact lowered from high to medium. The measured daily responses are only +2% fare per mile and +0.8% driver pay per engaged hour (weekday controls only).

R04-005 short-trip shift and R04-006 mode substitution: impact lowered from medium to low. The first is a 0.5-2.5 point shift in trip mix with no significant change in fare per trip; the second is only a calibration check on R04-002.

R04-002: the '+10-30% requests per rainy hour' figure was re-tagged from [S range] to a design range. No source gives it, and Brodeur & Nield count completed rides, not requests. Their +25%/+4% figures are still not re-read at source.

R04-004 and R04-009: the Uber hour-by-hour comparisons use the 4 Tue-Thu days with at least 0.4 in and have no trend control. Overnight hours also show +13% to +27%, so part of the gap is the upward trend within January.
R04-025 and the Summary: the 29 Sep 2023 speed drop of -29% to -35% is the citywide average for all yellow trips (mostly Manhattan), not a Manhattan-only measure.
R04-019 and R04-022: 104°F (2011) and -1°F (2016) are the 2009-2025 extremes in our copy, not all-time Central Park records (those are 106°F in 1936 and -15°F in 1934 [U]).
R04-060: four, not three, of the 12 wettest Central Park days in 2009-2025 fell in 2021-2023. Three of the 12 also fell in 2011, so this is weak evidence of a trend.
R04-039: Aurora's '~40% of the time weather-constrained in Texas in 2025' was re-read verbatim in the transcript copy; tag raised from [S] to [P*].

R04-050: Open-Meteo Previous Runs confirmed from Open-Meteo's own website source: lead offsets of 1-7 days and most models from January 2024. GFS 2 m temperature goes back to March 2021 and JMA to 2018, which gives some issued-forecast history for 2021-2023 replays.

New [uncertain] marks: R04-008 (the notebook's speed bins are in undocumented units, probably mm/h), R04-036 (computed glare dates are geometric-horizon dates; the published Manhattanhenge dates are about 28-30 May and 11-13 Jul; the NHTSA source is near-empty), the Waymo May 2026 recall, the Dec 2025 San Francisco outage, fueleconomy.gov's A/C wording, the subway suspensions on 29 Sep 2023, the Retrosheet rainout fields and the LCD unit options.
Impact ratings after the fact-check: 14 high, 28 medium, 19 low (before: 15 / 30 / 16). No variables removed or merged.
interactions: R01 Geography x R04: flood-prone links (FDR, BQE, parkways) are R01 road attributes that R04 closes (R04-025). Pedestrian density decides where rain raises street hails most (R04-007). Bridges and elevated roads ice first (R04-015). Snow-clearing state is tracked by borough (R04-014).

R02 Time x R04: the same rain matters more at 6 pm than at 3 am (R04-004), and seasons set the weather mix (R04-054). Daylight timing lives in R02-063; its driving-side effects are R04-035, and the night cycle also feeds the visualiser (R04-061).

R03 Events x R04: weather cancels or delays outdoor events (R04-032). Weather-driven subway suspensions and travel bans are disruptions whose objects R03 owns (R03-044 emergencies, R03-046 subway incidents, R03-049 airport disruptions, R03-020/R03-021 event cancellation and weather at let-out); R04 supplies the weather triggers (R04-016, R04-026, R04-031, R04-032). Official alerts belong in the same public information feed as event news (R04-051), so the with/without-information test should cross event information with weather information. Replayed storm days need the R03-064 memorisation guard.

R05 Riders and demand x R04: rain uplift, onset surge, short-trip shift, mode substitution and willingness to pay (R04-002 to R04-006, R04-045) are multipliers on the R05 demand generator. HVFHV data show only completed trips, so unserved rainy-day demand must be inferred.

R06 Supply and matching x R04: in our data yellow trips stay flat in rain while app trips rise, so taxi supply is capped and app supply responds through surge. R06-050 (weather supply response) and R06-058 (robotaxi limits) take R04-039 and R04-046 as inputs. Pickup ETA inflation (R04-009) is a validation target for the matcher.

R07 Fares and rules x R04: surge responds to the weather-driven shortage (R04-011), and the emergency surge cap (R04-012) switches on in declared emergencies. The yellow meter's time component (charged below 12 mph) partly offsets slow rainy traffic, but fare per engaged hour still fell about $1.4 on heavy-rain days.

R08 Vehicle and energy x R04: R08 owns the cost side of EV range and charging in cold and heat (R08-010) and of HVAC energy (R08-009); R04 supplies the hourly temperature and the curve evidence (R04-037, R04-038, R04-023). Crash and flood damage (R04-041, R04-043), winter maintenance (R04-018) and post-storm fuel shortages (R04-030) are R08 cost inputs driven by R04 weather.

R09 Driver x R04: whether to keep working in a storm (R04-047), heat and cold fatigue (R04-048) and log-off thresholds (R04-046). The 'take me home' behaviour should account for bans and floods before they start.

R10 Traffic x R04: the weather speed-penalty table (R04-008) feeds R10-006, and weather crash hazards feed R10-025. Flooded and snow-narrowed links change the network, and low-sun glare (R04-036) is a small link-level penalty.

R11 Fleet x R04: weather is a correlated shock that hits every car at once; storm power outages are one cause of R11-060 fleet-wide outages. A robotaxi fleet can lose all supply when it leaves its weather envelope (R04-039). Pre-positioning ahead of forecast rain (R04-053) is a fleet-level skill.

R12 Benchmark x R04: the weather information level (R04-049) is served as issued forecast vintages under R12-015. Replay versus synthetic weather with common seeds (R04-055), counterfactual pairs (R04-056) and data resolution (R04-057, R04-058) are harness settings. Replaying famous storm days risks rewarding memorisation, so dates may need to be hidden.

open_questions: Hourly calibration: the NOAA LCD and Open-Meteo hosts were blocked, so all our TLC weather effects are daily. Before hard-coding multipliers, re-run the analysis on hourly LCD precipitation to fit the onset curve (R04-003) and the intensity bins (R04-001/002).

Unserved demand: HVFHV files hold completed trips, not requests. Rainy-hour demand that went unserved, or was priced out by surge, is therefore invisible. Should the demand uplift be calibrated to completed trips plus an assumed unserved share, or to Brodeur and Nield's published estimates?

Snow evidence is thin: 2023 and early 2024 were nearly snowless in NYC. Once those TLC months are downloaded, the calibration should add big-snow days (1 Feb 2021, 14.8 in; 23 Jan 2016, 27.3 in; 25 Jan and 22-23 Feb 2026).

Robotaxi weather envelope for NYC: no operator publishes thresholds. The only hard number found (Aurora, about 40% of time limited by weather) is for trucks in Texas. Which robotaxi 'generation' should the default scenario use?

Fair public forecasts: archived forecasts at real lead times exist only from early 2024 (Open-Meteo Previous Runs). For 2019-2023 replays, should we use NOAA NBM/NDFD archives, IEM text products or synthetic forecast noise? Which of these counts as 'public information' under the benchmark rule?
Memorisation: replaying famous days (Ida, Sandy, the 2015 blizzard bust) may reward models that remember them. Should scenario dates be hidden, or the weather re-timed?

Spatial weather: is one Central Park station enough? Its wind sensor is sheltered (mean 5.3 mph), its GSOD thunder flag recorded 0 days in 2023, and summer storms are local. LGA/JFK data or radar may be needed.

Not verified at source (host blocked or search budget used up): Brodeur and Nield's +25%/+4%; Farber's rain-specific finding; the AAA/fueleconomy.gov EV and HVAC figures; details of the 2014 Uber surge cap; the 2015 and 2016 travel bans; NWS heat-advisory criteria; FloodNet data access.
Do riders choose robotaxis differently in bad weather (a dry, enclosed car versus distrust of AV performance in rain)? No evidence found.
How much of the rainy-day speed drop is caused by the extra ride-hail vehicles themselves (endogenous congestion, R10-007) rather than by the weather?

domains.summary: R05 Riders and demand has 69 variables in 10 sub-boxes (17 high, 26 medium, 26 low impact; 26 core, 30 extended, 13 stretch). Rider demand matters more for profit per hour than anything else: the zone-hour request rate, the destination matrix and how much each destination is worth for the next trip, airport arrival waves and queues, and rider sensitivity to price and to the quoted wait. For taxis the street-hail encounter process also matters a lot. Public NYC TLC trip records give a strong base layer: zone-level pickups and drop-offs, times, fares, tips and driver pay, plus HVFHV request and on-scene times and shared, WAV and Access-A-Ride flags (column lists confirmed from a verbatim GitHub copy of the schema). Those records hold only completed trips, though. They contain no cancelled or unserved requests and no cash taxi tips, so the simulator needs a latent-demand uplift and imputation, exposed as settings. Smaller realistic effects are covered too: no-shows, late riders, boarding time, party size, luggage, WAV, car-seat and pet requests, shared rides, multi-stop trips, tips (app vs card-default vs cash), ratings, cleaning fees, lost items, disputes, fare evasion, safety incidents, and for robotaxis the AV premium, AV preference, doors left open and rider help requests. Evidence is strongest for trip volumes, wait times, tipping and WAV rules. Price and wait-time elasticities and cancellation and no-show rates rest on a few studies or design guesses and should be swept as scenario knobs. Research limits: nyc.gov, arXiv, NBER and Wikipedia were unreachable from this session, and the shared web-search budget ran out before checking the NYC wait-time elasticity paper, Access-A-Ride e-hail volumes and driver assault statistics, so those items stay tagged [S] or [U].
key_corrections: R05-036/059: the taxi refusal rule is 35 RCNY 80-20, not 56-20, which is the Paratransit Drivers chapter. 80-20(a)(1) sets the mandatory destinations (NYC, Westchester, Nassau, EWR). 80-20(a)(4) bans asking the destination before the rider is seated. 80-20(b)(8) allows refusing EWR, Nassau and Westchester after 8 h of driving. Source: verbatim RCNY export [P*].

R05-031: the 90%-of-WAV-requests-within-10-min standard is in force (35 RCNY 59B-17(f)(3)(i), amended eff. 6 Mar 2025), not just proposed. The alternative is sending 25% of trips to WAVs. WAV requests were 0.15% of HVFHV trips in Jan 2023.

R05-038: on_scene_datetime is filled on 100% of Uber trips and ~0.1% of Lyft trips (Jan 2023), despite the dictionary's 'Accessible Vehicles-only' label. Rider lateness is a median of 0.8 min and a p90 of 2.0 min (0.5% over 5 min), not a 1-2 min median.
R05-017: access_a_ride_flag flags no trips in Jan 2023 (blank for Uber, 'N' for every Lyft trip), so it cannot measure paratransit volume.
R05-059: 4.5% of HVFHV trips end outside NYC or at EWR, and 0.7% of yellow trips do (was 1-3% [U]). Pickups outside NYC are almost nil, so returns run empty.
R05-029: yellow 2023 party size is 1 rider 75%, 2 riders 15%, 3-4 riders 6%, 5-6 riders 2% (was 70/15/10/2).

R05-048/050: zero-tip yellow records were 30% (Oct 2019) and 23% (2023), not over 40%. Card trips: 95% are tipped, with tips ~22% of fare_amount. Card share of trips was 73% (2019) and 78% (2023), replacing the undated 53% figure. Tip-button defaults differ by vendor [uncertain].
R05-016: nightlife-zone pickups peak at 00:00-02:00 and taper to 04:00. There is no 4 AM last-call spike.
R05-009: the drop-off/pickup ratio in busy weekday zone-hours is 0.45-1.45 (5th-95th percentile), not 0.3-3.
R05-001: Aug 2024 HVFHV was ~617k trips/day (19.13M rows), not ~580k/day. The busiest zone-hours (max 1,625 pickups) are East Village at weekend midnight and Midtown Center in the evening.

R05-064/062: JFK pickups go 39% to Manhattan, 24% Queens, 21% Brooklyn and 14% outside NYC. LGA pickups go 57% to Manhattan. Apps took 68% of JFK pickups and 78% of LGA pickups vs yellow (Jan 2023). Half of yellow JFK pickups use the $70 flat fare, which the data confirms.
R05-022: impact lowered from high to medium. Cancels cost about 1-3% of driver time, partly repaid by fees.
R05-023/068: Frechette, Lizzeri & Salz 2019 do not estimate rider multi-homing or retention, so that evidence is reattributed to [design].

Confirmed from TLC data [P*]: Uber 73.5% of HVFHV trips; HV +4.9% Dec 2024 to Dec 2025; yellow 81% of trips at 5 mi or less and $18 or less (Oct 2019); HVFHV mean 4.8 mi, median 15.0 min; wait mean 4.6 min (Jan 2023); app tips on 19-20% of trips (4.5-4.7% of fare); zone-hour variance ~2.6x Poisson.

Still uncertain (hosts blocked, search budget used up): Cohen et al. elasticity point values, the Buchholz wait-elasticity ratio (Prague data), Obi survey figures, UberX Share NYC date, Frechette openICPSR ID, Citi Bike 40%, 2026 TLC wait and WAV figures, current NYC no-show and cancel fees.
interactions: R01 Geography: intra-zone pickup points (R05-011) need building, curb and foot-traffic layers; purpose layers need POIs (hotels, hospitals, bars, campuses); designated pickup areas (R05-041) are map objects; hail density per street segment (R05-042) should come from pedestrian counts, which fits Devansh's 'roads vs foot traffic density' placeholder.

R02 Time and calendar: base rate (R05-001), purpose mix (R05-012) and every demand layer depend on hour, weekday, holiday and season: nightlife peaks at the 4 AM last call, the airport wave at 4-8 AM, campus demand follows the academic calendar, and lunch-hour trips are a small midday bump in business districts.

R03 Events and disruptions: event end times create bursts (R05-003) and return waves (R05-010) and use venue pickup zones (R05-041); subway outages shift some riders to cars (R05-026); flight delays move airport waves (R05-065). The with/without event-info prompt test changes these from hidden to public_or_forecast.

R04 Weather: rain raises Uber rides ~25% per rainy hour vs ~4% for taxis, whose supply cannot respond (Brodeur & Nield 2018 [S]); weather multiplies demand by segment and interacts with price elasticity and surge.

R06 Competing supply and matching: observed demand is already net of competitor supply; platform share (R05-004), multi-homing (R05-023), street-hail matching frictions with increasing returns (R05-042) and airport queues (R05-063) sit on the boundary; cancellations (R05-022) depend on matching ETAs.

R07 Fares, platform rules and regulation: price elasticity (R05-020) acts on R07 fares; cancellation, no-show, wait and cleaning fee amounts are R07 rules; mandatory destinations and the refusal ban (R05-036, R05-059), WAV standards (R05-031), the CBD congestion fee (shifts demand inside the zone), airport fees and taxi tip-screen defaults (R05-048).

R08 Vehicle and energy: product and vehicle eligibility (XL, WAV, car seat) and luggage capacity; EV range limits long out-of-city trips; robotaxis have no tips, cleaning downtime and door-closure failures (R05-045).

R09 Driver and agent decisions: accept/decline uses request info (R05-036) and destination value (R05-058); the 'take me home' destination filter uses R05-060; ratings feed deactivation risk (R05-051); safety incidents can end a shift.
R10 Traffic: trip duration (R05-008) and ETAs drive cancellations (R05-022) and conversion (R05-021); congestion makes Citi Bike more competitive on short trips (R05-025).
R11 Fleet of N cars: induced demand from good service (R05-068), rebalancing against directional imbalance (R05-009), WAV obligations, and cars of one fleet competing for the same requests.

R12 Benchmark settings and data: latent-demand uplift (R05-066), replay vs synthetic resampling (R05-069), information levels, seeds and the 10-day train / day-11 test split; replaying a known historical day lets a model use memorised knowledge.

open_questions: TLC files hold only completed trips. How big should the latent-demand uplift be, and can it be calibrated from public signals alone (wait-time spikes, surge proxies)? No public cancel or unfulfilled-request data was found.
What do NYC app drivers see at offer time in 2026 (destination, fare, rider rating)? This sets the observation schema in R05-036.
Which HVFHV licensees fill on_scene_datetime? The dictionary says accessible vehicles only; check in the Parquet files before using it for lateness and no-shows.
Yellow cash tips are unrecorded. Impute them as a scenario knob, or count only card tips (which understates taxi income)?
The ride product split (UberX vs XL vs Black) is not public. Set an assumption, or simulate one product in v1?
Price elasticity (Cohen et al.) comes from 2015 data in four cities, and wait-time elasticity evidence is thin (the NYC 37% figure is unverified). Should both be swept as settings in the eval?

There is no NYC driverless service yet (testing only), so robotaxi rider settings (AV premium, preference, door-left-open rate) must be carried over from SF, Phoenix and LA. How should we adjust them for NYC?
Persistent rider agents (tipper type, rating, retention) or independent requests? Persistent riders enrich the 10-day learn / day-11 test design but are harder to calibrate.
How should the JFK/LGA yellow holding lot and the app virtual queues be represented and calibrated (Port Authority dispatch counts)?
Current NYC cancellation, no-show and wait fee amounts and free windows ($5 vs $10; 2 vs 5 min) are unconfirmed for 2026; R07 should confirm them.

domains.summary: What a driver earns per hour depends mostly on how many other idle cars are close by when a request appears, and on the platform's matching rule, more than on anything the driver does alone. New York's market is large and lopsided: about 665k app trips a day in 2025 (Uber about 72%, Lyft about 28%), about 130k yellow-taxi trips a day from about 10,500 active medallions, and 82,225 licensed app vehicles. Our own estimate is about 15k app cars online on average [S/design]. The public app trip records carry no driver or vehicle ID, so competitor supply cannot be replayed. It has to be a calibrated population of bot drivers, fitted to the TLC monthly aggregates (unique drivers, vehicles per day, hours per vehicle) and to request-to-on-scene times by zone and hour. The variables with the most effect on profit per hour are the local ratio of idle cars to requests, the ping rate, utilisation (about 59% for NYC app cars), pickup time and the 'wild goose chase' regime when supply is thin, airport queue length and wait, how much of the offer a driver sees before accepting, how quickly rivals log on during surge, and platform log-on lockouts. Several NYC rules shape supply directly: the pause on new FHV licences since 2018; the 2024 Uber and Lyft lockouts, driven by a pay formula tied to utilisation; yellow cabs' monopoly on street hails; the 4-5 pm taxi shift change; and airport first-in-first-out queues with taxi short-return tickets. Robotaxis cannot carry passengers in NYC (Waymo's test permit lapsed on 31 Mar 2026), so robotaxi presence is a scenario setting. Waymo's US average of about 20 trips per car per day gives a realism check, and Uber's dispatch of Waymo cars in Austin and Atlanta is the template for mixed fleets. At fleet and multi-agent level, the fleet's share of total supply decides whether its cars just take the market as it is or change it, and the fleet's own cars take trips from each other. Scores should be reported under both fixed and responsive background supply. Evidence caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through this domain, and nyc.gov, TLC data hosts and most news sites were unreachable (no proxies used). Many figures are therefore search snippets [S] or background knowledge [U] and should be checked before they are hard-coded. 70 variables in 9 sub-boxes: 21 high, 38 medium, 11 low impact; 34 core, 26 extended, 10 stretch.
key_corrections: R06-054 lockouts: since 1 Aug 2025, 35 RCNY 59D-22(c) requires 72 h notice before restricting a driver for a day. A driver who logs on must stay available for at least 16 h (the 16 h restart after 8 h offline). There are exceptions, and the fine is $500 per violation. Mid-shift lockouts are now barred, so the variable depends on rule vintage [P*, verbatim RCNY copy on GitHub].

R06-036, summary and section 5: since Aug 2025 the pay floor divides by fixed applied utilisation rates (53.3% per minute, 68.5% per mile), not by each company's actual utilisation (35 RCNY 59D-22(b)). The 59% utilisation figure covers the Manhattan core only; the citywide figure for 2024 was about 58%.

R06-009: the TLC fatigue cap is 10 h of passenger time in any 24 h (reset after 8 h with no passengers) and 60 h per Monday-Sunday week (35 RCNY 80-14(f)). It replaces the earlier '[U: check exact caps]'.

R06-038, 001 and 069: Lyft fills on_scene_datetime for only about 0.3% of trips, so public pickup-time calibration is Uber-only. Uber Manhattan pickups (Jun 2024) took a median 3.0 min and a p90 6.6 min, replacing '3-8 min [U]'.

R06-001, 003 and 035: 2025 app trips were 243,589,684 (about 667k a day): Uber 176.0M (72%) and Lyft 67.6M (28%). The '~1,060 other bases' figure is a cumulative base list in a GitHub repo, not the count of active bases.

R06-001 and 004: the figure of 5-8k yellow cabs on the road in a daytime hour is too high for about 130k trips a day. The corrected figure is about 3-5k [design calc]. The active and stored medallion counts (10,520 and 3,069) sum to 13,589, not 13,587 [uncertain].
R06-045: 2025 app airport pickups were 4.92M at LGA and 4.07M at JFK, about 25k a day combined. This replaces '10-25k/day [U]'.

R06-025 and 028: NYC cabs may not refuse destinations in NYC, Nassau, Westchester or Newark Airport, and may not ask the destination before the rider is seated (35 RCNY 80-20). Off-duty cabs heading home have a legal 'going home' mode (80-19(a)(5)), so R06-028 now also applies to taxis.

R06-005 and 032: the green Hail Exclusionary Zone is Manhattan south of E 96th St and W 110th St plus the NYC airports, and green cars may not start pre-arranged trips in that Manhattan zone. The original statement was correct; its tag moved from [U] to [P*].

R06-030, 031 and 007: the raw columns are wav_request_flag, wav_match_flag, access_a_ride_flag, shared_request_flag and shared_match_flag. In 2025, WAV-requested and matched trips were about 0.3%, WAV vehicles served about 9% of trips, shared requests were 2.8% (all Uber) and 1.6% matched. Accessible taxis must accept dispatches (35 RCNY 53-08), so R06-030 now also applies to taxis.

R06-056, 057 and 059: the US Waymo fleet was about 3,000 cars in early 2026, and the 3,800 figure is unconfirmed. The trips-per-car range is now 19-24 a day. The Austin counts of about 100 (2025) and about 200 (2026) are analyst estimates, not Waymo disclosures.

Smaller fixes. R06-018: the 2011 drop at the 4-5 pm taxi shift change is 18.5%, not about 20%. R06-033: e-hail is partly visible in public data through payment_type = 0 (Flex Fare). R06-055: the cruising-cap figures (36% and then 31%), their hours and the fines were verified in the rule text. R06-024 (offer timeout) and R06-043 (taxi short-return window) are marked uncertain.

Method caveat: the web-search budget was already used up and most hosts were blocked, so 32 variables keep their original [S] or [U] evidence without re-checking. The TLC testimony and annual-report counts, the Gridwise, Schaller and AutoMarketplace figures, and the Uber platform rules are still unverified.
interactions: R05 Riders and demand: the ratio of idle cars to requests (R06) is demand divided by supply. Rider patience and cancellation when pickup times are long (R05) close the wild-goose-chase loop.

R07 Fares, pay and platform rules: surge (R07) is the signal that pulls rivals in and moves them around (R06). The TLC minimum-pay formula divides pay by company utilisation, which is why the platforms locked drivers out. The JFK flat fare and airport fees set what an airport queue is worth.

R03 Events and disruptions: rivals crowd venue exits, which wears away event surge. Strikes are supply events. In the with/without event-information test, the bots' knowledge of events must be set to match the agent's, or the comparison is biased.
R04 Weather: in rain, demand jumps while supply stays roughly flat (Farber). Heavy snow takes drivers off the road. Robotaxi operating limits suspend robotaxi supply in bad weather.
R02 Time and calendar: shift-start curves, the 4-5 pm taxi shift change, holidays, and Ramadan or Friday-prayer dips all depend on the calendar.

R01 Geography: zone polygons for the supply field, street-hail boundaries (the Manhattan core where only yellow cabs may hail), airport lots and geofences, drivers' home boroughs, and foot traffic for hail encounters.
R10 Traffic and routing: road travel times are the matching cost and set pickup time. Cruising empty cars add to congestion, so supply feeds back into traffic.

R08 Vehicle and energy: vehicle class sets which products a car can take (XL, Comfort Electric, wheelchair-accessible). EV and accessible cars are exempt from the licence pause. Robotaxi charging downtime cuts robotaxi supply.

R09 Driver as a person and agent decisions: the agent's own choices about multi-apping, accepting offers, the destination filter ('take me home') and airport queuing all act against the rival behaviour modelled here. Rivals' breaks mirror the agent's breaks.
R11 Fleet of N cars: own-fleet cannibalisation, whether the platform or the fleet picks which car takes a trip, rebalancing against background supply, and the fleet's share of the market.

R12 Benchmark settings and data: how background supply is generated, whether it responds to the agent, what the agent can see of rivals, common random numbers and seat rotation for multi-agent runs, and the public calibration targets.

open_questions: Are Uber and Lyft still locking drivers out, or running waitlists, in NYC as of Oct 2026, and did the TLC act on the NYTWA petition about lockout-period utilisation data?

Exact 2025-26 TLC monthly values (unique drivers, vehicles per day, hours per vehicle) are needed to fix the size of the supply field. The host was blocked here, so download the monthly CSV before the component-planning meeting.
Is inferring idle supply from request-to-on-scene times by zone and hour precise enough? Validate on a month where Chicago or the 2013 driver-ID data allow a cross-check.

Platform internals are not public: batch window, dispatch radius, offer timeout in NYC, forward-dispatch look-ahead, and whether acceptance rate changes dispatch priority. Should they be fixed design constants with sensitivity analysis, or a hidden randomised rule that agents must learn?
Should background bots get the same event information as the agent in the with/without event-awareness test? Asymmetric information changes how big the measured effect of event information is.
Should agent fleets displace background supply or add to it? This decides whether fleet-level scores are realistic for N in the hundreds or thousands.

Robotaxi scenarios: what share of supply to assume for a 'future NYC' and which operating limits (no freeways, weather pauses) to impose, given state law currently forbids driverless passenger service.
The NYC multi-apping share, green taxi active count and taxi e-hail share were not found. They need TLC data or a driver survey.
Holiday, Ramadan and Friday-prayer supply dips are only anecdotal (Paris 2017). Measure them in HVFHV on-scene times before treating them as more than low impact.
Rules for NYC TLC drivers picking up at Newark (EWR) and elsewhere in NJ, and their effect on airport strategy, are unverified.
Exact TLC driver fatigue caps (hours of passenger service per 24 h and per week) need confirming; the figures here are from memory.

domains.summary: This domain sets the money rules: what a rider pays, how much of it reaches the driver or fleet, and which rules limit what an agent may do. Most of it can be taken straight from law. The NYC taxi meter ($3.00 plus $0.70 per fifth of a mile or per slow minute), every taxi surcharge and flat fare, the taxi lease caps, the hail rules, the hours cap and the Uber/Lyft minimum-pay formula are all in the Rules of the City of New York, read here from a verbatim copy current through rules effective 13 Aug 2026. The biggest levers on profit per hour are four: the platform take rate (NYC drivers got about 79% of the base fare on average in 2025), the TLC pay floor (about $1.24 per passenger mile plus $0.63-0.69 per passenger minute since the 1 Aug 2025 reset; the per-minute figure is derived, not read), surge, and for taxis the lease cost of $105-129 per 12-hour shift. Also large are the JFK $70 flat fare, which hands the traffic risk to the taxi driver, street-hail legality by vehicle type and zone, airport queue rules, and what a driver may see before accepting. Smaller but real effects include the rush, night and LaGuardia surcharges, the $0.75 / $1.50 congestion-zone trip fee, rider-side taxes that change demand but never reach the driver, cancellation fees, quests, WAV premiums, fines and licence costs. The rules also block two shortcuts an agent might try: taking long routes on purpose, and refusing taxi riders by destination. Robotaxis need their own rule pack. NYC has no commercial pathway (testing permits expired 31 Mar 2026, and state law requires a hand on the wheel), so a NYC robotaxi track is a declared counterfactual priced like an FHV or like a Waymo city. Many numbers change every year (pay-floor CPI each 1 March, Green Rides targets each January, toll phase-ins), so the simulator has to version its rules by date. Research limits: the shared web-search budget was already used up, so no web searches were made, and nyc.gov, mta.info and most other hosts were blocked. Rule text came from a verbatim GitHub export of NYC rules [P*], pay-factor history from a verbatim copy of the Feb 2025 CNYCA report [P*], and app economics from secondary analyses of 2025 HVFHV data [S].
key_corrections: R07-045: NYC now has a just-cause deactivation law for Uber/Lyft drivers: Admin Code 20-1281 to 20-1290 (Local Law 52 of 2026, enacted 29 Jan 2026, effective 28 Jul 2026). It sets a 30-day probation, requires progressive discipline and 14 days' notice, counts restrictions of 72 h+ in a row or 168 h+ per year as deactivation, and makes economic layoffs follow reverse seniority. The dossier said no such law existed. R07-030 and R07-065 now cross-reference it.

R07-002 and the worked example: 35 RCNY 58-26(a)(1) prices the initial unit at $3.00 and each additional unit at $0.70. Read literally, fare = $3.00 + $0.70 x floor(units), not ceil, so the dossier formula overcharges by $0.70 per trip; for the example trip that is $14.90, not $15.60. Meter practice is marked uncertain and should be calibrated on yellow fare_amount.

R07-017: the taxi lease gas surcharge is not a fixed $21/shift ($126/week); that was the 2012 starting value. It is now banded on the trailing 6-month EIA NYC gasoline index: $16-31 per shift ($96-186 per week) for ordinary cabs and $13-28 for hybrid or diesel, reset 31 Jul and 31 Dec.

R07-006 / R07-015: per 35 RCNY 51-03, the $1.00 improvement surcharge is deposited into the City's Taxicab Improvement Fund, which funds WAV subsidies. It passes through the owner but is not owner revenue. The $0.50 MTA tax is now [P*] from 51-03.
R07-061: in Apr 2025 Waymo's premium was ~31% over Uber and ~41% over Lyft ($20.43 vs $15.58 vs $14.44), not '30-41% over Uber'. In late 2025 it was ~12.7% over Uber and ~27.3% over Lyft.

R07-016 / R07-065: 2 May 2025 is the latest amendment to section 58-21, not a change in the lease-cap amounts, which are long-standing. Medallion-only weekly caps were added ($952, or $994 hybrid, + $275/week for a conditional vehicle purchase).

R07-011: 2025 HVFHV average base fares are $73.18 for JFK pickups and $59.72 for LGA. The dossier's '$60-73 for JFK' mixed the two airports. Whether the airport fee applies on JFK flat-fare trips is uncertain.

R07-059: Vital City classes 28 states as permissive for driverless commercial service, not only the six states where Waymo operates. WA (Seattle has a local human-driver rule) and IL are ambiguous; NY, MA and NJ are effectively barred.
R07-032: impact downgraded from medium to low, because the cruising cap is reportedly annulled (Dec 2019) and off by default.

R07-048: yellow cabs do pick up at airports, but only through the taxi stands and feed lines; they may not cruise there. R07-053: the single-touch accept/cancel/arrived exception is written only for taxi e-hail apps (78-21(a)(2)). For all TLC drivers, 80-14(g) allows device use only while standing or parked.

R07-028: the factor history now includes the 13 Mar 2023 distance-only reset (+6.7% to $0.762, transport CPI) and the distance-factor steps. R07-062: partner launch dates fixed (Austin Mar 2025 and Atlanta Jun 2025 via Uber, Nashville 7 Apr 2026 via Lyft).

Uncertain, not resolved: the TLC's posted 2025-26 HVFHV floor rates (derived $1.24/mi and $0.63-0.69/min; these do not reproduce the ~5% raise news reported for Aug 2025), the 2026 yellow airport access fee ($1.75 or $2.00), the CRZ 2028 per-trip step-ups (about $1.00 / $2.00 [U]), the '~5-mile' average app trip, and the dates of California AB 1777. No web search budget remained and nyc.gov/mta.info were unreachable; all RCNY and Admin Code text was re-read verbatim from jehiah/nyc_code_archive.
interactions: R10 Traffic: the meter switches from distance to time at 12 mph (R07-001, R10-043). The NYC app floor pays per passenger minute (R07-026), so slow traffic is partly paid for app drivers. The JFK $70 flat fare (R07-011) puts airport-corridor traffic risk (R10-010) entirely on the taxi driver. The shortest-route rule (R07-052) limits route choice (R10-042), and floor pay counts actual miles and minutes. Toll amounts belong to R10-021; who pays them belongs here (R07-018, R07-038).

R05 Riders and demand: every rider-side fee (R07-005 to R07-009, R07-023), surge (R07-020) and the robotaxi premium (R07-061) feed price elasticity (R05-020) and robotaxi uptake (R05-027). Tips (R05-047/048) follow the pass-through rules (R07-037). Cancellations and no-shows (R05-022/037) trigger fees (R07-035/036). Airport demand (R05-061 to R05-064) meets the airport rules (R07-051) and flat fares.

R06 Competing supply and matching: surge (R07-020) depends on idle supply. Lockout rules (R07-030) and the FHV licence cap (R07-057) bound competitor supply. Platform take (R07-024) and the pay floor shape the offers that competitor drivers accept.

R09 Driver as a person: the hours cap (R07-047 = R09-005), refusals (R07-042 / R09-032), acceptance and cancellation consequences (R07-043/044 / R09-040), quests (R07-033 / R09-025), lockouts (R07-030 / R09-042), deactivation (R07-045 / R09-043) and the off-duty 'returning home' exception (R07-050 / R09-020). Merge these overlapping rows at synthesis: R07 keeps the rule values and fines, and R09 keeps the behaviour.

R08 Vehicle and operating costs: lease caps and add-ons (R07-016/017), licence fees (R07-055), insurance minimums and premiums (R07-056) and the Green Rides EV/WAV mandate (R07-057) are cost or eligibility inputs to the R08 cost ledger.
R02 Time and calendar: rush and night windows and legal holidays (R07-003/004), CRZ peak hours, annual CPI steps and rule effective dates (R07-028, R07-065).

R01 Geography: polygons for the 96th St congestion surcharge, the 60th St CRZ, the hail exclusionary zone (Manhattan south of E 96th / W 110th plus airports), airport zones 1/132/138, the city boundary for out-of-city fares and pay rates, and robotaxi ODD polygons (R07-060).
R03 Events and R04 Weather: events and rain raise surge (R07-020); severe weather can pause robotaxi service (R07-060); incidents can suspend AV permits (R07-063).

R11 Fleet of N cars: cruising cap (R07-032), utilization standards (R07-031), operator licence fees (R07-058), Green Rides quota (R07-057), partner revenue split (R07-062) and ODD (R07-060) all act at fleet level.

R12 Benchmark settings: rule vintage (R07-065), profit accounting (R07-066) and the city rule pack (R07-067) are harness settings. R12 should also decide how much of the rulebook the agent is told, for example whether it knows the pay-floor formula or sees the surge map.

domains.summary: Vehicle and energy costs decide how much of a driver's gross pay is profit, but most of them are fixed per week rather than tied to any one decision, and the benchmark has to keep the two apart. In an illustrative NYC cost stack for a full-time hybrid driver (700 miles in 50 online hours a week; gross about $34 per online hour, from January 2023 HVFHV driver pay of $57 per engaged hour [P] at roughly 59% time with a passenger [S]), vehicle costs take about 25-34% of gross: rental or ownership plus commercial insurance are $6-9 per hour, while energy is only $1-2 per hour (3-6% of gross) [design]. Energy per mile runs from about $0.08 (45-mpg hybrid at $3.40/gal) to $0.15-0.18 (EV on public DC fast chargers at $0.50-0.60/kWh), so in NYC an EV without home charging can cost more per mile in energy than a hybrid; the real EV penalties are range, charging downtime (18-45 minutes per fast charge plus queues) and winter range loss of 20-40% [U]. Tolls are mostly passed to riders (8.2% of 2023 yellow trips and 11-17% of January 2023 Uber and Lyft trips carried tolls, mean $5-10), but the driver pays on the empty return from the 4.5% of app trips that end outside the city or at Newark, where pickups are almost nil [P]. For robotaxis the cost structure flips: no driver wage, but capex of roughly $0.10-0.67 per mile, depot space, depot demand charges, operations staff, remote assistance and self-insurance, with fewer crashes but rare fleet-wide groundings [design/U]. The most consequential design choice here is the cost-accounting basis (marginal only vs including fixed costs), because it shifts profit per hour by roughly 14-28% of gross and changes incentives such as shift length. Evidence caveat: the shared web-search budget was used up before this researcher's first search, and nyc.gov, eia.gov, afdc.energy.gov and AAA were unreachable, so trip-record facts are primary [P] (computed from local TLC Parquet copies; scripts and outputs saved in /home/user/benchmark/research/research_notes/RoboTaxi Bench variables/R08_vehicle_costs_data/), cross-domain facts come from sibling dossiers [S], and most prices, rules and study figures are background knowledge [U] that must be checked before they are hard-coded. 70 variables in 10 sub-boxes: 9 high, 25 medium, 36 low impact; 20 core, 34 extended, 16 stretch.
key_corrections: R08-050 premise reversed: TLC rules make the rider pay 'all necessary tolls to and from the destination' on trips beyond NYC (35 RCNY 58-26(f)(2), 59A-23(b)(2)), and apps must pass to the driver any toll paid on a trip (59D-17(c)). Jan 2023 HVFHV data: 100% of Newark drop-offs carry a toll (median $21) and 56-62% of other out-of-city drop-offs do (median $20), although westbound Hudson crossings are free. Driver-paid tolls are mainly empty repositioning, so impact was lowered from medium to low. This also explains the $20/$21 toll values (99.9% are on out-of-city trips).

R08-042 taxi weekly lease caps are $630 (day) and $737 (night), not $667-800 (35 RCNY 58-21(c), amended May 2025). Shift caps of $105-129 confirmed; hybrids +$3 a shift or +$21 a week. Medallion-only cap $952 ($994 hybrid). Fuel surcharge $13-31 a shift, indexed to the EIA NYC gasoline price. Medallion Relief guaranty: principal up to $170k at up to 7.3%, payment up to $1,235 a month (58-51(e)).
R08-043 card processing is a flat $7 a shift or $49 a week (58-21(c)(5)(xi)), not about 5% of card fares.
R08-039 FHVs must be inspected three times a year (59A-26(a)), not once a year. Only new-licence and renewal inspections must be at the TLC facility.

R08-040 / R08-006: taxis retire 84 months after hack-up, with a 6-month hardship extension; accessible taxis may run on while they pass inspection (67-18). FHVs and green cars have no TLC retirement age (59A-28(d) repealed). Gap found: since 18 Oct 2024 only accessible models may be hacked up as yellow taxis (67-06(a)); added to R08-005 and R08-040.

R08-038 fees now from rule text: driver licence $84 a year (3-year term); FHV vehicle licence $275 a year (2-year term); Commercial Motor Vehicle Tax $800 per FHV term; TLC inspection $75 (FHV) or $90 (taxi). Total about $15-20 a week, not $5-15.
R08-044 FHVs (incl. Uber/Lyft) may not carry rooftop ads (59A-29(e)(2)); only taxis may, on a permitted fixture, with income to the medallion owner.
R08-051 every taxi and FHV must carry an MTA E-ZPass and drivers must use it (58-27, 59A-24, 80-15(d)), so toll-by-mail is an edge case for TLC cars.

R08-001 / R08-069: the Jaguar I-PACE uses 44.3 kWh/100 mi (EPA), not about 40, so robotaxi DC-fast energy is about $0.22-0.26/mi. Camry, Camry Hybrid, RAV4 Hybrid, Model 3 and Niro EV ratings confirmed from an EPA data copy.
R08-056 and R08-057 impact lowered from medium to low; expected crash cost is about $0.2-1 an hour (consistent with the R09 fact-check).

Verified from rule text: Green Rides quota of 5/15/25/40/60/80/100% for 2024-2030 (59D-13(c)); TLC insurance minimums of $100k no-fault, $100k/$300k bodily injury and $10k property damage, 24/7 (58-13, 59A-12); Taxi Improvement Fund hack-up payment of at least $20k plus $10k operating payments and $10 per accessible-dispatch trip; HVFHV pay floor per mile $1.061 for WAV trips vs $0.850; parking fines (19 RCNY 39-05) and bus-lane camera fines of $50-250 (39-18).

New [uncertain] marks: FHV Active list fields (make and model probably absent), the 2012 Sandy rationing exemption, the 2026 IRS rate, the Waymo May 2026 recall, the NYC eGRID factor (probably about 0.40 kg/kWh, not 0.25-0.35), and 2026 EV-only licence releases.
interactions: R04 Weather: temperature drives HVAC load (R08-009) and EV range and fast-charge speed (R08-010); rain, snow and road salt drive car-wash frequency (R08-048) and robotaxi sensor cleaning (R08-062); pothole season raises flat-tyre risk (R08-055).

R10 Traffic: link speeds from R10 set energy per mile through the drive-cycle curve (R08-007) and idle burn in queues (R08-008); stops per mile set brake wear (R08-047); trips to chargers and depots use R10-057; toll-avoiding routes (R10-021) trade minutes against driver-paid tolls (R08-050).

R01 Geography: fuel and charger POIs (R01-064, R01-065), toll crossings and directions (R01-020, R01-021), relief stands for free parking (R01-031), out-of-city empty returns (R01-059) and depot sites (R01-063) are the places where R08 costs are incurred.

R09 Driver: the refuel-or-charge action (R09-059) consumes R08 state; charging is best combined with meal breaks; the fatigue crash multiplier (R09-008) triggers R08-056 costs; home location (R01-061) plus home charging access (R08-029) set the starting charge; robotaxi cleaning, depot and remote assistance (R09-044 to R09-049) sit beside R08-061 to R08-066 in the fleet ledger.

R06 Supply: the background EV share sets charger queues (R08-025); vehicle-class pools (R06-007) depend on the agent's class (R08-002); the licence pause (R06-053) and Green Rides rules (R08-041) cap fleet growth; robotaxi operating limits (R06-058) and recalls (R08-060) remove supply.

R07 Fares and pay: product tier multipliers pair with service class (R08-002); toll pass-through rules decide who pays (R08-050); EV per-trip incentives (R08-021) and taxi card fees (R08-043) are pay-side items; NYC's minimum pay formula for app drivers is built on estimated vehicle expenses per mile [U], so R08 values should match the vintage of the pay rule.
R05 Demand: party size (R08-003), luggage (R08-004) and WAV requests (R08-005) filter which offers a car can take; rider preference for EV or robotaxi products links to R08-002.

R11 Fleet: procurement and mix (R08-069), spare ratio (R08-058), staggered depot charging under demand charges (R08-020), depot rent (R08-064) and operations overhead (R08-063) are fleet-level levers.
R03 Events: fuel price shocks and rationing (R08-015), protests that bring vandalism (R08-059) and recall or suspension news (R08-060).

R12 Benchmark settings: the accounting basis (R08-067), cost information level (R08-068) and simple vs itemised cost mode (R08-049) are experiment settings; data-era alignment (fuel prices, tolls and pay rules from the same period as the replayed trips) must match R10-064.
