open_questions: Rental, lease and insurance prices for NYC TLC cars are the largest cost items but have no public dataset; can the team run a quick market scan (fleet price lists, driver groups) or use a driver survey such as the TLC or IDG reports to pin them down?
Which cost-accounting basis is the headline score (marginal only, plus fixed per hour, or full economic cost)? It changes profit per hour by roughly 14-28% of gross and changes optimal shift length.

What are the frequent toll values of exactly $20.00 (about 214k HVFHV trips in Jan 2023), $21.00 and $3.00, and the many tiny Lyft values ($0.10-0.15)? They look like platform pass-through conventions or artefacts and must be understood before tolls are replayed.
Green Rides percentages and the current (late 2026) TLC licensing status for EVs and WAVs need re-reading on nyc.gov; they decide which vehicles a fleet agent may add.
TLC trip records have no vehicle or fuel field, so the EV share of app trips by year must come from the FHV Active vehicle list (no link to trips) or TLC reports; is a fleet-level share enough?
No public history of charger occupancy exists; should queues be simulated from an assumed background EV share, or should the scenario use live network APIs only for forward runs?

Robotaxi costs (capex, insurance, depot, operations) are unpublished; agree on two or three named cost scenarios (e.g. 2026 Waymo-like, next-gen, Cybercab-like) and run sensitivity rather than one guess.
If robotaxis operate outside TLC licensing in NYC, do they pay per-trip congestion charges, the daily CRZ toll, or neither? This changes robotaxi tolls (cross-check with R01-022 and R07).
Should multi-week runs model slow-moving states (battery degradation, depreciation, inspections, retirement), or should a run be short enough that these become fixed per-day charges?
Exact 2026 toll and fine values (MTA increase of about 6% in Jan 2026, PANYNJ, camera fines) should be read from primary pages before use.

domains.summary: R09 covers the human behind the wheel: shift timing and length, fatigue and legal hour caps, breaks (meals, bathroom, prayer), home location and the 'take me home' end of shift, income and hours targets, experience, safety worries, preferences, other jobs, and ratings and platform standing. For robotaxis it covers what replaces these: depot returns, cleaning, remote assistance and field recovery. It also lists 21 agent decisions (19 in section J, plus shift start and end). There are 70 variables in 10 sub-boxes: 12 high, 34 medium and 24 low impact. The decisions that move profit per hour most are when to work, where to wait or reposition, which offers to accept, and whether to join an airport queue; for a robotaxi the biggest is its duty cycle, since a car with no driver can stay in service about 20 h a day. Human limits act mainly as constraints and honest costs. NYC caps passenger time at 10 h per 24 h and 60 h per week, a TLC analysis found a 23.8% higher injury-crash rate above 12 h/day, and only 42 of 109 NYC relief stands are open to app drivers. Evidence on income targeting is mixed: Camerer et al. 1997 found negative wage elasticities, Farber 2015 found mostly positive ones, and Thakral & To 2021 found recent earnings raise stopping. We suggest treating targets as an optional persona and as a bias probe for the LLM. Experience is worth about 5-14% per hour (Haggag et al. 2017; Cook et al. 2021), which maps onto the planned 10-day memory test. Two caveats: the current TLC public yellow and HVFHV files have no driver ID, so per-driver shift behaviour must be calibrated from 2009-13 FOIL-era data, Chicago's taxi IDs or the published studies; and most evidence is [S], because nyc.gov, nber and arxiv were blocked and the shared search budget ran out before four final checks.
key_corrections: Method caveat: the web-search budget was used up and every non-GitHub host was blocked. Checks used verbatim NYC rules (jehiah/nyc_code_archive, current through 13 Aug 2026), the TLC schemas in toddwschneider/nyc-taxi-data, our own trip-file headers and zone lookup, and sibling dossiers. No proxy or mirror services were used.

R09-042 lockouts: since 1 Aug 2025, 35 RCNY 59D-22(c) requires 72 h notice and at least 16 h of access per session (restarting after 8 h offline), with exceptions for excessive cancellation or non-acceptance. The 2026 default is no in-shift lockouts, so impact drops from high to medium.

R09-051 safety operator: the [U] claim is now [P*]. 34 RCNY 4-17(d)(4) (eff. 7 Sep 2021) requires a test vehicle operator in the driver's seat, plus a $5,000/yr permit and $5M of insurance. Waymo's NYC permit expired 31 Mar 2026 [S], so a NYC robotaxi is a counterfactual. Impact rises from medium to high.

R09-003/R09-019: the late-return fee is no longer [U]. It is capped at $25 per hour and at one shift's lease in total (35 RCNY 58-21(c)(5)(iv)). The 12-consecutive-hour shift rule is verified (58-21(i)(1)(ii)).

R09-005: verified as 10 h passenger time per 24 h and 60 h per Mon-Sun week, with a single-trip defence. The '[final trip] counts toward the weekly total' claim is not in the rule. The rule also has an 8-hour reset and bars counting the same time toward both a daily and a weekly violation.

R09-017: taxis do have a 'take me home' rule. A logged-off driver returning to the garage or home may take only riders going directly along the route, and may ask their destination first (35 RCNY 80-19(a)(5), 80-20(a)(4)(i)).

R09-032/R09-063: refusal penalties completed (80-02(e)). First offence: $350 on a guilty plea or $500 after a hearing. Second within 24 months: $700 or $1,000 plus possible suspension up to 30 days. Third within 36 months: revocation. A driver may refuse Newark, Nassau and Westchester trips after 8 h of operation (80-20(b)(8)).
R09-061: the 2010 TLC case of 1.8 million overcharged trips was meter-rate-code fraud, not route detours. Taxis must take the 'shortest reasonable route' (80-16(a)).
R09-016: the cruising cap is verified in 59D-21 (36% from Feb 2020, then 31% from Aug 2020, per company, Congestion Zone). [U] A court annulled the cap in Dec 2019.
Impact ratings: R09-007 fatigue, R09-008 crash risk and R09-029 driving speed move from medium to low (only a few per cent of profit per hour). Totals are now 12 high, 31 medium, 27 low.

R09-002: the Hall & Krueger hours claim is reframed: about half of US Uber drivers drove 1-15 h/week in late 2014, pooled across markets [U]. Green-taxi files are confirmed to have no driver ID (own header) [P].

Marked [uncertain] (20 places): Chen et al. 'two-thirds' hours; Uber 2014 survey 52%/75%; ATUS share and 74 min; Farber 1/8; NIOSH 18/100k and sevenfold; Buchholz 53,000; Ashkrof $0.50-0.71; Waymo $50/$100 fees; destination-filter counting; Bronx share; deadhead shares; 92% foreign-born; ICPSR IDs; Chicago 2024+ id; Data Hub date; $63k median.
interactions: R02 Time: break timing (R09-010, R09-058) should fall in demand troughs, so its cost depends on the R02 demand curve. The 4-5 pm taxi shift change (R09-003) creates a supply dip that R02/R06 must replay. Friday prayers and the Ramadan calendar (R09-013) are calendar-driven.

R03 Events: whether event information helps depends on R09-067 (information gathering) and R09-030 (memory). Stuck robotaxis (R09-050) spike during blackouts and big events. Airport queues (R09-057) are fed by flight arrivals and disruptions.

R04 Weather: rain raises demand and slows traffic, which changes the value of each extra hour (R09-023) and the stopping decision (R09-002). Farber's 'taxi in the rain' paper sits at this junction. Heat and cold could raise fatigue (R09-007) [design].

R05 Riders: driver rating (R09-039), tips, no-show waits (R09-055), mess events (R09-046) and rider-interaction scoring (R09-064) all draw from the rider model. Rider ratings of drivers and driver ratings of riders (R09-065) are two sides of one mechanism.

R06 Competing supply: simulated competitor drivers need R09's human parameters (shift start, hours and income targets, experience, home location) so that supply ebbs and flows realistically. Multi-apping (R09-056) and lockouts (R09-042) link drivers to platform supply management.

R07 Fares, pay and rules: the TLC hour cap (R09-005), destination-filter quota (R09-017), Uber Pro thresholds (R09-040/041), service-refusal fines (R09-032), cancellation and no-show fees (R09-055), quests (R09-025) and the NYC utilization-based pay floor behind the lockouts (R09-042) are R07 rule values that R09 behaviour responds to.

R08 Vehicle and energy: refuel/charge timing (R09-059) is best combined with meal breaks; depot charging capacity (R09-045) limits the robotaxi duty cycle (R09-044); taxi lease and garage (R09-003, R09-019) tie the shift to the vehicle. Personal costs (R09-037) are kept separate from vehicle costs.
R10 Traffic and routing: commute deadhead (R09-016), route choice (R09-061), navigation skill (R09-028), driving speed (R09-029) and fatigue slow-down (R09-009) all act through R10 travel times.

R11 Fleet of N cars: with human drivers each car has its own home, fatigue, hour caps and break needs, so a fleet manager must stagger breaks and plan end-of-shift positions. With robotaxis these become depot, cleaning and remote-assistance queues (R09-045 to R09-049) shared across the fleet.

R12 Benchmark settings: persona choice (R09-004), value of time (R09-023), home-ending value (R09-020), memory (R09-030) and the information level (R09-067) are experiment settings. They need fixed defaults so results are comparable across models.

Within R09: fatigue (R09-007) links hours (R09-002), breaks (R09-058) and crash risk (R09-008); acceptance behaviour (R09-054) feeds acceptance rate (R09-040), which feeds airport queue place (R09-057) and lockout priority (R09-042); home location (R09-015) drives the destination-filter decision (R09-060) and the end-of-shift score (R09-020).

open_questions: Should the LLM driver be bound by human-body constraints at all? We suggest two personas scored separately: 'robot driver' (no fatigue, meals or bathroom) and 'human driver' (timers enforced). Mixing them in one leaderboard would confuse what is being measured.

How to calibrate shift behaviour without driver IDs: the current TLC files have none. Options are the 2010-13 FOIL-era data (check whether ICPSR 37254 keeps hashed IDs), Chicago's taxi IDs, or published moments (Farber 2015, Haggag et al. 2017). Which is acceptable under the 'public data only' rule?
Fatigue-to-crash dose response: the only NYC number found is a threshold (+23.8% injury-crash rate above 12 h/day). Is a smooth curve worth building, or is a step at 10-12 h enough?

Current platform rules need re-checking against primary sources: Uber's 12 h/6 h offline rule and Lyft's 14 h rule are 2018 reports; destination-filter limits (Uber 2/day, Lyft 2-6) come from blogs; Uber Pro thresholds differ by city and year.
Are NYC app lockouts still active in 2025-26? Sources show a 2024 deal to end Uber's lockouts; a 2023 newsletter says there were none that year. The default for R09-042 depends on this.
NYC rating deactivation threshold: Uber says it is city-specific and does not publish it. We need a default (e.g. 4.6) clearly marked [design].

Robotaxi remote-assistance intervention rate and cleaning cadence are not disclosed by Waymo; only Cruise 2023 figures (a session every 2.5-5 miles) and fleet-level staffing (about 70 agents for about 3,000 cars) are public.

Not verified because the shared search budget ran out: Farber 2005 (stopping tied to hours), Crawford & Meng 2011 (hours and income targets), the University of Washington Seattle study (time targets matter more than earnings targets), and Waymo's NYC testing-permit requirement for a safety specialist. A follow-up turn could finish these checks.
Bathroom and prayer detour times: no public data. A small driver survey or Chicago taxi gap analysis could give break-duration distributions.

Should income targeting be imposed on the agent (realism) or measured in it (a bias probe)? The second is more novel: log whether the LLM stops earlier on high-earning days, chases surges that have ended, or stays in an airport queue past the break-even point (sunk cost).

How should 'take me home' be scored: as a hard end location, a cost per minute of final deadhead, or a bonus? The choice changes optimal end-of-shift strategy and should be fixed before model comparisons.

domains.summary: Traffic is the denominator of every earnings number in RoboTaxi Bench. At Midtown speeds of about 4-5 mph (2017-2019) a car finishes far fewer paid trips per hour than on the same streets overnight, so the travel-time model effectively sets the whole economy of the simulation. The largest levers are: a time-dependent speed profile (by zone, road class and hour of week), the gap between the slow core and the rest of the city, bridge and tunnel chokepoints, and the step change from congestion pricing on 5 Jan 2025 (CBD speeds about 15% higher than in comparison cities; morning-peak crossing times 4-36% shorter). That step change means each scenario must be calibrated on trip data from the same era it replays. Medium effects come from travel-time noise and correlated slow days, pickup and drop-off dwell, curb friction and GPS pin errors, routing objective and toll choice, and the quality of the ETAs and traffic information the agent is shown. Small effects include NYC traffic rules (25 mph limit, right-on-red ban, busways, bus-lane and camera fines, anti-idling) and navigation slips. Deadhead is where agent skill shows: NYC app riders wait about 4.4-6.6 min on average, and about 41% of FHV time in Manhattan below 96th St had no passenger in 2019. Empty moves must therefore use the same engine as paid trips. Robotaxis need their own routing profile: Waymo only began freeway rides in Nov 2025, and a 2024 LA test found Waymo trips took about 2.2x as long as Uber/Lyft. For the engine I recommend OSM routing (Valhalla 5-minute weekly speed profiles, or hourly OSRM speed files) for route geometry and the live map, with edge times scaled so that zone-pair x hour medians match TLC trip durations. Raw router defaults (OSRM assumes 65 km/h on primary roads) underestimate Manhattan travel times several-fold. Evidence caveat: nyc.gov, the open-data portals, NBER and arXiv could not be reached from this sandbox, and the shared web-search budget ran out after about 45 searches. Most figures are therefore tagged [S] and should be re-read from the primary source before they are hard-coded. The only primary reads ([P]/[P*]) are the Valhalla docs, the OSRM car profile and the nyc-taxi-data schema. The dossier has 67 variables in 10 sub-boxes: 13 high, 33 medium and 21 low impact; 29 core, 28 extended and 10 stretch priority.
key_corrections: Method: web searches were used up and nyc.gov, the open-data portals, NBER, arXiv and news hosts were blocked, so no workaround services were used. The checks used real TLC trip records already in the session from SHA-256-verified GitHub copies (HVFHV Jan 2023, 18.5M trips; yellow taxi 2023, 38.3M trips) analysed with DuckDB, plus verbatim NYC rule text (jehiah/nyc_code_archive, current to 13 Aug 2026), OSRM and Valhalla source on GitHub, and NOAA Central Park daily weather. The scripts and their outputs are saved in R10_traffic_travel_time_data/.

Airport corridor (R10-003, R10-008, R10-010, R10-056): the 2023 weekday median from the Midtown core to JFK is 29 min at 3-5 AM, 54 min at 10-11 AM and 75 min at 4-5 PM, with P90 up to 94 min. This replaces the older 38 / 64 / 84 min figures. LGA median is 21-44 min (P90 up to 60) and EWR is 30-54 min.
Overnight speeds (R10-001, R10-003): Manhattan below 60th St averages 11.6-13.6 mph from 0-5 AM, not 15-25 mph. Overnight trips are 1.6-2.2x faster than midday, not up to 3x.

Travel-time noise (R10-008): the coefficient of variation across zone-pair x hour cells has a median of 0.28 (P10 0.20, P90 0.46), with sd(log) of 0.41 for trips under 1.5 mi and 0.21 for trips over 6 mi. The design range of 0.15-0.35 was too narrow. The day factor of 0.8-1.25 is confirmed: P5-P95 is 0.82-1.20, and UNGA week and early December are the slowest weekdays (R10-009, R10-004).

R10-006 weather-to-speed impact cut from medium to low: in 2023, rainy weekdays were no slower than dry ones in Manhattan below 60th St (median factor 0.99 on dry days, 1.07 on days with 1 in of rain or more). Hourly and snow effects are untested.

Pickup dwell (R10-035, R10-050): on_scene_datetime is filled for 100% of Uber trips and 0.14% of Lyft trips, so the data dictionary's 'accessible vehicles only' label is wrong in practice. The Uber median dwell is 0.8 min, not 1-2 min, and 17% of trips heap at 2.0-2.2 min, so the field appears censored at the 2-minute wait clock. Mean request-to-pickup time in Jan 2023 was 4.3-5.5 min by borough.

Router bias (R10-015, R10-061): OSRM's 65 km/h applies only to untagged primary roads. Roads with a speed tag get 0.8 x maxspeed and only 2 s per signal, and the 7.5 s turn penalty is an angle-based maximum. Raw OSRM times are about 3.5-7x too fast in Midtown, not 2-5x.

Rule text (R10-043, R10-032, R10-034, R10-051): the meter rule is 70 cents per 1/5 mile at 12 mph or more ('at', not 'above'). The 200-ft bus-lane exception is for right turns. Idling fines are $350-$2,000 (Admin Code 24-178), so the '$250+' figure was dropped. The cruising cap was 36% from Feb 2020 and 31% from Aug 2020, counts en-route time and exempts WAVs; it is still printed in 35 RCNY 59D-21 but was annulled in court [U].
NYPD crash rate (R10-025): ~190k crashes a year is the 2012-2021 average; years since 2020 run near 100k [U].

Newly confirmed from primary text: the right-on-red ban (34 RCNY 4-03); the 25 mph default and 15-20 mph school-zone limits (34 RCNY 4-06, Admin Code 19-177); $50 speed-camera and red-light-camera fines; bus-lane camera fines of $50-$250; relief stands limited to 1 h; only taxis may cruise for passengers; the AV test permit requires a safety driver (34 RCNY 4-17); and HVFHV records have no vehicle ID.

Flagged [uncertain] (15 claims), including: CBD speed 8.2 to 9.7 mph (that is +18%, not +15%); the later NBER +11%; Lincoln Tunnel -10% vs -5%; the single-trip LA Waymo 2.2x test; MTA ACE route counts and dwell thresholds; the Lyft wait-fee start; the claim that taxi stands require the driver to stay in the car.
interactions: R01 Geography x R10: R01 supplies the road graph, taxi zones and land use; R10 adds the dynamic layer on top (speeds by hour, turn costs, time-conditional access such as busways and car-free park drives).

R02 Time x R10: the hour-of-week and calendar index from R02 selects the speed profile; the midday lunch peak coincides with peak delivery double-parking (R10-038), and Gridlock Alert Days (R10-004) are calendar items.

R03 Events x R10: events create closures and egress surges (R10-027; Midtown under 4 mph in UNGA week); cross the event-information level (R12) with the traffic-information level (R10-045) so the benchmark can separate the value of each.

R04 Weather x R10: rain and snow cut speeds and raise crash rates (R10-006, R10-025) at the same time as they raise demand (R05); per-minute pay (R07) partly offsets slower trips, so the net effect on $/hour should come out of the simulation, not be assumed.
R05 Demand x R10: trip length and origin-destination mix set how much of the shift is spent in slow zones; slow speeds reduce effective supply, which lengthens waits and raises surge (R06, R07).

R06 Matching x R10: pickup ETA from this engine (R10-050) sets the matching radius and acceptance; competing vehicles add to hotspot curb queues (R10-040); the airport queue (R06) versus empty return (R10-056) is a direct trade-off.

R07 Fares x R10: time-versus-distance pay (R10-043; the yellow-taxi meter switches to time below 12 mph); tolls and congestion surcharges (who pays decides R10-021); long-haul rules versus routing objective (R10-042).
R08 Vehicle and energy x R10: stop-and-go traffic raises gas consumption per mile and favours EV regeneration; idling cost and the anti-idling limit (R10-034); charger and depot deadhead (R10-057).
R09 Driver x R10: home location drives return deadhead (R10-055); breaks need legal places to stop (relief stands, R10-054); fatigue could lower driving speed or raise navigation errors [design].

R11 Fleet x R10: sending many cars to one hotspot creates curb queues (R10-040); endogenous congestion only matters at very large N (R10-007); a fleet dispatcher needs fast many-to-many travel-time matrices from the same engine.

R12 Benchmark x R10: traffic-information level, ETA noise, common random numbers and data era are harness settings (R10-044, R10-045, R10-064, R10-067); the 'learn over 10 days, test on day 11' protocol only rewards learning if slow-day shocks are correlated and partly predictable (R10-009).

open_questions: Is on_scene_datetime populated for all HVFHV trips, or only for some platforms and accessible vehicles? The data dictionary says accessible vehicles only. This decides whether pickup dwell (R10-035) and en-route time (R10-050) can be calibrated from public data. The TLC file host was blocked here, so it could not be checked.
Which era should the default scenario replay: 2019 (pre-COVID), 2024 (pre-pricing) or 2025+ (post-pricing)? Speeds and demand must come from the same months (R10-064).

Are 263 taxi zones fine enough? Short intra-zone trips, wrong-side pickups and curb effects need a road graph, while OD calibration needs zones. The hybrid engine (R10-059 option c) is recommended but costs more to build.

Empty-vehicle speeds are unobserved: TLC records only paid trips and, as far as I know, carry no vehicle ID, so shifts cannot be rebuilt [U]. Is it acceptable to apply occupied-trip speeds to deadhead (R10-058)?

How should the robotaxi be set up for NYC, where there is no commercial service? The Aug 2025 Waymo test permit allowed 8 cars with safety drivers and no passengers, and its renewal was uncertain in Mar 2026. Should it borrow SF/LA ratios or treat them as a scenario knob?
Does the agent choose routes (R10-042) or only destinations? Exposing route choice adds realism (tolls, highways) but enlarges the action space and the token cost per step.

Several [S] numbers conflict across sources and need a primary read: CBD speed gain (15% vs 11% in a later NBER version), Lincoln Tunnel (10% vs 5% faster), speed-camera trigger (10 vs 11 mph over), bus-lane fine schedule (older $115-$150 vs current $50-$250).

No public measurement was found within budget for TNC curb dwell, airport pickup access times at JFK/LGA, red-light camera counts or 2024-2026 Midtown speeds. A follow-up search session, or direct analysis of TLC data, should fill these gaps.
Can Google-derived travel times (Congestion Pricing Tracker, Google Maps API) be used under the 'public data only' rule, or should calibration rely only on TLC and DOT data for licence reasons?
At what fleet size N do endogenous congestion (R10-007) and hotspot curb queuing (R10-040) need to be switched on?

domains.summary: At fleet level, profit per car depends less on any one car's choices than on how N cars are spread, charged and kept in service, and on how much the fleet's own cars compete with each other. Two NYC trip replays on GitHub give anchors: with greedy dispatch about 3,000 robotaxis served about 90% of ~150k Manhattan-internal weekday app requests and about 5,000 served all of them, while utilisation per car fell from 57% (1,500 cars) to 28% (6,000). In the same replay, forecast-driven repositioning cut waits by about 8% but raised empty miles per trip by about 87%. Charging is the second big lever: topping up in demand troughs served 3.4 points more riders at 15% lower energy cost than a fixed 20-80% threshold, 24 chargers run this way beat 72 run on the threshold rule, and with no charging policy 4-12% of demand went unserved. The biggest benchmark design choice is the control architecture: one LLM call per car every 5 minutes for 100 cars is about 28,800 calls a day, far beyond the ~$20 run budget, so v1 should be hierarchical, with the model setting zone targets, charging and the active fleet every 5-15 simulated minutes and a coded matcher assigning trips every ~30 s. Other high-impact variables are who dispatches (platform or own app), the decision epoch, own-car herding, uptime, the labour model and shift roster, fixed cost per car-day, the fleet's effect on prices at large N, correlated fleet-wide outages, and whether the score is profit alone or profit with a service floor. New York adds the 2026 ban on passenger robotaxis, the FHV licence pause, wheelchair-access rules, base affiliation, taxi lease caps and garages in western Queens, each with a counterpart elsewhere. Evidence caveat: only github.com resolved (the shared search budget was spent and arXiv, Nature, PNAS, nyc.gov, Wikipedia and waymo.com failed DNS), so literature figures are unverified [U] and NYC numbers come from simplified third-party simulators [S] whose median wait was 2.4 times the real operator's. Counts: 69 variables in 10 sub-boxes; 18 high, 38 medium, 13 low impact; 29 core, 34 extended, 6 stretch.
key_corrections: R11-059: the WAV rule is not 'most requests within 10-15 min'. Each FHV base must either send at least 25% of its trips to accessible vehicles or join an approved accessible-vehicle dispatcher that serves at least 90% of WAV requests in under 10 min (35 RCNY 59B-17(c)(1)(v), (f)(3)), and HVFHS apps must offer WAV requests (59D-13(b)) [P*]. The yellow-cab 50% conversion schedule in 58-50(a)-(d) now reads 'Reserved', so that goal is marked uncertain.

R11-051: the lease caps are exactly $105-129 per 12-hour shift ($108-132 for hybrids) and $630-737 a week (35 RCNY 58-21(c)) [P*], not 'about $100-130'. FHV rentals have no rate cap (Admin Code 19-553 covers disclosure only).
R11-049: Waymo's fleet partners are Moove (Phoenix, Miami), Avomo (Austin, Atlanta, Uber-dispatched rides) and Lyft (Nashville) [S]. 'Avis' was not supported by any source read.
R11-015: 'taxi garages see cars only at shift change' is not supported. NYC taxi technology systems must log each logged-on cab's position at least every 30 s (35 RCNY 66-03(h)) [P*].

Impact ratings: R11-012 (decision epoch) moved from high to medium, because fleetsim shows the strategic layer moves waits only about 8% once a coded matcher dispatches. R11-021 (reach cap) moved from low to medium, because fleetsim shows the cap changed repositioning from -1.2% wait for +6.6% empty miles to -8.0% for +87%. Totals are now 17 high, 40 medium and 12 low.
offpeak numbers: peak charging load is 2.2-3.6 MW, not 3.1-3.6 (R11-039). The ablation baseline is 96.2%, not 96.1% (R11-041). The 550 cars serve a 20% demand sample (R11-034).

fleetsim numbers: pickup deadhead is 0.85-1.10 mi per trip (R11-022). HVFHV on_scene_datetime is missing for Lyft trips, so wait calibration rests on Uber rows (R11-057). All other fleetsim figures, including the fleet sweep, batching, repositioning, oracle, charging, fairness-weight, latency and runtime results, were confirmed by re-reading the README.
R11-042: 20-22 h a day is 83-92% availability, not 75-90%.

Dossier summary: New York has no legal path for passenger robotaxis, rather than a '2026 ban'. State law requires a hand on the wheel, NYC permits expired on 31 Mar 2026, and the Feb 2026 Hochul proposal, which excluded NYC, was withdrawn. 34 RCNY 4-17 allows testing only with an operator in the driver's seat. The greedy simulator's median wait was 2.4-3 times the real operator's, not 2.4 times.

Upgraded from [U] to [P*] using the verbatim NYC rules export on GitHub (jehiah/nyc_code_archive, current through rules effective 13 Aug 2026): Green Rides quotas of 5/15/25/40/60/80/100% for 2024-2030 (59D-13(c)); inspections, taxis every 4 months and FHVs 3 times a year (58-29, 59A-26); taxi retirement at 84 months, with the FHV retirement rule repealed (67-18, 59A-28(d)); base affiliation, one base per FHV, with a $500 a year base fee (59A-04, 59B-07); 12-hour lease shifts (58-21); the licence-pause basis (Admin Code 19-550).

Could not be checked: web search budget spent; nyc.gov, NYC Open Data, NHTSA, AFDC, Con Edison, NYISO and news sites unreachable. Still [U] and marked uncertain: literature figures (Alonso-Mora, Vazifeh, Lin et al.), news items (Cruise permit and festival stall, SF blackout, LA fires, May 2026 recall and the 3,800-car figure), NYC minimum wage, FTA spare ratio, Revel, NYC Open Data dataset IDs.
interactions: R06 Competing supply: the fleet's share of local supply (R06-061) decides whether fleet profits add up linearly or cannibalise (R06-062, R11-030) and whether the fleet moves prices (R11-056); report fleet scores under fixed and elastic background supply (R06-068); matcher-side intra-fleet dispatch flag is R06-063, agent-side action set is R11-010; rival-fleet messaging R06-065 vs own-fleet sharing R11-016.

R05 Riders and demand: directional imbalance (R05-009) creates the rebalancing need; better fleet service induces demand (R05-068, R11-057); trip records show only served demand (R05-066), so replays understate what a large fleet could capture.

R08 Vehicle, energy and costs: battery size, charging power, taper and electricity price feed charger ratio, schedule and queue (R11-034 to R11-041); in the offpeak replay the hourly wholesale price signal added nothing in NYC because cheap hours already coincide with low demand, and a -5 C week erased the smart policy's cost advantage (link to R04).

R10 Traffic: travel-time matrices set repositioning and charger-trip costs; empty fleet miles add congestion (R10-007), which neither GitHub simulator modelled; robotaxi freeway limits (R10-023) constrain airport allocation (R11-024).

R01 Geography: depots and garages (R01-063), charger sites (R01-065), legal waiting spots (R01-032) and the robotaxi geofence (R01-008) are the map layers for R11-023, R11-037 and R11-043; whether empty repositioning trips into the congestion relief zone (R01-022) pay anything is open.

R03 Events and R04 Weather: events drive pre-positioning (R11-025); blackouts, festival cellular congestion, floods and heavy weather can ground many robotaxis at once (R11-060); event information on/off is the with/without event awareness test in R11-017.

R07 Fares, pay and regulation: surge is what a large fleet suppresses (R11-056); TLC rules set licence caps, WAV obligations, lease caps, base affiliation and minimum pay (R11-008, R11-049, R11-051, R11-055, R11-059).

R09 Driver and agent: single-car versions live in R09 (repositioning R09-052/053, duty cycle R09-044, depots R09-045, cleaning R09-046/047, remote assistance R09-048/049, stuck vehicles R09-050, home R09-015, memory R09-030); R11 adds pooling, queueing and roster effects across N cars.

R02 Time: shift roster and active fleet size follow the hourly demand curve; dead hours (R02-014) are the natural charging and maintenance window; the taxi 4-5 pm shift change (R02-044) is a fleet-wide handover cost.

R12 Benchmark settings: information levels, token budget, latency handling, seeds, scoring, multi-run variance and the 10-days-then-day-11 learning test apply to fleet runs; R11-009 to R11-017 and R11-064 to R11-069 are the fleet-specific settings.

open_questions: How would a NYC robotaxi fleet be licensed (FHV base or a new TLC class), and would empty repositioning trips into the congestion zone pay a toll, a per-trip charge or nothing?
Which control architecture keeps a 100-car run under ~$20? Measure tokens per decision on a cheap open model before fixing the decision epoch (R11-012) and the per-car override quota.

Can the matcher reproduce the real HVFHV wait distribution? A third-party greedy simulator had a median wait of 8.9 min against 3.0 min observed; forward dispatch and better travel times may be needed before fleet results mean anything.
Robotaxi uptime, charging hours per day, cleaning cadence and remote-assistance call rates are not public: which ranges should be fixed and which swept?
Should fleet scores use fixed or elastic background supply and prices, and how do we stop large-N models scoring well just by crowding rivals out?
How far can a fleet operator legally direct contractor drivers in NYC, and what compliance rate (R11-018) is realistic?
Which baselines come first (proportional LP, MPC or an orchestrated charging rule), and can FleetPy (MIT) modules be ported without bringing in GPL code from AMoDeus?

Verify numbers that could not be checked because the web was blocked: Zhang and Pavone (about 8,000 robotaxis for Manhattan taxi demand), Alonso-Mora et al. (about 3,000 four-seat cars for about 98% of NYC taxi demand), Spieser et al. (Singapore with about one third of its vehicles), Fagnant and Kockelman (one shared AV replacing about 11 cars), Bauer et al. 2018 (Manhattan automated electric taxi fleet costs), Revel's current NYC status, TLC WAV response-time standards, lease caps and inspection cadence.
Depot land and grid capacity in NYC: is there public data on Con Edison hosting capacity for multi-MW depots?
For the visual demo, should the map show the fleet's target distribution against its actual distribution, so that herding is visible?

domains.summary: RoboTaxi Bench scores a model, but the score also depends on experiment settings that are easy to leave unstated. These include which public information the agent may query, how often it is called, whether sim time stops while it thinks, which days it is tested on, whether demand is replayed or generated, how runs are paired and normalised, and how much each run may cost. The biggest levers on measured profit are the model itself, the information level, the action space and decision cadence, the scenario and day-type mix, the data era, and the scoring rules (floor, ceiling and aggregation). We analysed the official TLC January 2023 files [P] (byte-identical to the TLC originals by SHA-256). Ten days are enough to learn the ordinary weekday pattern: predicting day-11 zone-hour pickups from the six prior non-holiday weekdays gives WAPE 0.134, against a 0.120 floor with 19 weekdays. But ten days hold only 2-3 examples of a weekend day, and naively averaging all ten days (including the New Year holidays) nearly doubles the error (0.238). Citywide app-driver pay per engaged hour is very stable across weekdays (about $54, CV 1.4%), while daily trip volume swings 12%. So every model must face the same days (common random numbers) and be compared by paired differences. Leakage is a first-order risk. NYC taxi data is among the most reused public datasets, frontier models can recall famous tables, and the TLC publishes each month about two months late. The 'public at decision time' rule must therefore exclude the replayed day's own trip records and the realised weather, serve forecasts as they were issued, and draw test months from after each model's training cutoff. Run cost is driven by calls per sim-day times context size. The team's $20 per run covers a 10-day run only at a lean cadence (40 calls of 8k tokens per day: about $7 on Opus 5.5, $17 on Fable 5.1); a standard cadence costs $31-73 per run. Recommended setup: a frozen-harness headline with paused sim time, scoring net profit per online hour normalised between a passive floor and a hindsight oracle, aggregated by interquartile mean with bootstrap CIs. Side panels cover risk, compliance, efficiency, information value and cost. The live map needs a per-vehicle path-and-timestamp log with model colours, which deck.gl's TripsLayer already animates for NYC, though without day/night lighting. Caveat: the shared web-search budget was used up before R12 started, and the NYC/NY data portals, eia.gov, afdc.energy.gov and weather.gov were unreachable. Dataset IDs were therefore confirmed only through GitHub copies [S], and most licence terms are [U].
key_corrections: 0.120 zone-hour WAPE is the error of a plain mean of 19 other January weekdays, some after the target day. It is a reference level, not a proven floor, so 'a learner cannot beat it' and 'gains beyond it are memorisation' were overstated (summary, analysis, R12-014, R12-033, R12-037, R12-047, R12-066).

R12-041: with 5 unpaired runs the smallest detectable gap is about 1.77 x the CV, so CVs of 0.07-1.0 give about 0.12-1.8x the mean, not 0.35-1.8x. The impact is on ranking reliability, not on expected profit.
R12-028: ProsusAI vending-bench charges 5-75 sim-minutes per tool call (5 for reads, 25 for email, search and payments, 75 for stock and collect), not 5-45.

R12-002: the Kimi K2 Thinking provider gap ($1,296 vs $649) comes from phase-1 dossier B via a GitHub copy of the leaderboard, not from D11. It holds for the mean only; on minimum net worth the order flips ($418.54 vs $354.00).

R12-001: $9.2k-$15.5k is the Vending-Bench 2 top 7 of 66 entries (29 Sep 2026); the top 10 spans about $7.5k-$15.5k. R12-003: Opus 4.8 scoring higher at High than at Max effort was on Vending-Bench 2.
R12-059: the HVFHS cruising cap (35 RCNY 59D-21) binds app companies, not drivers, and was reported annulled in court in Dec 2019 [U]. It is a fleet or robotaxi scenario toggle only.

R12-068 and the data table: NREL is now the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The AFDC API moved to developer.nlr.gov, and developer.nrel.gov stopped resolving on 29 May 2026. Open-Meteo's free API is for non-commercial use only (data CC BY 4.0, code AGPLv3).

R12-048: the Chicago tables cited are closed series (taxi wrvz-psew 2013-2023; TNP m6dm-c72p 2018-2022). Newer data are in ajtu-isnz (taxi, 2024 onward) and n26f-ihde (TNP, 2023-2024). taxi_id is confirmed [S].

R12-016: NYC Permitted Event Information (tvpp-9vvx) covers approved events within the next month and has 13 columns. Back-tests need bkfu-528j, and ticketed events on private property need venue schedules.
Data table: the Pedestrian Counts API resource is cqsj-cfgu (2de2-6x2h is the map page). DOT Traffic Speeds data change several times a minute, but the portal's update frequency is listed as Daily.

R12-006: Haiku 5.5's $0.10 / $0.50 price applies only to prompts of 100K tokens or fewer, and its tokenizer counts about 30% more tokens, so per unit of text it costs about 1/31 of Opus 5.5, not 1/40. All other prices and cost-table cells were recomputed and match.
R12-011 and the analysis: yellow total_amount includes card tips only, and 'engaged hour' means passenger-on-board time (trip_time), not the drive to the pickup.

Impact ratings: R12-051 and R12-052 drop from high to medium, and R12-055 from medium to low, because reference baselines not used for normalisation do not change the measured profit. New totals: 24 high, 38 medium, 10 low.

R12-024: '(MIT)' after LPSim is its licence, not its institution. R12-049: whether arena rankings differ from solo ones is uncertain (mixed evidence in D07). R12-072: the 18-of-1,000 vLLM result is real, but 'identical requests' is not stated in the README.
interactions: R01 Geography x R12: the spatial unit (R01-009) sets the action granularity (R12-025) and forces coordinate synthesis within taxi zones (R12-067); a masked or mirrored city (R12-044) must keep R01's geography while hiding names.

R02 Time x R12: holiday and weekday flags define the 10-day training window, the day-11 test strata and the scenario mix (R12-035, R12-036, R12-042); holidays inside the window nearly double a naive learner's error (WAPE 0.238 vs 0.134).

R03 Events x R12: the event-awareness arm (R12-008) and the event calendar (R12-016) are the team's headline information experiment; attendance and outcomes must be as known before the event (R12-022), and event days need their own stratum and information-value metric (R12-042, R12-061).
R04 Weather x R12: forecasts served as issued from archived vintages, never realised weather (R12-015); bad-weather days form a test stratum; real dates let models recall the weather (R12-044).
R05 Riders x R12: replay vs synthetic demand (R05-069 / R12-039) and demand censoring (R05-066) decide what the generator can claim; the offer content (R05-036) is part of the observation (R12-023).

R06 Competing supply x R12: the number of competing model fleets (R06-060) is the arena mode (R12-049); the 10-15 s offer timeout (R06-024) is why latency coupling matters (R12-027); bots double as baselines (R12-050, R12-051); surge and queue displays are an information choice (R12-019).
R07 Fares and rules x R12: fares, fees and commissions feed the net-profit headline (R12-056); TLC rules feed the compliance panel (R12-059); the role framing selects the rule pack (R12-011).

R08 Vehicle and energy x R12: all operating costs enter the headline (R12-056); EV range and charging raise difficulty (R12-047); EIA fuel, EIA electricity and AFDC charger data come through the pipeline.

R09 Driver x R12: persona, home and value of time (R09-004, R09-020, R09-023) set role framing and the go-home rule (R12-011, R12-032); memory (R09-030) and information gathering (R09-067) are governed by R12-033, R12-034 and R12-028.

R10 Traffic x R12: the traffic-information level (R10-045) should be crossed with the information ladder (R12-013); data era (R10-064) and common random numbers (R10-067) are shared settings; the travel-time engine backs the map tools (R12-018).
R11 Fleet x R12: the fleet control interface (R12-030) sets cost (one call per car multiplies cost by N); OR planners and the hindsight oracle need fleet versions (min-cost flow; R12-052, R12-053).

open_questions: What exactly does '10 days x 100 runs' mean: 100 independent 10-day runs with fresh memory, or 100 passes over the same 10 days with accumulating notes? The second rewards memorising replayed requests unless demand is redrawn each pass (R12-037).

Is day 11 meant to be the next calendar day or a harder unseen day type? Our TLC analysis shows a 10-day window teaches weekdays well (WAPE 0.134 vs 0.120 floor) but weekends, holidays and event days poorly.

Budget: $20 per run covers a 10-day run only at a lean cadence (about 40 calls of 8k tokens per day) at Opus or Fable prices. Should the headline use a shorter horizon, a lean cadence, or a bigger budget? Is the $10k total firm?

Should the headline use real NYC names and dates (credits legitimate public world knowledge) or a masked or mirrored city (blocks recall of specific days)? Proposal: real names with masked dates, plus an anonymised track.

Is the driver-app surge heatmap 'public'? Every driver sees it, but it is platform data. Proposal: allowed for the app-driver and robotaxi roles, generated by the simulator rather than taken from any platform.
Headline in paused time or latency-charged time? Paused is fairer to slow reasoning models; latency-charged is more realistic, since ride offers expire after 10-15 s.
What minimum effect size should the benchmark detect (e.g. 3% profit per hour)? This sets runs per model by power analysis after a pilot on a dev model.
Which archive provides NYC forecast vintages back to 2019 (NCEI NDFD archive, Open-Meteo historical-forecast products)? This could not be checked from this sandbox.
Licences: do NYC Open Data and TLC terms allow redistributing derived demand files, and does OSM's share-alike clause apply to a shipped road graph with calibrated speeds?
Human baseline: can real NYC drivers be recruited to play the interface, and is the Chicago taxi table (with taxi IDs) a usable source of real per-shift earnings?
TLC records hold completed trips only: how much latent-demand uplift (R05-066) should the generator add, and how would that be validated?
The existing 'Rideshare Bench' by the Malaysian developer could not be found by GitHub search; the team should share its link so its settings and gaps can be checked.
