variables.name: Event-window scoring metrics
variables.description: Measures of how well the agent used event information.
variables.values_or_range: Profit per hour overall; profit within +/- 2 h and 2 km of let-outs; value of information = L1 - L0; information-use efficiency = (L1 - L0)/(L3 - L0)
variables.impact_evidence: [design]; event-window version of R12-061 (information-value metric)
variables.how_to_model: Tag each trip with its event window; report per arm with paired seeds

variables.sub_box: Public event information and the with/without-info experiment
variables.name: Out-of-NYC event scenario (Coachella-style)
variables.description: A portable event module for a festival town with no public trip data, to test whether event skill generalises.
variables.values_or_range: Coachella: Empire Polo Club, Indio CA, two April weekends, ~125k a day, rideshare lot with long waits [U]; alternative calibration: Chicago TNP trips plus Lollapalooza [U] [uncertain: Coachella site, dates and capacity not re-checkable this session]
variables.data_source: Chicago Transportation Network Providers - Trips (data.cityofchicago.org m6dm-c72p; ID S via the City of Chicago developer blog on GitHub; later years may sit in a successor table, uncertain)
variables.how_to_model: Synthetic town graph plus event templates from NYC and Chicago residuals

variables.sub_box: Public event information and the with/without-info experiment
variables.name: Event visual overlays
variables.description: Map overlays that show events, closures and alerts in the live visualisation.
variables.values_or_range: Venue pulse sized by attendance; closure polygons; subway status ticker
variables.impact_evidence: [design]
variables.how_to_model: Render event objects on the map timeline

variables.name: Precipitation state and hourly intensity
variables.description: Whether it is dry, raining or snowing in each hour, and how hard; the master input that drives the demand, speed, risk and robotaxi rules.
variables.values_or_range: dry; trace (<0.01 in/h); light (<0.10 in/h, ~2.5 mm); moderate (0.10-0.30 in/h); heavy (>0.30 in/h); extreme (>1 in/h, Ida 2021 ~3.15 in in one hour [U]). Central Park 2009-2025 per year: 126 days >=0.01 in, 80 >=0.1 in, 56 >=0.25 in, 34.5 >=0.5 in, 13.6 >=1 in, 2.5 >=2 in; mean 50.5 in/yr [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: Brodeur & Nield 2018: Uber rides +25% per rainy hour vs taxi +4% [S] [uncertain: IZA/JEBO hosts unreachable and the search budget was exhausted, so the +25%/+4% figures were not re-read at source]; our TLC Jan 2023: Uber trips +6.3% on wet days (t=2.3), yellow -0.5% [P]
variables.data_source: NOAA NCEI Local Climatological Data (hourly), Central Park USW00094728 https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/local-climatological-data ; GHCN-Daily https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/datasets/GHCND/stations/GHCND:USW00094728/detail ; IEM ASOS https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/request/download.phtml
variables.how_to_model: Hourly series per scenario day (replayed from LCD or generated), binned into 5 intensity classes that index the demand, speed, crash and robotaxi tables.

variables.name: Rain demand uplift for app requests
variables.description: Extra ride requests when it rains; completed app trips rise but completed taxi trips do not, because taxi supply is fixed and fully used [uncertain: an inference; TLC files cannot show taxi occupancy or unmet hails].
variables.values_or_range: App ride volume +10-30% per rainy hour [design range anchored on Brodeur & Nield's +25% for Uber] [corrected by fact-check: was 'requests' tagged [S range]; no source gives this range, and Brodeur & Nield count completed rides, not requests]; daily, wet day (>=0.10 in) vs dry, Jan 2023: Uber +6.3% (t=2.3), Lyft +3.9% (t=1.5), yellow -0.5% (n.s.) [P]; heavy rain larger than light [U]
variables.impact_evidence: Brodeur & Nield 2018 IZA DP 9986: Uber +25%/rainy hour vs taxi +4% [S] [uncertain: IZA/JEBO hosts unreachable and the search budget was exhausted, so the +25%/+4% figures were not re-read at source]; our own TLC x NOAA daily regressions with weekday and trend controls [P]
variables.applies_to: human app driver, robotaxi, fleet; taxi (as latent hail demand)
variables.data_source: NYC TLC HVFHV and yellow trip records https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page joined to NOAA LCD hourly precipitation
variables.how_to_model: Multiply the zone x hour request rate by m_rain(intensity, hour, day type), fitted by Poisson regression of HVFHV counts on hourly rain with hour-of-week fixed effects.

variables.name: Rain onset surge and decay
variables.description: Demand jumps most in the first hour or two after rain starts, when people are caught out, then fades as trips are postponed or already made.
variables.values_or_range: First-hour peak 1.2-1.6x, decay half-life 1-3 h [design guess]; 29 Sep 2023 flood: yellow trips +46% to +63% from 05:00-09:00, back to about -3% to +5% by 12:00-15:00 vs 4 reference Fridays [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Our TLC hourly event study of 29 Sep 2023 [P]; curve shape is a [design guess]
variables.data_source: TLC trip records + NOAA LCD hourly or IEM 1-minute ASOS for onset times
variables.how_to_model: Multiplier = 1 + a*intensity + b*exp(-(t - onset)/tau); fit a, b, tau by event study on rain onsets.

variables.name: Rain effect by hour, day type and trip purpose
variables.description: The same rain raises demand more at some hours and on some day types (errands, evening, nightlife) and can cut discretionary weekend trips when heavy.
variables.values_or_range: Uber, wet vs dry Tue-Thu, Jan 2023: +2% to +6% at 05:00-09:00, +14% to +25% at 10:00-23:00 [P, not trend-adjusted] [corrected by fact-check: 'wet' here means the 4 Tue-Thu days with >=0.4 in (3, 19, 25 and 26 Jan) against dry Tue-Thu days; hours 00:00-04:00 also show +13% to +27%, so part of the gap is the upward trend within January, not rain]; heavy-rain Sunday 30 Apr 2023: yellow -24% to -29% at 19:00-21:00 [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Our TLC hourly comparisons [P]; R02 notes rain at 6 pm hits a market already short of cars [design]
variables.data_source: TLC trip records + NOAA LCD hourly
variables.how_to_model: Interact the rain multiplier with hour-of-week buckets and trip-purpose shares (commute vs discretionary) from R05.

variables.name: Shift toward short trips in bad weather
variables.description: Rain and cold add short trips that people would otherwise walk, changing the trip-length mix and the number of pickups per hour.
variables.values_or_range: Yellow share of trips under 1 mile: 20.5% on dry days; +0.5 pp light, +1.2 pp moderate, +1.4 pp heavy rain; +2.5 pp on cold days (max <=35°F); Uber +1.1 pp on wet days (base 10%) [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Our 2023 yellow daily regressions, t=2.7 to 6.2; Uber Jan 2023 t=3.7 [P] [corrected by fact-check: impact lowered from medium to low; the shifts are 0.5-2.5 points of the trip mix and the yellow fare per trip did not change significantly (heavy rain +$0.1, t=0.7), so the effect on profit per hour is small]
variables.data_source: TLC trip records (trip_distance, trip_miles) + NOAA GHCN-Daily
variables.how_to_model: Weather-dependent re-weighting of the trip-distance / OD distribution toward intra-zone and adjacent-zone trips.

variables.name: Mode substitution from walking, cycling and transit
variables.description: Bad weather moves trips off walking, Citi Bike, e-bikes and outdoor bus waits onto cars; this is the pool the extra car demand comes from.
variables.values_or_range: Citi Bike trips drop sharply on rainy days (order of -30% to -60%) [U]; subway ridership dips in storms [U]
variables.impact_evidence: Background knowledge of Citi Bike and MTA ridership on rain days; not computed here [U] [corrected by fact-check: impact lowered from medium to low; this variable is only a calibration check, and its demand effect is already carried by R04-002]
variables.data_source: Citi Bike System Data https://citibikenyc.com/system-data ; MTA Daily Ridership https://data.ny.gov/
variables.how_to_model: Use Citi Bike and subway drops on weather days as a calibration check on the car-demand uplift, not as a separate generator.

variables.name: Street-hail intensity in rain (taxi)
variables.description: How many more people try to hail a yellow cab per mile cruised when it rains, mostly in high-foot-traffic zones.
variables.values_or_range: Hail attempts +20-50% in rain in the Manhattan core [design guess]; completed yellow trips flat on wet days (-0.5%), so the cab is full rather than demand-limited [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Our TLC: yellow completed trips flat while app trips rise [P]; Farber 2015 'Why You Can't Find a Taxi in the Rain' [U for rain result]
variables.data_source: TLC yellow trip records; R01 pedestrian density
variables.how_to_model: Raise the street-hail arrival rate per road segment by weather, scaled by pedestrian density, so the hail-encounter probability per cruising minute rises.

variables.name: Weather speed-penalty table (input to R10-006)
variables.description: How much slower traffic moves in each weather class; R10 applies it to link speeds.
variables.values_or_range: NYC DOT sensors 2023-2025, median speed vs dry baseline (same sensor, day type, hour): light rain 0.95, moderate 0.91, heavy 0.91; light snow 0.91, moderate 0.80, heavy 0.51 [S] [uncertain: the ratios were re-read in the notebook output (0.946, 0.914, 0.913; 0.908, 0.798, 0.513), but its bins use thresholds of 2.5 and 10 (rain) and 2 and 5 (snow) in undocumented units, probably mm per hour, with each sensor matched to its nearest LCD station, so its classes do not map exactly onto the in/h bins in R04-001]. Our TLC: heavy-rain days -0.4 mph (t=-2.2); 29 Sep 2023 08:00-09:00 7.5-8.4 vs 11.6-11.8 mph (-29% to -35%); snow 16 Jan 2024 08:00-10:00 -14% to -23% [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Jususs/NYC_Big_Data notebook joining NYC DOT speeds to NOAA LCD [S]; our TLC hourly speeds [P]
variables.data_source: NYC DOT Traffic Speeds NBE https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Transportation/DOT-Traffic-Speeds-NBE/i4gi-tjb9 + NOAA LCD; TLC trip speeds
variables.how_to_model: Lookup multiplier by precipitation class x road class (highway vs street) x hour, applied on top of the R10 weekly profile.

variables.name: Pickup ETA inflation in rain
variables.description: Rain lengthens the time from request to driver arrival; the curb dwell after arrival does not change.
variables.values_or_range: Uber median request-to-on-scene +0.23 min on wet days (base 2.6 min, +9%, t=3.0); 17:00-20:00 wet 2.6-3.1 vs dry 2.0-2.5 min (+22% to +40%) [corrected by fact-check: this evening comparison uses the 4 Tue-Thu days with >=0.4 in against dry Tue-Thu days, without a trend control; only the +9% daily figure uses the >=0.10 in definition with weekday and trend controls]; on-scene-to-pickup dwell 0.79 min, unchanged (t=0.2) [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Our TLC HVFHV Jan 2023 analysis [P]
variables.how_to_model: Emerges from matching (R06) under slowed speeds and tighter supply; use +9% daily and +22% to +40% in the evening as validation targets.

variables.name: Weather-driven cancellations and no-shows
variables.description: Riders cancel when ETAs grow or they find another car; drivers cancel long or flooded pickups.
variables.values_or_range: Cancellation rate +2 to +5 pp in heavy rain [design guess]; public TLC files contain completed trips only
variables.impact_evidence: No public data found [design guess]
variables.data_source: none found (TLC HVFHV has completed trips only)
variables.how_to_model: Rider cancel hazard rising with ETA, scaled up in rain; driver-side cancel exposed as an agent action.

variables.name: Surge response to weather
variables.description: How much app prices and driver pay rise when rain creates a supply shortage; the yellow meter does not change.
variables.values_or_range: Uber daily averages on wet days, Jan 2023: base fare per mile +$0.09 (+2%, t=1.4), driver pay per engaged hour +$0.46 (+0.8%, t=1.8) [P] (weekday controls only, no trend control); hourly peaks much larger [U]; yellow tariff fixed
variables.impact_evidence: Our TLC HVFHV analysis [P]; Brodeur & Nield: surge lets app supply respond to rain [S] [corrected by fact-check: impact lowered from high to medium; the measured daily price and pay responses are only 1-2%, and the larger hourly surge peaks are unmeasured [U]]
variables.how_to_model: Surge multiplier from zone demand/supply ratio (R07); weather enters only through demand and speed, not as a separate weather fee.

variables.name: Emergency surge cap
variables.description: During New York state-declared emergencies Uber agreed to cap surge pricing, and state price-gouging law applies.
variables.values_or_range: July 2014 Uber agreement with the NY Attorney General to cap surge in state-declared emergencies [S] (fact-check: a news sentence in the cited public dataset confirms an agreement 'to put a ceiling on surge pricing during state-declared emergencies' announced in July; the year 2014 is inferred from context); cap reported as the 4th-highest multiplier of the prior 60 days [U]; NY General Business Law 396-r [U]
variables.impact_evidence: News text in a public GitHub corpus describing the 2014 agreement [S]
variables.data_source: NY Attorney General press releases https://ag.ny.gov/ (not fetched)
variables.how_to_model: When a declared-emergency flag is on, cap the surge multiplier at a configurable ceiling.

variables.name: Snowfall rate and accumulation
variables.description: How much snow falls per hour and in total, which slows traffic, changes demand and can stop robotaxis.
variables.values_or_range: Central Park 2009-2025: mean 28.9 in/season (2.3 in 2022-23 to 61.9 in 2010-11); per year 10.8 days >=0.1 in, 6.9 >=1 in, 2.7 >=4 in, 1.4 >=6 in, 0.4 >=10 in; record 27.3 in on 23 Jan 2016 (fact-check: with 0.2 in on 22 Jan the storm total is 27.5 in [P*], the largest Central Park storm on record [U]); 2026: 11.4 in on 25 Jan, 19.7 in on 22-23 Feb [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: NYC DOT sensor speed x0.51 in heavy snow [S]; 16 Jan 2024 (1.3 in): yellow trips -5%, morning speeds -14% to -23% [P]
variables.data_source: NOAA GHCN-Daily Central Park (SNOW, SNWD) via GitHub copy https://github.com/toddwschneider/nyc-taxi-data ; NOAA LCD present-weather codes
variables.how_to_model: Hourly snowfall rate and running depth drive speed (R04-008), demand (R04-017), crash risk (R04-041) and robotaxi limits (R04-039).

variables.name: Snow cover and plowing state after a storm
variables.description: Snow left on roads and curbs for days after a storm: narrower lanes, blocked curbs and slow side streets.
variables.values_or_range: Snow depth >=1 in on 22.5 days/yr at Central Park [P*]; side streets 1-3 days to clear [U]
variables.impact_evidence: Depth statistics [P*]; clearing times [U]
variables.data_source: GHCN-Daily SNWD; NYC DSNY snow-plow tracking (PlowNYC) [U, URL not verified]
variables.how_to_model: Per-borough 'cleared' state that recovers over 1-3 days, adding speed and pickup-dwell penalties on uncleared streets.

variables.name: Freezing rain, sleet and black ice
variables.description: Icy precipitation and refreezing that make bridges and ramps slippery and raise crash risk more than snow does.
variables.values_or_range: A few days per year [U]; highest crash multiplier of any weather type [U]; bridges and elevated roads ice first [U]
variables.impact_evidence: Road-weather background knowledge; FHWA pages unreachable [U]
variables.data_source: NOAA LCD present-weather codes (FZRA, PL); NWS winter weather advisories (IEM archive) https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/
variables.how_to_model: Precipitation-type flag that applies the snow speed penalty plus a higher crash multiplier, larger on bridges and elevated links.

variables.name: Weather-triggered emergencies, travel bans and transit suspensions
variables.description: Official orders in big storms that ban non-emergency driving, suspend subway or bus service, or close bridges. Weather thresholds and examples only; the emergency object itself is R03-044.
variables.values_or_range: Jan 2016 travel ban during the 27.3 in storm [U]; 26-27 Jan 2015: travel ban and full subway shutdown for a storm forecast at 20-30 in that gave 9.8 in at Central Park [U for ban and forecast; P* for 9.8 in]; above-ground subway lines suspended in heavy snow [U]
variables.impact_evidence: Snowfall totals [P*]; ban and shutdown details [U]
variables.data_source: NYC Emergency Management / NYC Notify; MTA service alerts; no machine-readable archive found
variables.how_to_model: Scenario flag with start and end time: ban stops new trips except exempt classes (configurable); transit suspension boosts car demand on affected corridors (R04-026).

variables.name: Snow-day demand mix
variables.description: Snow changes who travels: closed schools and remote work cut commutes, while people who must travel switch from walking and buses to cars.
variables.values_or_range: Small snows (0.1-1.3 in), 2023-24: yellow trips -3% (n.s.); 16 Jan 2024 -5% [P]; big storms likely -30% or more during the storm, rebound afterwards [U]; NYC public schools now go remote on snow days [U]
variables.impact_evidence: Our TLC daily regressions [P]; big-storm effect [U]
variables.data_source: TLC trip records + GHCN-Daily; NYC public school closure announcements
variables.how_to_model: Snow multiplier on demand by trip purpose: commute down, airport and medical stable, short trips up.

variables.name: Winter road damage and salt
variables.description: Potholes, road salt and slush add tyre, alignment, corrosion and car-wash costs in late winter.
variables.values_or_range: Pothole complaints peak Feb-Apr [U]; +$5-15 per week in washing and wear in winter [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [U] and [design guess]
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, robotaxi, fleet
variables.how_to_model: Seasonal maintenance cost-per-mile multiplier (cross-link R08).

variables.name: Hourly air temperature, humidity and heat index
variables.description: Outdoor temperature (with dew point for heat index and wind for wind chill) each hour.
variables.values_or_range: Central Park 2009-2025 mean daily max 39.6°F (Jan) to 86.0°F (Jul); per year 62.9 days with min <=32°F, 18.1 days max >=90°F, 2.8 days >=95°F; highest 104°F on 22 Jul 2011 [P*] [corrected by fact-check: this is the 2009-2025 maximum in our copy, not the all-time record; the Central Park record is 106°F on 9 Jul 1936 [U]]
variables.impact_evidence: Our climate statistics from GHCN-Daily [P*]; drives EV energy, demand and comfort
variables.data_source: NOAA LCD hourly dry-bulb and dew point; GHCN-Daily TMAX/TMIN
variables.how_to_model: Hourly series feeding the demand (R04-020), HVAC energy (R04-023) and EV range (R04-037) functions.

variables.name: Temperature demand effect
variables.description: How hot and cold days change the number of rides and how short they are.
variables.values_or_range: Yellow trips vs 51-80°F days, with month and weekday controls, 2023: max >=90°F +22% (t=1.9), 81-89°F +11% (t=1.6), max <=35°F +4% (n.s.); short-trip share +2.5 pp on cold days (t=5.2), +1.3 pp on hot days (t=3.2) [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Our 2023 TLC regressions, small samples (12 hot, 9 cold days) [P]
variables.how_to_model: Temperature-band multipliers on demand and short-trip share, refitted on several years before use.

variables.name: Heat waves and heat advisories
variables.description: Multi-day hot spells with official advisories that raise short-trip demand, strain power and transit, and tire drivers.
variables.values_or_range: NWS NYC heat advisory roughly heat index >=95°F for 2+ days or >=100°F [U]; 2.8 days/yr >=95°F [P*]; subway heat and A/C failures [U]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] frequency; effects [U]
variables.data_source: NWS alerts (IEM archive) https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/ ; NOAA LCD
variables.how_to_model: Heat-event flag raising short-trip demand, A/C energy and fatigue, with a small chance of correlated power or transit outages.

variables.name: Extreme cold and wind chill
variables.description: Very cold hours that cut EV range, slow charging, fail weak batteries and push people into cars.
variables.values_or_range: Daily min <=20°F on 14.6 days/yr, <=10°F on 2.1 days/yr; lowest -1°F on 14 Feb 2016 [P*] [corrected by fact-check: this is the 2009-2025 minimum in our copy, not the all-time record; the Central Park record low is -15°F in Feb 1934 [U]]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] frequency; effects via R04-037/038 [S]/[U]
variables.how_to_model: Cold flag triggering EV range and charging penalties, a small 12V battery failure chance [design guess] and the short-trip shift.

variables.name: Cabin climate-control energy cost (temperature input to R08-009)
variables.description: Fuel or battery used for A/C and heating, including while idling between trips. R08-009 owns the HVAC energy cost; R04 supplies the hourly temperature that drives it.
variables.values_or_range: Gas car: A/C can cut fuel economy by more than 25% on short trips in very hot weather [uncertain: fueleconomy.gov's wording recalled as 'more than 25%', not 'up to'; page unreachable]; cold cuts short-trip city mpg ~15-24% [U]; idling ~0.2-0.5 gal/h [U]; NYC 3-min anti-idling limit (R10-034)
variables.impact_evidence: fueleconomy.gov hot/cold pages, unreachable here [U]
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, robotaxi, fleet
variables.how_to_model: HVAC energy per minute as a U-shaped function of outdoor temperature, applied while driving and idling.

variables.name: Thunderstorms and lightning
variables.description: Short, intense, often local summer storms that cause sudden demand spikes, airport ground stops and street flooding.
variables.values_or_range: Mostly May-Sep afternoons; 30-120 min; rain rates can exceed 1 in/h [U]; GSOD thunder flag shows 0 days in 2023 at Central Park, so station flags are unreliable [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: [U]; station-flag check [P*]
variables.data_source: NOAA LCD weather-type codes (TS); NEXRAD on AWS https://registry.opendata.aws/noaa-nexrad/ ; NWS warnings (IEM)
variables.how_to_model: Convective-cell generator: short heavy-rain bursts over a subset of zones, coupled to airport delays (R04-031).

variables.name: Flash flooding and flooded roads
variables.description: Extreme rain that floods parkways, underpasses and basements, closing links for hours.
variables.values_or_range: Central Park extreme days: 7.13 in (1 Sep 2021, Ida), 5.48 in (29 Sep 2023), 4.45 in (21 Aug 2021); >=2 in on 2.5 days/yr [P*]; flood-prone FDR, BQE, Major Deegan, Grand Central and Bronx River parkways [U]
variables.impact_evidence: 29 Sep 2023: yellow-trip average speeds at 08:00-09:00 -29% to -35% [P] [corrected by fact-check: all yellow trips citywide (mostly Manhattan), not a Manhattan-only measure]; Waymo fleet recall May 2026 after flooded-road incidents [S, via R06] [uncertain: not re-checked at source; news hosts unreachable]
variables.data_source: FloodNet NYC street-flood sensors https://www.floodnet.nyc/ [U]; NYC 311 street-flooding complaints; GHCN-Daily
variables.how_to_model: When hourly rain passes a threshold (e.g. 1.5 in/h [design guess]), close or slow a list of flood-prone links for 1-6 h; entering a closed link carries damage risk (R04-043).

variables.name: Weather-driven transit disruption (weather cause of R03-046)
variables.description: Subway and rail suspensions caused by flooding, snow, heat or storms, which push riders onto cars. R03-046 owns the subway-incident object; R04 supplies the weather trigger and its demand evidence.
variables.values_or_range: 29 Sep 2023 flood with subway suspensions [uncertain: the suspensions are background knowledge; only the trip changes come from our data]: yellow trips +17% for the day and +46% to +63% from 05:00-09:00 [P]; full MTA shutdowns for Irene (2011), Sandy (2012) and the Jan 2015 blizzard [U]
variables.impact_evidence: Our TLC hourly event study [P]
variables.data_source: MTA ridership https://data.ny.gov/ ; MTA GTFS-realtime alerts (no historical archive found)
variables.how_to_model: Disruption event that boosts car demand in the catchment of suspended lines (cross-link R03, R05).

variables.name: Wind speed and gusts
variables.description: Wind that brings down trees and branches and triggers bridge restrictions; little direct effect on cars otherwise.
variables.values_or_range: Central Park mean daily wind 5.3 mph (sensor sheltered by trees; LGA/JFK windier); 2023: 5 days with gusts >=30 kn, max 34 kn (gusts reported on only 213 of 365 days); Sandy day mean 18.8 mph [P*]; bridge wind limits mostly hit trucks and motorcycles [U]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] station data; restrictions [U]
variables.data_source: NOAA LCD (LGA USW00014732, JFK USW00094789); NOAA GSOD
variables.how_to_model: Gust threshold triggers random tree-down link closures and bridge restrictions.

variables.name: Hurricanes, tropical storms and nor'easters
variables.description: Rare multi-hazard storms combining heavy rain, wind, storm-surge flooding, power cuts and transit shutdowns over 1-3 days.
variables.values_or_range: About one major event every few years [U]; Irene 28 Aug 2011 (3.99 in; 6.87 in over 27-28 Aug), Sandy 29 Oct 2012 (mean wind 18.8 mph), Henri and Ida Aug-Sep 2021 [P*]; evacuation zones 1-6 [U]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] station data; scenario consequences [U]
variables.data_source: NOAA NHC HURDAT2 https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/ ; NYC hurricane evacuation zones (NYC Open Data) [U]
variables.how_to_model: Scripted scenario pack combining R04-025/026/029/030, with demand collapse during the storm and a surge afterwards.

variables.name: Weather-related power outages (a cause of R11-060)
variables.description: Storm or heat outages that turn off traffic signals and EV chargers. R11-060 covers fleet-wide outages of any cause.
variables.values_or_range: Dark signals act as all-way stops; Sandy left lower Manhattan dark for days [U]; Waymo cars stalled at dark signals in the Dec 2025 San Francisco outage [U] [uncertain: news recollection, not re-checkable this session; R03 and R11 flag the same claim]
variables.data_source: Con Edison outage map (live only) [U]; none historical found
variables.how_to_model: Outage polygon: links inside get a signal-out speed penalty, chargers inside go offline, robotaxis may stop.

variables.name: Post-storm fuel and charging shortages
variables.description: Fuel or charging scarcity after a major storm.
variables.values_or_range: Odd-even gas rationing in NYC in Nov 2012 after Sandy [U]
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, robotaxi, fleet
variables.how_to_model: Fuel-availability flag: refuelling takes longer or fails (cross-link R08).

variables.name: Airport weather delays and cancellations (weather cause of R03-049)
variables.description: Thunderstorms, snow, wind and low cloud cause ground stops and cancellations at JFK, LGA and EWR, shifting airport pickup demand in time. R03-049 owns the airport-disruption object.
variables.values_or_range: Summer thunderstorm ground stops; mass cancellations in snowstorms [U]; airport pickup share did not change on rain days in 2023 (+0.2 to -0.4 pp, n.s.) [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Our TLC airport share [P]; delay mechanisms [U]
variables.data_source: BTS Airline On-Time Performance https://www.transtats.bts.gov/ ; FAA airport status (live)
variables.how_to_model: Weather perturbs flight-arrival banks: delays shift airport demand later, cancellations remove it (cross-link R01-052, R05-063).

variables.name: Weather cancellation and delay of outdoor events (input to R03-020, R03-021)
variables.description: Rainouts, rain delays and postponed outdoor concerts move or remove event egress surges. R03-020/R03-021 own event cancellation and weather-at-let-out effects.
variables.values_or_range: Baseball rainouts and delays; outdoor concerts and parades postponed [U]
variables.data_source: Retrosheet game logs (rainouts) https://www.retrosheet.org/ [uncertain: game logs list games played; postponements and their reasons are recalled to sit in Retrosheet's schedule files, not re-read]; NYC permitted events (NYC Open Data)
variables.how_to_model: Event cancel/delay probability conditioned on rain forecast and observed rain; shifts or removes the R03 egress surge.

variables.name: Fog and low visibility
variables.description: Fog and mist that slow traffic slightly, raise crash risk, limit robotaxis and delay flights.
variables.values_or_range: Central Park 2023 (GSOD): fog flagged on 27 days; daily mean visibility <5 mi on 18 days, <3 mi on 2, never <1 mi [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] station data; effects [U]
variables.data_source: NOAA LCD visibility; NOAA GSOD FRSHTT flags
variables.how_to_model: Visibility class adds a small speed and crash penalty and feeds robotaxi limits (R04-039) and airport delays (R04-031).

variables.name: Wildfire smoke and air quality alerts
variables.description: Smoke or ozone episodes that push people from walking and cycling into cars and cancel outdoor events.
variables.values_or_range: 7 Jun 2023 Canadian smoke (AQI near 480 at worst [U]): yellow trips +4.8% for the day, +15% to +17% at 14:00-15:00 vs nearby Wednesdays [P]; NYS air quality health advisories on several summer days a year [S]
variables.impact_evidence: Our TLC event comparison [P]; NYS DEC advisory texts in a public dataset [S]
variables.data_source: EPA AirNow API https://docs.airnowapi.org/ ; EPA AQS https://aqs.epa.gov/aqsweb/documents/data_api.html ; Open-Meteo air-quality API
variables.how_to_model: AQI series; above ~150, shift walking and cycling trips to cars, cancel outdoor events, raise driver discomfort.

variables.name: Daylight and darkness (driving side)
variables.description: Light level through the day, which affects crash risk, robotaxi perception and riders' sense of safety; the timing effect on demand sits in R02-063.
variables.values_or_range: Day length 9.2 h (21 Dec) to 15.1 h (21 Jun); earliest sunset 16:27 (5 Dec), latest 20:31 (24 Jun); civil twilight 28-34 min (2026, our calculation) [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Astronomical calculation [P]; night crash effect [U]
variables.data_source: Astronomical calculation (astral library, NOAA solar calculator); LCD sunrise/sunset fields
variables.how_to_model: Sun elevation from date and time; feeds crash risk, robotaxi limits and the visualiser's night cycle.

variables.name: Low-sun glare
variables.description: Low sun shining straight down a street blinds drivers and cameras, especially along Manhattan's crosstown grid.
variables.values_or_range: Sunset azimuth ~299° (grid-aligned) around 24-25 May and 17-18 Jul; sunrise ~119° around 2-3 Dec and 8-9 Jan (2026, our calculation) [P] (fact-check: reproduced with an independent NOAA solar-position calculation) [uncertain: these are dates for the sun at the geometric horizon; the published 'Manhattanhenge' dates, with the sun just above the real horizon, are about 28-30 May and 11-13 Jul, recalled not re-read; glare risk spans several days around both]; camera-based driving struggles in glare and low visibility (NHTSA probe) [S]
variables.impact_evidence: Sun-angle calculation [P]; NHTSA FSD low-visibility probe reported in news [S] [uncertain: the cited GitHub source is near-empty on re-check; the probe was opened in Oct 2024 [U] and its later status was not re-checked]
variables.data_source: astral sun position; OSM street bearings https://download.geofabrik.de/north-america/us/new-york.html
variables.how_to_model: When sun elevation <10° and street bearing within ±10° of sun azimuth, small speed and crash penalty on those links.

variables.name: EV range loss in cold and heat (temperature curve for R08-010)
variables.description: How much more energy per mile an electric car uses in cold or hot weather. R08-010 owns the vehicle-side cost; R04 supplies temperature and the curve evidence.
variables.values_or_range: At 20°F with heater on, range -41% (AAA 2019, cited by fueleconomy.gov) [S]; at 20°F without HVAC about -12%, at 95°F with A/C about -17% [U] (fact-check: -41% is the cold extreme; Central Park has a daily minimum of 20°F or lower on about 15 days a year (R04-022), so typical NYC winter losses are smaller)
variables.impact_evidence: AAA/fueleconomy.gov figure quoted in public GitHub code [S]
variables.data_source: fueleconomy.gov cold-weather page https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/coldweather.shtml ; AAA 2019 EV test
variables.how_to_model: kWh/mile multiplier as a U-shaped function of outdoor temperature (lowest near 65-75°F), applied to battery state of charge.

variables.name: Cold-battery charging speed and preconditioning (see R08-010)
variables.description: Cold batteries charge slowly unless warmed first; hot batteries can throttle. Shared with R08-010.
variables.values_or_range: DC fast-charge power reduced with a cold battery; preconditioning 10-30 min uses energy [U]
variables.data_source: AFDC station locator https://afdc.energy.gov/stations ; no public charging-curve-by-temperature data found
variables.how_to_model: Charging-power curve scaled by battery temperature; agent may precondition while driving to a charger at an energy cost.

variables.name: Robotaxi weather operating envelope
variables.description: Weather limits beyond which robotaxis stop taking rides, return to base or restrict their area.
variables.values_or_range: Thresholds e.g. rain >0.3 in/h, any snow accumulation, visibility <0.5 mi, flash-flood warning, high winds [design]; Aurora: weather constrained its driverless trucks in Texas ~40% of the time in 2025 until rain, fog and wind were validated [P*]; Waymo says its 6th-gen sensors handle rain, fog and snow and it is expanding to snowy cities [S]
variables.impact_evidence: Aurora Q4 2025 earnings call transcript, 11 Feb 2026 [P*] (fact-check: re-read verbatim in the GitHub transcript copy, 'During 2025, inclement weather of all types constrained our driverless operations in Texas roughly 40% of the time'; tag raised from [S]); Waymo technical summaries [S]
variables.data_source: none public (operator internal); CPUC/DMV filings partial [U]
variables.how_to_model: ODD table: weather class -> normal / restricted zones or speeds / no new pickups / return to base; 'robotaxi generation' scenario knob.

variables.name: Robotaxi sensor degradation, cleaning and cautious driving
variables.description: Rain, snow and salt spray on sensors make robotaxis drive more cautiously, call remote help more often and stop to clean.
variables.values_or_range: Extra speed penalty -5% to -15% beyond human drivers in rain or snow; more remote-assistance stops; cleaning stops [design guess]; Waymo simulates raindrops on sensors and glare [S]
variables.impact_evidence: [design guess]; Waymo simulation description [S]
variables.how_to_model: Robotaxi-specific multipliers on speed, stop probability and minutes lost per hour by weather class.

variables.name: Weather crash-risk multiplier for the agent's car
variables.description: Higher chance that the agent's own car crashes in rain, snow, ice or fog, with repair cost and lost days.
variables.values_or_range: NYC crashes per hour in rainy vs dry hours at the same hour of day (2023-2025, not exposure-adjusted): about -1% to +5% at 08:00-17:00, about +10% at 00:00, 07:00 and 18:00, and +20% to +34% at most hours from 19:00 to 06:00 [S] [corrected by fact-check: was '10-35% higher' at every hour; the notebook output shows almost no difference in daytime, and its 'rain' hours include trace amounts]; snow and ice higher [U]; cost: deductible $500-2,500 plus 2-10 days off the road [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: Jususs/NYC_Big_Data notebook joining NYPD crashes to NOAA LCD [S] [corrected by fact-check: impact lowered from medium to low; crashes are rare per driver-hour, so even a 20-30% weather multiplier changes expected profit per hour very little, though one crash can dominate a single run [design guess]]
variables.data_source: NYPD Motor Vehicle Collisions https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Public-Safety/Motor-Vehicle-Collisions-Crashes/h9gi-nx95 + NOAA LCD
variables.how_to_model: Poisson crash hazard per mile x weather multiplier; a crash ends the shift and charges cost (cross-link R08, R10-025).

variables.name: Interior cleaning and wet-car downtime
variables.description: Wet or slushy riders soil the car, needing cleaning time or money.
variables.values_or_range: Robotaxi cleaning detour 5-15 min after a soiled ride [design guess]; more car washes in winter [U]
variables.impact_evidence: [design guess]
variables.how_to_model: Per-trip probability of a soiled interior rising with precipitation, triggering a cleaning detour.

variables.name: Flood water damage and stranding risk
variables.description: Chance that driving into standing water stalls or wrecks the car.
variables.values_or_range: About 6 in of water can stall a car; flood-damaged cars are often written off [U]
variables.data_source: FloodNet depths https://www.floodnet.nyc/ ; no damage data found
variables.how_to_model: If the route crosses a flooded link above a depth threshold, stochastic stall: car stuck for hours plus repair cost.

variables.name: Tipping response to weather
variables.description: Whether riders tip more in bad weather; in the data they barely do.
variables.values_or_range: Yellow card tips 22.3% of fare on dry days; rain days +0.1 to +0.2 pp (n.s.); Uber tip incidence 19.6%, +0.3 pp on wet days (n.s.) [P]; sunnier days slightly higher tips (Devaraj & Patel 2017) [U]
variables.impact_evidence: Our 2023 yellow and Jan 2023 HVFHV regressions [P]
variables.data_source: TLC tip_amount (card trips) and HVFHV tips
variables.how_to_model: Keep tip rates weather-independent by default; optional small multiplier.

variables.name: Rider willingness to pay in bad weather
variables.description: Riders accept higher prices when it is wet or very cold, so surge loses fewer of them.
variables.values_or_range: Price elasticity 10-30% lower in rain [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [U] general ride-hail pricing literature; none NYC-specific found
variables.how_to_model: Weather term in the rider price-acceptance function (R05, R07).

variables.name: Driver weather log-off thresholds
variables.description: How human drivers (competitors and the agent's persona) cut hours in snow, ice or floods, which they do not do in ordinary rain.
variables.values_or_range: Rain: taxi supply about flat (Farber 2015) [U]; heavy snow: supply -10% to -40% [U, as R06-050]; NYC cab drivers respond positively to higher earnings opportunities (Farber 2015 abstract) [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: Farber 2015 QJE abstract via NBER metadata copy [P*] (fact-check: confirmed in the NBER w20604 metadata, Oct 2014; the abstract does not mention rain, so the rain result stays [U]); snow numbers [U]
variables.applies_to: taxi, human app driver, competitor supply
variables.data_source: TLC trip records (no driver IDs in current files); Farber used 2009-2013 TLC data
variables.how_to_model: Weather-dependent log-off hazard in the competitor supply model (cross-link R06-050).

variables.name: Decision to work through severe weather
variables.description: The agent's choice to start, continue or stop driving when a storm hits, trading higher utilisation and surge against delay, crash and damage risk.
variables.values_or_range: Work / pause / go home, at any time, triggered by alerts or observed conditions [design]; 29 Sep 2023: trips +17% but fare per engaged hour $55-57 vs $68 in the 08:00-09:00 peak [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Our TLC event study shows the trade-off [P]; decision design [design]
variables.how_to_model: Action space includes go-offline and return-home at any time; payoff emerges from the simulator.

variables.name: Driver comfort and fatigue in heat and cold
variables.description: Extreme heat or cold makes a human driver tire faster.
variables.values_or_range: Fatigue rate +10-20% on extreme-temperature days [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [design guess]; cross-link R09-007
variables.how_to_model: Temperature term in the fatigue accumulation function.

variables.name: Weather information level given to the agent (see R12-015)
variables.description: What weather the agent can see: none, current conditions only, a public forecast, or perfect foresight. R12-015 owns serving forecast vintages; this variable defines the weather view levels.
variables.values_or_range: L0 none; L1 current conditions at own location; L2 L1 plus hourly forecast 0-48 h; L3 perfect future weather (oracle, ablation only) [design]
variables.impact_evidence: [design] mirrors the team's with/without event-information test
variables.data_source: NWS API https://api.weather.gov ; Open-Meteo forecast and Previous Runs APIs
variables.how_to_model: Harness injects the chosen weather view into the observation each step.

variables.name: Forecast error and lead time (feeds R12-015)
variables.description: How wrong the public forecast was, in timing and amount, at each lead time. Forecasts must be served as issued (R12-015).
variables.values_or_range: Open-Meteo Previous Runs API stores forecasts at 1-7 day lead offsets, processed from early 2024; its Historical Forecast API (from 2021-22) stitches first forecast hours, so it is closer to observed weather than to a forecast [P*] (fact-check: confirmed in Open-Meteo's own website source on GitHub: lead offsets of 1-7 days, most models archived from January 2024, GFS 2 m temperature from March 2021, JMA GSM/MSM from 2018 [P*]); Jan 2015 blizzard forecast 20-30 in vs 9.8 in observed [U, P*]
variables.impact_evidence: Open-Meteo documentation copy [P*]; blizzard bust [U]
variables.data_source: Open-Meteo Previous Runs API https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/previous-runs-api ; IEM archived NWS text products https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/ ; NOAA NBM/NDFD archives [U]
variables.how_to_model: Give the agent the forecast actually issued before each time (from archives), or a synthetic forecast = truth plus calibrated timing and amount noise.

variables.name: Official alerts and warnings feed
variables.description: Time-stamped public warnings the agent could read: flash flood, winter storm, heat, wind, fog and air-quality alerts.
variables.values_or_range: NWS watches, warnings and advisories; NYS air-quality health advisories; NYC Notify; phone emergency alerts [U]
variables.data_source: IEM NWS watch/warning archive https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/request/gis/watchwarn.phtml [U]; NWS API alerts https://api.weather.gov/alerts
variables.how_to_model: Alert events in the agent's news feed alongside R03 public event information.

variables.name: Spatial weather awareness
variables.description: Whether the agent sees weather only where its car is, a citywide summary, or a radar-style zone map.
variables.values_or_range: Own location / citywide / zone grid [design]
variables.impact_evidence: [design]
variables.data_source: NOAA MRMS radar precipitation https://mrms.ncep.noaa.gov/ [U]; NEXRAD on AWS
variables.how_to_model: Observation granularity switch; matters only when the simulator models spatial weather (R04-057).

variables.name: Pre-positioning ahead of forecast weather
variables.description: Moving one car or a fleet before rain or a storm arrives toward zones where demand will jump, or home before a ban.
variables.values_or_range: Lead 15-120 min; share of a fleet staged near hubs and nightlife before forecast rain [design]
variables.impact_evidence: [design]; value depends on onset dynamics (R04-003) and information level (R04-049)
variables.how_to_model: Ordinary repositioning actions; the benefit comes from forecast information and onset dynamics.

variables.name: Seasonal climate mix per scenario day
variables.description: How likely each weather type is in each month, which sets how often each effect appears in randomly drawn scenario days.
variables.values_or_range: Central Park 2009-2025: wet-day (>=0.01 in) probability 0.28 (Sep) to 0.39 (May, Dec); snow-day probability Jan 0.11, Feb 0.13, Mar 0.05, Dec 0.06; days >=90°F per month Jul 8.1, Aug 4.8, Jun 2.7; freezing nights Jan 19.7 [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: Our GHCN-Daily climate statistics [P*]
variables.how_to_model: Scenario-day sampler stratified by month and weather type; report the weather class with every score.

variables.name: Weather replay vs synthetic generator, and seeds (see R03-064)
variables.description: Whether a scenario replays the real weather of a historical day (matched to its TLC demand) or uses generated weather, and how weather randomness is shared across runs. Pair with the R03-064 memorisation guard.
variables.values_or_range: Replay (realistic; models may remember famous days such as Ida) / stochastic (Markov chain on hourly classes fitted to Central Park) / hybrid; same weather seed for all models in a comparison [design]
variables.impact_evidence: [design]; memorisation risk noted by R05
variables.how_to_model: Weather module interface replay(date) or generate(month, seed); common random numbers across models.

variables.name: Weather counterfactual and ablation pairs
variables.description: Running the same demand day with and without weather effects, or with rain injected at a chosen time, to measure how much of an agent's earnings come from handling weather.
variables.values_or_range: Weather on/off; rain injected at time t; information level L0-L3 crossed with weather on/off [design]
variables.impact_evidence: [design]
variables.how_to_model: Harness toggles weather multipliers while holding other random draws fixed.

variables.name: Spatial resolution of weather
variables.description: Whether one station represents the whole city or weather varies by zone.
variables.values_or_range: One station (Central Park) / 4-5 stations (Central Park USW00094728, LGA USW00014732, JFK USW00094789, EWR USW00014734, Teterboro USW00094741) / 1-km radar grid [P* station IDs; design]; summer storms can be very local [U]
variables.impact_evidence: Station list from a public NOAA LCD analysis [P*]; locality [U]
variables.data_source: NOAA LCD for the listed stations; NOAA MRMS radar
variables.how_to_model: Nearest-station or radar interpolation to taxi zones.

variables.name: Temporal resolution of weather
variables.description: Daily, hourly or minute weather data; coarse data hide most of the rain effect.
variables.values_or_range: Daily (GHCN) / hourly (LCD routine reports at :51) / 1-5 min (ASOS); our daily estimate (+6% Uber on wet days) vs ~+25% per rainy hour in Brodeur & Nield [P, S] [uncertain: the Brodeur & Nield figure was not re-read at source]
variables.impact_evidence: Comparison of our daily estimate with the hourly literature [P, S]
variables.how_to_model: Hourly by default; finer only for onset dynamics.

variables.name: Weather data join and cleaning rules
variables.description: Rules for turning raw weather files into simulator inputs aligned with trip records.
variables.values_or_range: LCD 'T' = trace precipitation; report types FM-15 (routine hourly), FM-16 (special), SOD (daily summary); LCD exports in metric or imperial units [uncertain: not re-checked; NOAA host blocked]; align to America/New_York local time [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: Public LCD cleaning notebooks [P*]
variables.how_to_model: Pipeline step with unit tests: hourly bins aligned to TLC pickup hour; trace treated as 0.001 in.

variables.name: Climate trend in extremes
variables.description: Whether to include more frequent extreme rain in 'future NYC' scenarios.
variables.values_or_range: 4 of the 12 wettest Central Park days in 2009-2025 fell in 2021-2023 (21 Aug, 1 Sep and 26 Oct 2021; 29 Sep 2023), 5 counting 23 Mar 2024 [corrected by fact-check: was '3 of the 12'; 3 of the 12 also fell in Aug-Sep 2011, so this clustering is weak evidence of a trend]; seasonal snowfall swings 2.3-61.9 in [P*]; heavier downpours in the Northeast long-term [U]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] ranking; trend [U]
variables.data_source: NOAA GHCN-Daily; NYC Panel on Climate Change reports [U]
variables.how_to_model: Optional scenario knob raising extreme-rain frequency.

variables.name: Weather and daylight rendering on the live map
variables.description: Showing rain, snow, fog, floods and night lighting on the live map so clips show why earnings jumped.
variables.values_or_range: Rain/snow overlay, fog dimming, night lighting by sun elevation, flooded links highlighted [design]
variables.impact_evidence: [design]; team notes on night/day cycle and clippable visuals
variables.data_source: Simulator weather state; astral sun elevation
variables.how_to_model: Visualiser reads the same weather state as the simulator.

variables.name: Base request rate by zone and hour
variables.description: Expected number of ride requests starting in each taxi zone in each hour, split by day type, which is the main input that drives all earnings.
variables.values_or_range: Citywide ~18M HVFHV trips in Aug 2024 [corrected by fact-check: 19.13M raw HVFHV rows in Aug 2024, about 617k/day rather than ~580k/day; TLC's '>18M' is consistent] plus ~3M yellow (~97k/day; confirmed, 2.98M rows = 96k/day); Jan 2023: 18.48M HVFHV trips (~596k/day). Per zone-hour (HVFHV Jan 2023): median 64, p99 ~560, max 1,625 pickups/hour [corrected by fact-check: the busiest zone-hours are East Village (zone 79) at 00:00-02:00 on weekend nights and Midtown Center (zone 161) at 19:00-21:00, not generic 'Midtown peaks']; 263 taxi zones plus code 264 (Unknown) and 265 (Outside of NYC)
variables.impact_evidence: [S] TLC testimony 27 Sep 2024: HV sector >18M trips in Aug 2024 (~90% of 2019), yellow ~3M (~50% of 2019); [P*] monthly row counts from a SHA-256 catalog of the TLC files (R02 data folder) and own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (HVFHV Jan 2023)
variables.data_source: NYC TLC trip records (yellow, green, HVFHV; PULocationID x pickup hour) https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page
variables.how_to_model: Non-homogeneous Poisson rate per zone x 15-min slot x day type, fitted from served trips, then lifted for unserved demand (R05-066)

variables.name: Day-to-day demand randomness (overdispersion)
variables.description: How much realised demand in a zone-hour scatters around its average, beyond pure Poisson noise, because of shared daily shocks.
variables.values_or_range: Coefficient of variation 10-30% per zone-hour on comparable days [fact-check: confirmed. HVFHV Jan 2023, Tue-Thu, zone-hours with >=50 trips: median CV 15% (IQR 12-20%) vs 9% from Poisson noise alone, variance about 2.6x the mean; citywide daily total CV ~11%]; one citywide daily shock plus zone-level shocks
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (HVFHV Jan 2023): variance ~2.6x Poisson, so Poisson alone understates spread; matters for robustness across 100 runs
variables.data_source: NYC TLC trip records (daily counts by zone)
variables.how_to_model: Gamma-Poisson (negative binomial) mixture: daily city multiplier x zone multiplier x Poisson arrivals, seeded per run

variables.name: Bursty, clustered request arrivals
variables.description: Requests arriving in bursts within minutes when crowds leave a venue, a flight bank lands or a train line stops, rather than spread evenly.
variables.values_or_range: Bursts of 5-500 requests within 10-30 min at one zone [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [design] arrivals cluster at event end times; cross-link R03 Events
variables.data_source: Event schedules (R03), flight schedules (BTS), MTA service alerts
variables.how_to_model: Batch or Hawkes-process arrivals triggered by scheduled event end, flight arrival and outage times

variables.name: Platform share of city demand
variables.description: The fraction of all city ride demand that reaches the platform the simulated driver or fleet works on.
variables.values_or_range: Uber 73.5%, Lyft 26.5% of HVFHV trips in Jan 2023 [fact-check: confirmed from data, HV0003 13.58M vs HV0005 4.90M trips; earlier '~70-75% [U]' holds]; yellow and green taxis are separate channels; robotaxi operator share is a scenario knob 0.01-0.5
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies, field hvfhs_license_num (HV0003 Uber, HV0005 Lyft), HVFHV Jan 2023
variables.data_source: NYC TLC HVFHV trip records, field hvfhs_license_num
variables.how_to_model: Thin total demand by platform share before matching; cross-link R06 for competitor capture

variables.name: Demand level of the replay year
variables.description: Which year and month the scenario replays, which sets the overall demand level and the taxi versus app split.
variables.values_or_range: Yellow ~50% and HVFHV ~90-95% of 2019 levels (Aug 2024 vs Aug 2019 raw rows: yellow 49%, HVFHV 95%; 2019 HVFHV rows also include Via and Juno); HV trips +4.9% Dec 2024 to Dec 2025 [fact-check: confirmed, 21.07M to 22.11M rows]; yellow +17% over the same months (3.67M to 4.31M rows)
variables.impact_evidence: [S] TLC testimony Sep 2024; [S] TLC license pause report Feb 2026; [P*] TLC monthly row counts via SHA-256 catalog of the original files (R02 data folder)
variables.data_source: TLC trip records and monthly aggregated reports https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/aggregated-reports.page
variables.how_to_model: Scenario chooses base year/month; a global scale factor rescales all rates

variables.name: Destination choice matrix
variables.description: Probability that a request from a given zone at a given hour goes to each destination zone.
variables.values_or_range: 263 x 263 zone matrix (~69k cells) per hour band and day type, very sparse outside Manhattan
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] PULocationID and DOLocationID confirmed in local HVFHV and yellow Parquet files; destination sets where the driver ends up
variables.data_source: NYC TLC trip records (PU/DO zone pairs)
variables.how_to_model: Empirical conditional OD with Bayesian smoothing; gravity-model fallback for sparse pairs

variables.name: Trip distance distribution
variables.description: Spread of trip lengths, from short Midtown hops to long airport and out-of-city runs.
variables.values_or_range: Yellow Oct 2019: mean 3.05 mi, median 1.67 mi, 85% of trips 5 mi or less, 81% both 5 mi or less and fare $18 or less (confirms the '~80%' claim); yellow 2023: mean 3.5 mi, median 1.8 mi, 82% 5 mi or less; HVFHV Jan 2023: mean 4.8 mi, median 2.9 mi, 70% 5 mi or less, p99 ~26 mi [fact-check: all recomputed from TLC files; the earlier [U] means are confirmed]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (yellow Oct 2019 and 2023, HVFHV Jan 2023); [S] NYC Data Science 2019; trip length sets fare per trip versus time between trips
variables.how_to_model: Emerges from OD plus routing; calibrate against empirical distance histograms by hour

variables.name: Trip duration distribution (validation target)
variables.description: Distribution of in-car time per trip, used to check that simulated trips take as long as real ones.
variables.values_or_range: Yellow 2023: median 12.8 min, mean 16.5 min; HVFHV Jan 2023: median 15.0 min, mean 18.1 min [fact-check: confirmed from data, was [U]]; longer in PM peak
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (trip_time, pickup/dropoff times); time per trip is the denominator of profit per hour; cross-link R10
variables.how_to_model: Not generated directly; harness compares simulated vs empirical duration by OD and hour

variables.name: Directional imbalance by zone and hour
variables.description: Net flow of trips into versus out of each zone, such as morning inflow to Midtown and late-night outflow from bar districts.
variables.values_or_range: Drop-off to pickup ratio 0.3-3 per zone-hour [corrected by fact-check: in HVFHV Jan 2023, weekday zone-hours averaging >=50 pickups/day have a ratio of 0.45-1.45 (5th-95th percentile, IQR 0.78-1.11); values near 0.3 or 3 occur only in small zones, at airports or in event hours]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (PU vs DO counts by zone and hour); imbalance drives deadhead and stranding
variables.how_to_model: Emerges from OD matrix; harness exposes it as a derived heatmap and tracks the agent's deadhead

variables.name: Return-trip coupling (tour chains)
variables.description: People who travel out for a concert, dinner or flight later make a predictable return trip.
variables.values_or_range: P(return by car within 2-8 h) 0.3-0.6 for leisure trips [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [design] reverse wave after events; cross-link R03
variables.data_source: none found (infer from paired OD flows in TLC data)
variables.how_to_model: Rider tours home-activity-home, or an event-linked return wave scheduled at event end

variables.name: Exact pickup and drop-off point within a zone
variables.description: Where in a taxi zone the rider actually stands or is dropped, since TLC data gives only zone IDs.
variables.values_or_range: Zones ~0.3-2 mi across [U]; points weighted by buildings, foot traffic and historic GPS [corrected by fact-check: coordinates were dropped from July 2016 onward; yellow and green files up to June 2016 carry GPS points]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] Schneider nyc-taxi-data README: 'Starting in July 2016, the TLC no longer provides pickup and dropoff coordinates'

variables.name: Nightlife demand layer

In nightlife zones (East Village 79, Lower East Side 148, West Village 249) Sat/Sun HVFHV pickups peak at 00:00-02:00 (~3,500/h for the three zones), are ~2,000 at 03:00 and ~950 at 04:00 (Jan 2023); there is no closing-time spike at 4 AM]

variables.sub_box: D. Price, wait and mode choice
variables.name: Price elasticity to surge or fare level
variables.description: How much demand falls when the quoted price rises.
variables.values_or_range: Elasticity about -0.5 near 1.2x surge and below 1 in magnitude at higher surges (UberX, 2015, Chicago, LA, NYC, SF) [uncertain: point value comes from course notes; the paper is usually summarised as inelastic demand of roughly -0.4 to -0.6 across surge levels [U]; NBER unreachable]

variables.data_source: Published estimates only (no public NYC data)

variables.sub_box: D. Price, wait and mode choice
variables.name: Sensitivity to quoted pickup ETA
variables.description: How much fewer people request a ride when the app shows a longer wait.
variables.values_or_range: Price elasticities ~4x waiting-time elasticities (ride-hail auctions) [uncertain: ratio not re-read; Buchholz et al. use Prague (Liftago) data, not NYC]; one NYC study claims +1.5 min delay cuts demand ~37% (unverified)

variables.how_to_model: Multiply conversion by exp(-beta x ETA) per segment; key for fleet positioning

variables.sub_box: D. Price, wait and mode choice
variables.name: Rider cancellation after match
variables.description: Chance that a rider cancels after a driver accepts, rising as the wait drags or the car moves the wrong way.
variables.values_or_range: 5-15% of matched requests [design guess]; many cancels in the first minute; free window ~2 min then fee
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Spare 2019: many cancels come very quickly; [S] Wang, Zhang & Zhang 2024 (Operations Research): long pickups cause cancels [uncertain: citation not located]; [corrected by fact-check: impact lowered from high to medium. At 5-15% of matches and ~2-5 min lost per cancel, partly repaid by fees, the loss is about 1-3% of driver time [design arithmetic]; kept core because cancels feed fleet ETA and conversion]
variables.applies_to: human app driver, robotaxi, fleet, taxi e-hail
variables.data_source: none found (TLC data holds completed trips only)
variables.how_to_model: Hazard model over time since match with ETA-slip term; pays cancel fee per R07 rule

variables.sub_box: D. Price, wait and mode choice

variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, robotaxi, fleet
variables.how_to_model: Rider samples k options and picks lowest generalised cost (price + value of time x ETA)

variables.sub_box: D. Price, wait and mode choice

variables.how_to_model: Multinomial logit over products using price ratio and party size; vehicle eligibility from R08

variables.how_to_model: P(cash | zone, hour) from payment_type

variables.name: Ratings riders give the driver
variables.description: Star ratings riders leave, driven by wait, route, cleanliness and conduct, feeding the driver's rating.
variables.values_or_range: Mostly 5 stars; 1-3 low ratings per 100 trips rising with delays [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [design]; matters through deactivation risk in R09
variables.how_to_model: P(rating | service quality) updates driver rating state (R09)

variables.name: Rider rating shown to driver
variables.description: The rider's own rating shown on the offer, a weak signal of no-show, mess or low tips.
variables.values_or_range: Average rider ~4.89 (third party); NYC riders get the lowest ratings [uncertain: not re-checked]; low-rated riders can lose access (Uber, 2019)
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Uber 2019 announcement (USA Today); [S] third-party FAQs
variables.how_to_model: Request attribute correlated with no-show, incident and tip propensity

variables.sub_box: H. Incidents, disputes and side income
variables.name: Rider safety incidents
variables.description: Rare assaults, robberies or harassment involving riders or drivers.
variables.values_or_range: 99.9% of Uber US trips had no reported safety incident (2017-18); 20 physical-assault deaths in 2019-20 (15 riders) [uncertain: rider/driver split not re-checked]
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Uber US Safety Reports (press coverage)
variables.how_to_model: Rare event with night and zone multipliers; trip lost, downtime, may end shift (R09)

variables.sub_box: H. Incidents, disputes and side income
variables.name: Vomit, mess and cleaning fee
variables.description: A rider makes a mess, the car goes off duty for cleaning and the rider is charged a fee.
variables.values_or_range: Uber tiers $20 small, $40 vomit, $80 large spill, $150 heavy bodily fluids; 1 per 500-2,000 late-weekend trips [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Uber fee tiers via local news on 'vomit fraud'
variables.how_to_model: P(mess | nightlife, hour) leads to 30-90 min downtime plus fee and dispute chance

variables.sub_box: H. Incidents, disputes and side income
variables.name: Lost items and return fees
variables.description: Items riders leave behind, which the driver can return for a fee.
variables.values_or_range: $20 return fee to driver (Uber Canada 2023; older $15); 0.5-1% of trips [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Uber Canada 2023 Lost and Found Index; Tile 2024 analysis
variables.how_to_model: Bernoulli lost item; agent decides return detour vs keep driving

variables.sub_box: H. Incidents, disputes and side income
variables.name: Fare disputes, refunds and chargebacks
variables.description: Riders who complain about route or fees and get money back, sometimes clawed from the driver.
variables.values_or_range: 0.5-2% of trips disputed [design guess]; complaints of false cleaning fees rising
variables.impact_evidence: [S] BBB-cited 'vomit fraud' complaints in press
variables.how_to_model: Dispute chance rises with detour vs shortest path and ETA slip; payout rule from R07

variables.sub_box: H. Incidents, disputes and side income
variables.name: Non-payment and fare evasion
variables.description: Taxi riders who run off without paying or whose card fails.
variables.values_or_range: 0.1-0.5% of cash taxi trips [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [design]
variables.how_to_model: Bernoulli loss of fare on cash trips, higher late night

variables.sub_box: I. Destination value, stranding and airports
variables.name: Destination re-dispatch value
variables.description: Expected wait for the next paying trip after dropping off in a zone, which makes some fares worth more than their price.
variables.values_or_range: Manhattan core 1-5 min vs outer Queens or Staten Island 10-30+ min [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [design] computable from TLC pickups and drop-offs; central to accept/decline and positioning
variables.how_to_model: Emerges from demand plus supply; harness logs idle time after each drop

variables.sub_box: I. Destination value, stranding and airports
variables.name: Out-of-city trips and stranding
variables.description: Trips to Nassau, Westchester, New Jersey or Newark that pay well but leave the car far from demand.
variables.values_or_range: Taxis must serve NYC, Nassau, Westchester and Newark Airport [fact-check: confirmed, 35 RCNY 80-20(a)(1); a driver who has operated more than 8 h may refuse EWR, Nassau and Westchester, 80-20(b)(8)]; [corrected by fact-check: 4.5% of HVFHV trips end outside the city (3.9% in zone 265 + 0.6% at EWR; avg 16.6 mi, avg driver pay $44.6, Jan 2023) and 0.7% of yellow trips (2023), not '1-3% [U]'; HVFHV pickups in zone 265 are ~0.005% of trips, so the return is almost always empty]; empty return 30-90 min [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 80-20 (verbatim RCNY copy); [P*] taxi zone lookup: 1 = Newark Airport, 265 = Outside of NYC; [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (also R08 data folder)
variables.data_source: TLC DOLocationID (1 = EWR, 265 = Outside of NYC; confirmed in zone lookup); yellow RatecodeID 3 Newark, 4 Nassau/Westchester, 5 negotiated
variables.how_to_model: External destination nodes; low return-match chance; tolls on return (R07)

variables.sub_box: I. Destination value, stranding and airports
variables.name: Trips heading toward the driver's home
variables.description: How many requests go toward the driver's home area at shift end, for the 'take me home' feature.
variables.values_or_range: P(match toward home within 15 min) 0.1-0.6 by home zone and hour [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [design] from team notes; destination filter decision in R09
variables.how_to_model: Filter demand by heading; harness measures end-of-shift deadhead saved

variables.sub_box: I. Destination value, stranding and airports
variables.name: Airport-bound demand (departures)
variables.description: Requests to JFK, LGA and EWR, tied to flight departure times.
variables.values_or_range: Early-morning wave: airport-bound share of weekday HVFHV trips peaks at 24-28% at 04:00-06:00; volume peaks at 05:00 with a second bump at 13:00-16:00 [fact-check: own calc, Jan 2023]; JFK yellow flat fare $70 (Dec 2022 rule) [fact-check: confirmed in 2023 yellow records, RatecodeID 2 fare $70]
variables.impact_evidence: [S] TLC 2022 fare rule coverage: JFK flat fare $52 to $70; [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies; [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26 (via R07)
variables.data_source: BTS on-time and schedule data https://www.transtats.bts.gov/; TLC DOLocationID 132 JFK, 138 LGA, 1 EWR (confirmed in zone lookup)
variables.how_to_model: Departures by hour minus 2-3 h lead, x origin shares from TLC

variables.sub_box: I. Destination value, stranding and airports
variables.name: Airport arrival demand
variables.description: Requests from arriving passengers, driven by flight arrival waves and how many choose a taxi or app car.
variables.values_or_range: LGA 42% by cab + 14% black car (2012-14); 41% of JFK and 63% of LGA travellers use taxi/limo/e-hail [uncertain: survey shares not re-read]; [fact-check: Jan 2023 airport pickups per day: JFK ~11,170 app vs ~5,160 yellow (app 68%), LGA ~9,920 app vs ~2,880 yellow (app 78%); airports are 8.6% of yellow pickups but 3.5% of HVFHV pickups, consistent with ride-hail taking airport share]
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Port Authority survey via PANYNJ indicators; [S] 2021 airport access study; [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies
variables.data_source: BTS arrivals; PANYNJ traffic reports; 'Taxis Dispatched at Port Authority of NY NJ Airports' dataset (data.gov)
variables.how_to_model: Arrivals x passengers per flight x mode share, released 20-60 min after landing at terminal pickup areas

variables.sub_box: I. Destination value, stranding and airports
variables.name: Airport queue dynamics
variables.description: How long a car waits in the airport taxi holding lot or app virtual queue before getting a passenger.
variables.values_or_range: JFK taxi lot waits up to 2-3 h (2013-15 reports); Uber JFK virtual FIFO queue with visible position, free parking up to 3 h
variables.impact_evidence: [S] amNY 2014-15; Queens DA case; [S] Uber JFK driver page
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, robotaxi, fleet
variables.data_source: Port Authority taxi dispatch counts (data.gov); Uber airport pages
variables.how_to_model: FIFO queue fed by driver arrivals and drained by passenger demand; agent sees queue position

variables.sub_box: I. Destination value, stranding and airports
variables.name: Airport passenger destination and fare mix
variables.description: Where airport passengers go (Manhattan, Brooklyn, Long Island, NJ) and so what the trip pays.
variables.values_or_range: JFK to Manhattan flat $70 (yellow, confirmed); LGA metered; [corrected by fact-check: Jan 2023 yellow plus HVFHV airport pickups go JFK -> Manhattan 39%, Queens 24%, Brooklyn 21%, outside NYC 14%; LGA -> Manhattan 57%, Brooklyn 15%, Queens 15%, outside NYC 9%; half of yellow JFK pickups use the flat fare (RatecodeID 2)]
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies; [S] 2022 TLC rate rule coverage
variables.data_source: TLC trips with PULocationID 132, 138, 1 (zone IDs confirmed)
variables.how_to_model: Empirical destination distribution for airport pickups

variables.sub_box: I. Destination value, stranding and airports
variables.name: Flight delays shifting airport demand
variables.description: Late or cancelled flights move or remove arrival waves.
variables.values_or_range: Waves shift 15-180 min; storm days cancel banks [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [design]; cross-link R03 and R04
variables.how_to_model: Replay real arrival times per scenario day

variables.sub_box: J. Latent demand and demand feedback
variables.name: Latent vs observed demand (censoring)
variables.description: Trip data shows only served trips, so real demand in busy, short-supplied places is higher than the records.
variables.values_or_range: Unserved share 5-20% at peaks [design guess]; zero cancelled requests in TLC files
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Gammelli et al. 2020 censored Gaussian processes; [P*] local HVFHV Parquet schema has no cancel or unserved-request field
variables.how_to_model: Lift demand where supply was tight (long waits, surge) using a censored model; expose uplift as a scenario knob

variables.sub_box: J. Latent demand and demand feedback
variables.name: Request-to-pickup wait (calibration target)
variables.description: Real time from request to pickup, used to check the simulated balance of riders and cars.
variables.values_or_range: Citywide HVFHV average 5.4 min (Jan 2026) [S]; 4.5-6.6 min range since 2018 [S]; [fact-check: Jan 2023 completed trips: mean request-to-pickup 4.6 min, median 3.9 min, matching TLC's 4.7 min for Jan 2023]
variables.impact_evidence: [S] TLC license pause reports Feb 2023 and Feb 2026; [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (request_datetime to pickup_datetime)
variables.how_to_model: Harness compares simulated vs empirical wait by zone and hour

variables.sub_box: J. Latent demand and demand feedback
variables.name: Induced demand and rider retention
variables.description: Better service (short ETAs, few cancels) brings more requests later, and bad trips drive riders away.
variables.values_or_range: Zone demand multiplier 0.9-1.1 responding to recent ETA [design guess]
variables.impact_evidence: [design]; [corrected by fact-check: Frechette et al. 2019 show increasing returns to scale in taxi matching, which supports density effects but says nothing about rider retention]
variables.how_to_model: Zone demand multiplier tied to moving-average served ETA; rider churn after bad trips

variables.sub_box: J. Latent demand and demand feedback
variables.name: Demand replay vs synthetic resampling
variables.description: Whether a scenario replays a real day's trips exactly or draws new trips from fitted distributions.
variables.values_or_range: Modes: exact replay, bootstrap resample, parametric synthetic; seeded
variables.impact_evidence: [design] exact replay risks memorisation and caps demand at served trips; cross-link R12
variables.how_to_model: Harness option per run; held-out day 11 uses a different seed or month

variables.sub_box: A. Background supply volume and mix
variables.name: Competitor cars online by zone and hour
variables.description: Number of other app cars and taxis logged on (busy or idle) in each taxi zone in each 15-minute slot.
variables.values_or_range: NYC app cars online: about 15k on average (15-17k if utilisation is nearer 53%), about 25-30k at the evening peak, about 4-6k before dawn [design calc: ~667k trips/day x ~19 min / ~0.58 utilisation]; plus about 3-5k yellow taxis on the road in a daytime hour [corrected by fact-check: was 5-8k [U]; ~130k yellow trips/day x ~16 min / ~0.5-0.6 occupancy gives ~2.5-3k on average, x ~1.5 at peak [design calc]; check against TLC monthly vehicles_per_day and avg_hours_per_day_per_vehicle]; 0 to ~1,500 per zone.
variables.impact_evidence: Matching collapses into long pickups when idle supply thins (Castillo, Knoepfle & Weyl 2017) [P, re-read by fact-check]; 243M app trips in 2025 (TLC budget testimony, Mar 2026) [S] [corrected by fact-check: a count of the 2025 HVFHV records gives 243,589,684 trips, about 667k/day; S, FerrisSearch analysis on GitHub]; online totals are [design] arithmetic.
variables.data_source: TLC monthly report CSV (vehicles_per_day, avg_hours_per_day_per_vehicle, unique_drivers) https://www.nyc.gov/assets/tlc/downloads/csv/data_reports_monthly.csv ; HVFHV trip records https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page
variables.how_to_model: Supply field per zone x 15 min, scaled so citywide vehicle-hours match the TLC monthly report and local pickup times match HVFHV request-to-on-scene times [corrected by fact-check: Uber rows only; Lyft (HV0005) leaves on_scene_datetime empty on ~99.7% of trips, S, fleetsim notes on GitHub].

variables.sub_box: A. Background supply volume and mix
variables.name: Idle cars per open request (local balance)
variables.description: Ratio of idle competing cars to unserved requests in a zone at a moment; it sets how fast any one driver gets a ping and whether surge fires.
variables.values_or_range: 0.2 (shortage: surge, long pickups) to >10 (glut: long idle); about 1/3 of taxi and app cars in the Manhattan core are empty at any moment (2013-2017 data).
variables.impact_evidence: Schaller, Empty Seats, Full Streets (2017): about one-third of vehicles in the Manhattan CBD empty [S]; thin idle supply triggers wild goose chases [P, re-read by fact-check].
variables.how_to_model: Computed each tick from idle background cars and pending requests per zone; feeds ping rate, the surge model (R07) and pickup ETAs.

variables.sub_box: A. Background supply volume and mix
variables.name: Trip market shares by service
variables.description: Share of trips served by Uber, Lyft, yellow taxis, green taxis and other bases, which sets how many requests flow through each channel the agent can use.
variables.values_or_range: 2025: app (HVFHV) about 667k trips/day (243.6M), Uber ~72% (176.0M) and Lyft ~28% (67.6M) [corrected by fact-check: full-year counts of the 2025 HVFHV records, S, FerrisSearch analysis on GitHub] (Lyft 27.7% in Sep 2025); yellow about 130k/day (+16% 2024 to 2025, 57% of the 2019 level); green ~1-2k/day [U]; other bases (black car, livery, luxury) are small [corrected by fact-check: the ~1,059 'other' entries are a cumulative base-number list kept in a GitHub repo, not a count of bases active in 2025].
variables.impact_evidence: TLC testimony 17 Mar 2026 (243M app trips; taxi trips +16%, 57% of 2019) [S]; Uber/Lyft split from third-party analysis of TLC data [S]; a base map lists 30 Uber, 2 Lyft, 2 Via, 4 Juno and 1,059 other base numbers [S, re-read on GitHub by fact-check]; licence codes HV0002 Juno, HV0003 Uber, HV0004 Via, HV0005 Lyft [S, re-read].
variables.data_source: TLC trip records (hvfhs_license_num: HV0003 Uber, HV0005 Lyft); FHV Base Aggregate Report https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Transportation/FHV-Base-Aggregate-Report/2v9c-2k7f ; https://github.com/toddwschneider/nyc-taxi-data
variables.how_to_model: Split generated requests into channels by zone-hour shares from trip records; each channel has its own matcher and background fleet.

variables.sub_box: A. Background supply volume and mix
variables.name: Active yellow taxi fleet
variables.description: How many of the 13,587 medallions are actually on the road, competing for street hails and taxi e-hails.
variables.values_or_range: About 10,520 active and about 3,069 in storage (Sep 2025) [uncertain: these sum to 13,589, not 13,587; source not re-checked]; over 1,000 medallions back on the road since Sep 2024; about 3-5k on the road in a daytime hour [corrected by fact-check: was 5-8k [U], which ~130k trips/day cannot keep busy; design calc as in R06-001].
variables.impact_evidence: AutoMarketplace analysis of TLC data, Sep 2025 [S]; 13,587 medallion total [U].
variables.how_to_model: Scale the yellow bot fleet to the scenario date; each taxi bot has a shift schedule and a cruising policy.

variables.sub_box: A. Background supply volume and mix
variables.name: Green taxi fleet and hail zone
variables.description: Size of the green (boro taxi) fleet, which may street-hail only outside Manhattan south of E 96th / W 110th St and outside the airports.
variables.values_or_range: Small: ~1-2k trips/day and a few hundred to ~1,000 active cars [U]; the hail-exclusion zone is fixed: Manhattan south of E 96th St and W 110th St plus the NYC airports; green cars also may not start pre-arranged (base or app) trips in that Manhattan zone, though they may at airports [P*, 35 RCNY 51-03 and 82-13, verified by fact-check].
variables.impact_evidence: Green volume shrank as app trips grew; no 2025-26 vehicle count found [U].
variables.data_source: TLC green trip records; TLC monthly report (Green rows)
variables.how_to_model: Small bot fleet restricted to outer-borough and upper-Manhattan hail polygons; matters only if the agent plays a green taxi.

variables.sub_box: A. Background supply volume and mix
variables.name: Licensed pool versus active supply
variables.description: Headroom between licensed cars and drivers and those actually working, which limits how many extra cars can flood in for surge or events.
variables.values_or_range: 82,225 licensed app (HVFHV) vehicles; 179,670 licensed taxi and FHV drivers (TLC 2025); a fraction works on any one day (~40-60% [U]).
variables.impact_evidence: TLC annual report 2025 [S]; daily share from TLC monthly vehicles_per_day vs unique_vehicles [U values].
variables.data_source: TLC annual report https://www.nyc.gov/assets/tlc/downloads/pdf/annual_report_2025.pdf ; TLC monthly report
variables.how_to_model: Cap on total background drivers who can log on; the entry model draws from the inactive pool.

variables.sub_box: A. Background supply volume and mix
variables.name: Competitor product and vehicle-class mix
variables.description: Share of competing cars eligible for each product (standard, XL, Comfort, Black/Lux, wheelchair-accessible, Green/EV), since dispatch only matches within eligible classes.
