variables.data_source: TLC driver survey summary (nyc.gov/assets/tlc/downloads/pdf/driver_survey_summary.pdf) [S]; Hall & Krueger 2018 ILR Review 71(3).
variables.how_to_model: Scenario config picks a profile that loads availability windows, home zone, hour caps and cost items.

variables.sub_box: B. Fatigue and legal hour caps
variables.name: TLC passenger-time cap
variables.description: NYC rule that limits how long a taxi or for-hire driver may carry passengers.
variables.values_or_range: At most 10 h of passenger time in any 24 h (the count resets after 8 consecutive hours with no passengers) and 60 h per Monday-Sunday week; only time carrying passengers counts (not time between trips); a single trip begun before the limit is a defence [corrected by fact-check: the rule does not say this trip counts toward the weekly total; it bars counting time used for a daily violation toward the weekly limit]; fines from $50/$75 for up to 1 h over, rising (R07-047).
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 80-14(f) (verbatim copy, current through rules eff. 13 Aug 2026) [upgraded by fact-check]; [S] TLC fatigued-driving FAQ; the 2017 draft used 12 h/72 h of total driving instead [S, not re-checked].
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi (NYC; other cities have different or no caps)
variables.how_to_model: Track rolling 24 h and weekly passenger time; refuse new trips (or fine) once over; apply the single-trip defence and the 8-hour reset.

variables.sub_box: B. Fatigue and legal hour caps
variables.name: Platform driving-time cap
variables.description: App rule that forces the driver offline after long driving.
variables.values_or_range: Uber (2018): 12 h driving time, then 6 h offline; time online but stopped (e.g. airport lot) not counted. Lyft (2018 report): 14 h in driver mode, then 6 h.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] TechCrunch/VentureBeat Feb 2018 (not re-checkable; matches background knowledge [U]); Uber at the NYC Council (Sept 2024): exceeding maximum driving hours is a compliance-deactivation reason.
variables.how_to_model: Per-platform counter; forced logout for 6 h when reached. Multi-apping can get around one app's cap but not the TLC cap.

variables.sub_box: B. Fatigue and legal hour caps
variables.name: Fatigue level
variables.description: Hidden driver tiredness that grows with hours on duty, time awake and night hours, and falls with breaks and sleep.
variables.values_or_range: 0-1 scale; about +0.06-0.10 per hour driven; x1.5 between 02:00 and 06:00; a 30 min break recovers about 0.1-0.2 [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [corrected by fact-check: was medium; its profit effect runs only through crash risk (R09-008) and speed (R09-009), both small, and the legal cap (R09-005) binds first] [S] TLC fatigue-rule presentation: taxi drivers working over 12 h/day had a 23.8% higher injury-crash rate (2014-15 data); Singapore survey links fatigue to more than 10 h/day.
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, fleet (per driver)
variables.data_source: TLC presentation (nyc.gov/assets/tlc/downloads/pdf/presentation_fatigued_driving_rule.pdf) [S]; no public dose-response curve found.
variables.how_to_model: Two-process score (time awake plus circadian dip) updated each tick; feeds crash risk and a small speed penalty. The agent sees only hours worked.

variables.sub_box: B. Fatigue and legal hour caps
variables.name: Crash and incident risk from fatigue and hours
variables.description: Chance per hour of a collision that ends the shift, rising with fatigue and night driving.
variables.values_or_range: Base hazard by zone and hour; x1.24 when over 12 h/day; cost = rest of shift lost + deductible $500-2,500 + repair days [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [corrected by fact-check: was medium; design calc: at roughly one crash per 5,000-10,000 driving hours [U] and $2,000-5,000 total cost, expected cost is about $0.2-1 per hour even with the x1.24 multiplier] [S] TLC: +23.8% injury-crash rate above 12 h/day; Dalziel & Job 1997 (Accident Analysis & Prevention, Sydney taxi drivers) [U]: more total break time, fewer accidents.
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi (robotaxi uses an AV incident rate, R08)
variables.data_source: NYC Open Data Motor Vehicle Collisions (opendata.cityofnewyork.us, h9gi-nx95) [U, blocked here]
variables.how_to_model: Bernoulli draw each tick with hazard = base(zone, hour) x fatigue multiplier; on a crash end the shift and charge costs.

variables.sub_box: B. Fatigue and legal hour caps
variables.name: Fatigue effect on driving performance
variables.description: Tired drivers drive a little slower and make more navigation errors.
variables.values_or_range: Speed -0 to -5%; route-error rate +0 to +10% at high fatigue [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [design] no driver-level public evidence found.
variables.how_to_model: Multiply travel time by (1 + k x fatigue); add an occasional detour.

variables.name: Meal breaks: timing and duration
variables.description: When the driver eats and for how long.
variables.values_or_range: 1-2 meals per 10-12 h shift, 15-45 min each; general-population peaks 12:00-13:00 and 18:00-19:00; drivers often move meals off demand peaks.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] USDA ERS ATUS module 2006-08: over 35% of Americans eat as a main activity at noon-1 pm and 6-7 pm [uncertain: share not re-checkable; the peaks themselves are well established (U)]; ATUS 2024: 74 min/day eating and drinking [uncertain: recent ATUS values are about 1.1-1.25 h (66-75 min) a day (U)]; a Wuhan study detects cab drivers' meal stops from GPS.
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, fleet (per driver)
variables.data_source: BLS ATUS https://www.bls.gov/tus/ ; ERS Eating and Health Module https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/eating-and-health-module-atus/
variables.how_to_model: Hunger timer; after 5-6 h without a meal apply a rising fatigue or discomfort penalty; a meal action takes 15-45 min in a zone with food.

variables.name: Bathroom need interval
variables.description: How often the driver must stop for a toilet.
variables.values_or_range: Every 2-4 h [design]; shorter with more fluids.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Columbia News Service 2023: many NYC drivers urinate in bottles for lack of access; worse for women drivers.
variables.how_to_model: Timer that forces a 5-15 min stop plus search time (R09-012) when it runs out; any break resets it.

variables.name: Time to find a bathroom and a legal place to stop
variables.description: Extra minutes to reach a usable restroom and stop legally, which depends on the zone.
variables.values_or_range: 5-30 min detour [design]; NYC has 109 relief stands but only 42 are open to app drivers (2023) [S]; airport lots have facilities; taxi relief time at a taxi stand at most 1 h, and posted vehicle-type and time limits apply at relief stands (35 RCNY 80-19(d)(5), (7)) [P*].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Columbia News Service 2023 (109 and 42); Documented (33 of 74 in an earlier count); Fortune 2025: TLC seeking new relief-stand sites; [P*] 35 RCNY 80-19(d).
variables.data_source: TLC/DOT relief-stand list [U]; NYC Parks public restrooms on NYC Open Data [U]; OpenStreetMap amenity=toilets https://www.openstreetmap.org
variables.how_to_model: Per-zone restroom access-time table; breaks in the Manhattan core cost more minutes than at airports or outer-borough gas stations.

variables.name: Prayer and religious observance
variables.description: Prayer stops, Friday midday prayers and Ramadan fasting that some drivers observe.
variables.values_or_range: 5 daily prayers of about 10-15 min at sun-based times; Friday Jumu'ah about 45-60 min at midday; Ramadan iftar stop of 30-60 min at sunset.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] In The Fray: roughly half of NYC's taxi drivers are Muslim (anecdotal); Religion News Service 2023: drivers combine prayers when they cannot park; CNN: drivers give up '$30 or $40' in the iftar hour.
variables.data_source: Astronomical prayer-time calculation [U]; Islamic calendar for Ramadan dates [U]
variables.how_to_model: Optional persona schedule of fixed-time breaks that need a parking spot or mosque zone; a Friday midday block.

variables.name: Parking and ticket cost during breaks
variables.description: Cost and risk of tickets when stopping for meals, the bathroom or prayer where parking is scarce.
variables.values_or_range: NYC parking or standing fines about $65-115 [U]; ticket chance per stop 0-30% by zone [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Jamiat and RNS reports: parking tickets are routine for NYC drivers stopping to pray; Fortune 2025: drivers ask for placards for brief stops.
variables.data_source: NYC Open Data Open Parking and Camera Violations [U]; NYC Department of Finance fine schedule [U]
variables.how_to_model: Ticket probability per break minute by zone x fine; zero at relief stands and airport lots.

variables.sub_box: D. Home, commute and end of shift
variables.name: Driver home location
variables.description: Where the driver lives, which sets start and end deadhead and the 'take me home' target.
variables.values_or_range: NYC app drivers: Queens about 35%, Brooklyn about 24% (TLC, 2018); most of the rest in the Bronx [uncertain: Bronx share and share living outside NYC (NJ, Long Island, Westchester) not checked]; few in Manhattan.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Brooklyn Eagle 2018 citing TLC: 35% live in Queens and 24% in Brooklyn.
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi owner-driver, fleet (each car its own home)
variables.data_source: ACS PUMS (taxi drivers and chauffeurs by residence PUMA) https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/microdata.html [U]; TLC figures [S]
variables.how_to_model: Assign each driver a home taxi zone drawn from a borough/PUMA distribution; store it as a persona attribute.

variables.sub_box: D. Home, commute and end of shift
variables.name: Commute deadhead at shift start and end
variables.description: Unpaid miles and minutes from home to the first pickup and from the last drop-off back home.
variables.values_or_range: 0-60 min each way in NYC [design]; idle miles about 30% of all miles (Gridwise 2025); nearly half of miles without a passenger (UCS) [uncertain: neither re-checkable; both national or multi-city, not NYC].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Gridwise 2025; UCS; TLC voted to cut allowed Manhattan cruising time from 41% to 31% [P*: 35 RCNY 59D-21 sets 36% from 1 Feb 2020 and 31% from 1 Aug 2020 for HVFHV cars in the Congestion Zone, 6 am-11 pm, measured per company; the 41% baseline is S; (U) a New York court annulled the cap in Dec 2019, so enforcement is uncertain although it remains in the rule text].
variables.data_source: TLC trip records (HVFHV trip_miles and trip_time, passenger miles only) https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page; none at driver level
variables.how_to_model: Emerges from routing home to first zone and last zone to home; costed per mile (R08) and per hour of time (R09-023).

variables.sub_box: D. Home, commute and end of shift
variables.name: Destination filter quota and mechanics
variables.description: App feature that only offers trips heading toward a chosen destination, with a daily limit; taxis have a legal on-route-home equivalent.
variables.values_or_range: Uber: 2 uses/day, resets at midnight, a use counts when you arrive [uncertain: when a use is counted]; Lyft: 2-6/day in pilots [uncertain: sources conflict; R06 cites 6/day]; matching is slower while on. Taxi [corrected by fact-check: was 'no filter']: a logged-off driver returning to the garage or home may pick up a passenger whose destination is directly on the route, after recording 'Returning to garage (or home)', and may then ask the destination first (35 RCNY 80-19(a)(5), 80-20(a)(4)(i)) [P*].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Rideshare Guy and RidesharingDriver blogs (Uber 2/day; Lyft cut from 6 to 2 in pilots); drivers report longer waits with the filter on; [P*] 35 RCNY 80-19(a)(5).
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi (garage/home return rule)
variables.data_source: 35 RCNY 80-19 via https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive [P*]; platform help pages only for apps
variables.how_to_model: While active, offer only trips whose drop-off cuts the ETA to the destination by at least X%; decrement the quota on arrival; lower offer rate. Taxi: an on-route-home flag limits street hails to riders going toward the garage or home.

variables.sub_box: D. Home, commute and end of shift
variables.name: Hard stop or return deadline
variables.description: A time by which the driver must be home or finished (childcare, other job, garage return).
variables.values_or_range: None, or a fixed time such as 15:00 school pickup, 17:00 taxi handover or 23:00 [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Lyft destination mode has an 'arrive on time' deadline option; taxi day drivers leave Manhattan early to avoid late fees (capped at $25/h, 35 RCNY 58-21 [P*]).
variables.how_to_model: Persona constraint with a per-minute late penalty or forced logout; the agent must plan its last trips toward home.

variables.sub_box: D. Home, commute and end of shift
variables.name: Taxi garage location and late-return fee
variables.description: Leased yellow cabs start and end at a garage, usually outside Manhattan.
variables.values_or_range: Garages mostly in Queens and Brooklyn (R11 notes a cluster in western Queens [U]); late fee at most $25 per hour, capped at one shift's lease (35 RCNY 58-21(c)(5)(iv)) [P*] [corrected by fact-check: was 'per hour [U]'].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Shift-change reporting: most trips are in Manhattan but most garages are in Brooklyn and Queens, so day drivers leave Manhattan early; [P*] 35 RCNY 58-21 late charge and return-to-premises term.
variables.data_source: TLC licensed agent and fleet addresses on NYC Open Data [U]; 35 RCNY 58-21 via https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive [P*]
variables.how_to_model: For the lessee persona the garage zone replaces home; the shift ends at the garage by the handover time; late return accrues up to $25/h.

variables.sub_box: D. Home, commute and end of shift
variables.name: Value of ending near home ('take me home')
variables.description: How much the score rewards finishing the shift close to home.
variables.values_or_range: 0 (pure profit) up to an explicit cost of the final trip home, e.g. home deadhead time valued at $20-30/h plus per-mile cost [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [design] team notes ask for a 'take me home' feature; Onde vendor page says drivers go offline early to avoid ending far from home [S].
variables.how_to_model: Score = profit minus the cost of the final drive home (time at reservation wage + per-mile cost); reported separately.

variables.name: Daily income target (reference point)
variables.description: A daily income goal at which a human-like driver tends to stop.
variables.values_or_range: None, or $150-350/day, adapting to recent earnings [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Camerer et al. 1997 QJE: wage elasticity of -0.5 to -1 (target earning); Farber 2015 QJE 130(4) on all 2009-13 NYC trips: elasticities mostly positive, only about 1/8 of wage variation unanticipated [uncertain: the 1/8 figure not re-checkable]; Thakral & To 2021 AER: stopping rises with recent earnings.
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, competitor drivers (R06)
variables.data_source: TLC 2009-2013 trip data (used by Farber and Thakral & To)
variables.how_to_model: Optional prompt variant, or a stopping rule for simulated competitors; also a probe: does the LLM itself stop early on good days?

variables.name: Daily hours target
variables.description: A planned number of hours after which the driver stops, whatever the earnings.
variables.values_or_range: 4-12 h [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] University of Washington Seattle ride-hail study: time targets affect stopping more than earnings targets; Farber 2005 (JPE 113(1)) tied stopping mainly to hours worked, not income [U; matches background knowledge, not re-checked].
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, competitor drivers
variables.data_source: none at driver level for NYC today (no IDs); 2009-13 FOIL trips; Chicago taxi IDs
variables.how_to_model: Stopping hazard that rises with hours worked; used for competitor supply and as a persona constraint.

variables.name: Reservation wage (value of the driver's time)
variables.description: What an hour of the driver's time is worth, used to judge whether one more hour is worth working.
variables.values_or_range: $0 (pure revenue) or $15-35/h varying by hour (higher late night and weekends) [design]; NYC 2018 pay standard was $17.22/h after expenses.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Chen et al. 2019: reservation wages vary hour to hour and flexibility more than doubles driver surplus; Parrott & Reich 2018: $17.22/h standard (matches background knowledge [U]).
variables.how_to_model: Objective = revenue - costs - sum of hours x w(t). This makes 'when to stop' a real trade-off instead of 'work 24 h'.

variables.name: Cumulative earnings and hours today
variables.description: Running totals the agent sees during the shift.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Thakral & To 2021: recent cumulative earnings drive human stopping decisions.
variables.how_to_model: Dashboard state in every observation; also input to competitor stopping rules.

variables.name: Incentive and quest progress
variables.description: Progress toward platform bonuses such as trip-count quests and consecutive-trip bonuses.
variables.values_or_range: e.g. $X for N trips per day or week (amounts in R07).
variables.impact_evidence: [U] Uber and Lyft run quest and streak bonuses; amounts belong to R07.
variables.how_to_model: Counters that raise the effective pay per trip near thresholds; tests whether the agent works longer to hit a quest.

variables.name: Experience level
variables.description: Lifetime trips and shifts, which raise earnings per hour through better search and timing.
variables.values_or_range: New (<100 trips) to veteran (>2,500 trips); 0-120+ shifts.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Cook et al. 2021 REStud: drivers with >2,500 trips earn about 14% more per hour than those with <100 (secondary summary; matches background knowledge [U]); Haggag, McManus & Paci 2017 (AEJ: Applied 9(1)): NYC taxi novices earn about 5% less per hour and catch up in about 100-120 shifts (AEA summary, not re-checked).
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, competitor drivers
variables.data_source: Haggag et al. replication data https://openicpsr.org/openicpsr/project/113636/version/V1/view [S, project id not checked]; Cook et al. NBER w24732
variables.how_to_model: For the LLM, experience is what it learned in the training days (R09-030); for simulated competitors, a search-efficiency multiplier that rises with trips.

variables.name: Zone familiarity (local knowledge)
variables.description: Knowledge, per neighbourhood, of where the next fare is likely to be after a drop-off.
variables.values_or_range: 0-1 per taxi zone (263 zones [P*, zone lookup]) [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Haggag et al. 2017: neighbourhood-specific experience improves search; novices lose most after drop-offs in difficult areas and at slow times.
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, competitor drivers
variables.data_source: Haggag et al. replication; TLC taxi zone shapefile
variables.how_to_model: For bots, a zone-level search-time multiplier; for the LLM, it emerges from its memory notes.

variables.name: Navigation skill and route efficiency
variables.description: How close the driver's routes are to the fastest route.
variables.values_or_range: 0.95-1.10 x optimal travel time [design]; app navigation by default.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Ashkrof et al. 2020 focus groups: drivers name an 'unreliable navigation algorithm' as a drawback.
variables.how_to_model: Multiplier on travel time when the agent does not choose a route; the route-choice action (R09-061) overrides it.

variables.name: Driving speed and aggressiveness
variables.description: How fast the driver drives relative to traffic, trading time against ticket and crash risk.
variables.values_or_range: -5% to +5% versus flow speed [design]; NYC speed-camera fine about $50 [U].
variables.impact_evidence: [corrected by fact-check: was medium; the 2.2% speed difference explains about half of a 7% gap, i.e. about 3-4% of hourly earnings, similar to R09-028 (low)] [S] Cook et al. 2021: men drive about 2.2% faster, which explains about half of the 7% gender gap in hourly earnings.
variables.how_to_model: Persona speed factor on link travel times; adds ticket and crash hazards.

variables.name: Cross-day memory and learning store
variables.description: Whether, and how much, the agent can save learnings between simulated days.
variables.values_or_range: Off; free-text notes up to N tokens; structured hotspot table; kept across 10 training days, then frozen for the day-11 test.
variables.impact_evidence: [design] team plan: run 10 days 100 times, store learnings, test on day 11; human analogue is learning by driving [S].
variables.how_to_model: Harness gives read_notes and write_note tools with a size budget; compare cold start against warm start.

variables.sub_box: G. Personal safety, preferences and life constraints
variables.name: Personal safety risk by zone and time
variables.description: Chance of robbery, assault or a dangerous rider, which varies by area, hour and cash handling.
variables.values_or_range: Rare, about 1e-5 to 1e-4 events per hour [design]; taxi and limo drivers' violent work deaths 18 per 100,000 per year (2003-13) [uncertain].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] NIOSH via ISHN: 18 per 100,000 taxi and limo drivers (2003-2013); risk factors are cash, working alone and late night; cameras cut homicide rates about sevenfold [uncertain: rate and camera effect from a trade-press summary, not re-checked against NIOSH papers].
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi (cash raises risk)
variables.data_source: NYPD Complaint Data on NYC Open Data [U]; BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries https://www.bls.gov/iif/ [S]
variables.how_to_model: Low-probability incident hazard by zone x hour x cash share; an incident ends the shift. It matters mostly through the persona's avoidance choices.

variables.sub_box: G. Personal safety, preferences and life constraints
variables.name: Avoided areas and hours, and the legality of refusing
variables.description: Areas or times a driver persona will not serve, and the penalty where refusing is illegal.
variables.values_or_range: A list of zones and hours. NYC taxi refusing a destination in NYC, Westchester, Nassau or Newark Airport [corrected by fact-check, 35 RCNY 80-02(e), 80-20, P*]: first offence $350 on a guilty plea or $500 after a hearing; second within 24 months $700 or $1,000 plus possible suspension up to 30 days; third within 36 months licence revocation. After more than 8 h of operation in 24 h a taxi may refuse Newark, Nassau and Westchester (80-20(b)(8)). App drivers may decline before accepting (but see R09-040).
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 80-20, 80-02(e); [S] NBC New York / amNY: outer-borough refusals are illegal; enforcement by complaints, secret shoppers and GPS checks.
variables.how_to_model: Persona blacklist limits repositioning and acceptance; a taxi refusal after a hail draws the tiered fine with complaint probability p.

variables.sub_box: G. Personal safety, preferences and life constraints
variables.name: Trip-length preference
variables.description: Whether the driver favours long trips (airport, out of town) or short quick ones.
variables.values_or_range: Prefers trips over 45 min and airport runs, or short Manhattan hops [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Seattle stated-preference study: trips over 45 min, surge and higher rider ratings raise acceptance; Ashkrof et al. 2022: pickup time is the strongest negative.
variables.data_source: HVFHV trip_miles and trip_time distribution (TLC) [P*, fields verified]
variables.how_to_model: Persona prior for simulated drivers; for the agent it is revealed by accept and decline choices (R09-054).

variables.sub_box: G. Personal safety, preferences and life constraints
variables.name: Language and communication
variables.description: The driver's English and other languages, which affect rapport, ratings, tips and special requests.
variables.values_or_range: English fluent or limited, plus 1-3 other languages; about 92% of NYC licensed drivers born abroad, over 100 languages [uncertain].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] TLC filings: about 92% of licensees foreign-born; licensing tests in English, Spanish, Bengali and Urdu [uncertain: neither re-checked; 'over 90% immigrants' is widely reported (U)]. Effect on tips is a [design] guess.
variables.how_to_model: Small modifier on rating and tip draws when the rider's language matches.

variables.sub_box: G. Personal safety, preferences and life constraints
variables.name: Other job and availability windows
variables.description: Times when the driver cannot drive because of another job or commitment.
variables.values_or_range: e.g. weekdays 09:00-17:00 blocked, weekends free [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Uber 2014 survey: 75% of part-time drivers had other jobs [uncertain: not re-checked]; Chen et al. 2019: the value of the work lies in flexible timing.
variables.how_to_model: Blocked time windows in the persona; the agent must choose the best remaining hours.

variables.sub_box: G. Personal safety, preferences and life constraints
variables.name: Childcare and family constraints
variables.description: Fixed family duties, such as school runs, that split or end the shift.
variables.values_or_range: e.g. 07:30-08:30 and 15:00-16:00 blocked and the driver must be at home [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Cook et al. 2021: part of the earnings gap comes from where and when people can drive (interpretation).
variables.how_to_model: Like R09-035 but with a location: be in the home zone at time t.

variables.sub_box: G. Personal safety, preferences and life constraints
variables.name: Personal running costs
variables.description: The driver's own costs that are not tied to the car: phone, data, mount, food and drinks.
variables.values_or_range: Phone and data $40-100/month; food $10-25/shift [design/U].
variables.impact_evidence: [design] no public NYC survey found; IRS mileage rates cover the car only [U].
variables.how_to_model: Fixed per-shift and per-meal costs deducted from profit.

variables.sub_box: G. Personal safety, preferences and life constraints
variables.name: Demographic persona traits (age, gender)
variables.description: Traits that correlate with when and where people drive and how they handle safety.
variables.values_or_range: Not used directly; vary behaviour through experience, speed and time-place choices instead.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Cook et al. 2021: the 7% male-female hourly gap is explained by experience, speed and where/when people drive; no discrimination by Uber or riders found.
variables.how_to_model: Generate heterogeneity among simulated drivers through behaviour parameters, not protected traits (fairness).

variables.name: Driver rating
variables.description: Average of rider ratings, which can trigger warnings, lost perks or deactivation.
variables.values_or_range: 1-5 stars; average of the last 500 rated trips; city-specific minimum (not published); Uber Pro requires 4.85 or more.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Uber help text: rating is the average of the 500 most recent rated trips, with warnings near the local minimum (matches background knowledge [U]); Uber Pro criteria (Gridwise, Uber UK).
variables.applies_to: human app driver (robotaxi: trip ratings for the fleet)
variables.how_to_model: Each trip draws a rating from the rider model (R05) given wait, route, cleanliness and service; rolling 500-trip mean; thresholds trigger events.

variables.name: Acceptance and cancellation rates
variables.description: Share of offers accepted, and of accepted trips the driver cancels, used for tiers, queues and access.
variables.values_or_range: Acceptance 0-100% (Uber Pro historically 85% or more); cancellation 0-100% (4% or less for Pro; keep under 10%).
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 59D-22(c)(3): an NYC platform may restrict a driver's access without the usual 72 h notice for excessive cancellation or non-acceptance; [S] Uber JFK driver page: declining several requests in a row or cancelling several rides loses your FIFO queue place; under upfront fares, declines reportedly no longer count (Gridwise).
variables.data_source: 35 RCNY 59D-22 via https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive [P*]; platform thresholds none found
variables.how_to_model: Rolling counters; thresholds change tier, airport queue place and (if enabled) access restriction.

variables.name: Loyalty tier (e.g. Uber Pro)
variables.description: Status level earned from points and quality metrics that unlocks perks.
variables.values_or_range: Blue, Gold, Platinum, Diamond; point thresholds vary by city (UK example: 600, 1,100, 1,600).
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Uber Pro UK page; Uber blog: the new Uber Pro lowers Gold criteria and adds a Driving Insights score.
variables.how_to_model: Points per trip with peak multipliers; perks modelled as small pay or priority bonuses.

variables.name: Login access and lockouts
variables.description: Whether the app lets the driver go online at all; NYC platforms restricted this to manage utilization, and since Aug 2025 NYC rules limit it.
variables.values_or_range: Open; restricted by time and zone; priority by acceptance or tier (forum rule of thumb: 90%+ acceptance). [corrected by fact-check: since 1 Aug 2025, 35 RCNY 59D-22(c) (P*) requires 72 h notice before restricting a driver on a calendar day and at least 16 h of access once a driver goes online (restarting after 8 h offline), with exceptions for licensing, rule breaches, misconduct and excessive cancellation or non-acceptance; in-shift lockouts are a 2023-24 replay scenario, not the 2026 default.]
variables.impact_evidence: [corrected by fact-check: was high; the 2025 rule bars in-shift lockouts, so the high effect applies only to a 2023-24 replay] [P*] 35 RCNY 59D-22(c); [S] NYC Comptroller and Documented: Uber and Lyft locked drivers out to raise utilization and lower mandated pay; Uber paused lockouts in Sept 2024 under a deal with the city.
variables.data_source: 35 RCNY 59D-22 via https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive [P*]; TLC utilization data (Data Hub) [S]; no lockout logs public
variables.how_to_model: Scenario toggle; when on (2023-24 replay), the platform admits drivers by a priority score once supply exceeds a utilization target. Default 2026: restrictions announced 72 h ahead, no cut-off within 16 h of going online.

variables.name: Deactivation and compliance risk
variables.description: Risk of losing app access through compliance problems, a low rating or rule breaches.
variables.values_or_range: Uber NYC: 99% of deactivations are compliance-related (e.g. not on the TLC active list, over maximum hours).
variables.impact_evidence: [S] NYC Council transportation committee hearing, 27 Sept 2024 (citymeetings.nyc summary). Rare but ends earnings entirely.
variables.how_to_model: Terminal event if hour caps or the rating minimum are breached repeatedly; ends the run with a large penalty.

variables.sub_box: I. Robotaxi: what replaces the human
variables.name: Robotaxi duty cycle (no fatigue, no breaks)
variables.description: Hours per day a driverless car can stay in service, limited only by charging, cleaning, maintenance and demand.
variables.values_or_range: Up to about 20-22 h/day [design]; depots run 24/7 with three staff shifts. NYC: driverless passenger service is not currently legal (R09-051), so NYC runs are counterfactual.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] WSMV Oct 2026: the Waymo-Lyft Nashville depot runs around the clock with three shifts to charge, clean and maintain hundreds of cars a day.
variables.how_to_model: Replaces the human shift, break and home variables with an availability schedule driven by battery (R08), cleanliness (R09-046) and maintenance windows.

variables.sub_box: I. Robotaxi: what replaces the human
variables.name: Depot locations and capacity
variables.description: Where robotaxis go to charge, be cleaned and park, and how many each depot can serve at once.
variables.values_or_range: 1-5 depots per city [design]; e.g. an SF site with 19 chargers serving 2 cars each; about 70 workers per depot.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Understanding AI (SF depot, 19 dual chargers); Jalopnik (fleet over 3,800 cars, depots of about 70 staff each).
variables.data_source: none public; AFDC stations as proxies https://afdc.energy.gov/stations [U]
variables.how_to_model: Depot nodes with charger and cleaning-bay queues; the deadhead to the depot is unpaid.

variables.sub_box: I. Robotaxi: what replaces the human
variables.name: Interior cleanliness and mess events
variables.description: State of the cabin, and the chance a rider leaves a mess or item that takes the car out of service.
variables.values_or_range: Clean, dirty or unusable; mess chance 0.1-1% per trip, higher late on weekend nights [design]; rider fee $50 if self-reported, $100 if not (Waymo) [uncertain: not re-checkable]; Tesla $50-150.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Waymo One rider rules; Jalopnik on fleet handlers; Dec 2025 reports on Tesla robotaxi fees.
variables.applies_to: robotaxi (human drivers face the same via cleaning fees, R07)
variables.how_to_model: Per-trip mess draw by hour and nearby events, revealed when a rider reports it; a severe mess forces a depot return; the fee partly offsets the loss.

variables.sub_box: I. Robotaxi: what replaces the human
variables.name: Cleaning schedule and dwell time
variables.description: How often each car gets routine cleaning and how long it takes.
variables.values_or_range: Every 8-24 h or every N trips; 10-30 min per clean [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [design] no public cadence found; a 2020 report says Waymo was studying cleaning between rides [S].
variables.how_to_model: Cleanliness decays per trip; cleaning jobs queue at the depot.

variables.sub_box: I. Robotaxi: what replaces the human
variables.name: Remote-assistance request rate and latency
variables.description: How often a robotaxi asks a remote human for guidance, and how long it waits for an answer.
variables.values_or_range: Cruise 2023: a session every 2.5-5 miles per the NYT, every 4-5 miles per Cruise, many brief; Waymo: not disclosed; wait 0-5 min [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] CNBC on the 2023 NYT report (Cruise) and Vogt's reply; TechCrunch Mar 2026: companies refuse to say how often their AVs need remote help.
variables.how_to_model: Poisson events per mile, more in complex zones and at events; each adds a delay that grows when agents are busy (queue).

variables.sub_box: I. Robotaxi: what replaces the human
variables.name: Remote-assistance staffing ratio and cost
variables.description: Remote agents per vehicle and their hourly cost, the main labour cost left in a robotaxi.
variables.values_or_range: Waymo: about 70 agents on duty for about 3,000 cars (about 1:43); Cruise: 1 per 15-20 cars; wage about $15-40/h depending on location [design guess, not sourced] (about half of Waymo's agents are in the Philippines).
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Waymo Senate Commerce testimony, Feb 2026, and its reply to Sen. Markey (Newsweek, Axios, GovTech); CNBC 2023 for Cruise.
variables.how_to_model: Fleet cost = agents x hourly wage; fewer agents lengthen remote-assistance waits (R09-048).

variables.sub_box: I. Robotaxi: what replaces the human
variables.name: Stuck vehicle and field recovery
variables.description: Events where a robotaxi stops safely but cannot continue and needs a field team.
variables.values_or_range: About 0.1-1 per 1,000 vehicle-hours; recovery 20-90 min; spikes during blackouts and big events [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [design]; public incidents belong to R03.
variables.data_source: none found (California DMV and CPUC AV reports as a proxy [U])
variables.how_to_model: Hazard per hour by zone; the car is out of service until a recovery team arrives.

variables.sub_box: I. Robotaxi: what replaces the human
variables.name: Safety-operator requirement
variables.description: Whether local rules require a human operator on board, which brings back a wage and human limits.
variables.values_or_range: None, or required. NYC [corrected by fact-check: was 'reportedly [U]']: 34 RCNY 4-17(d)(4) (added 7 Sep 2021) requires a trained test vehicle operator in the driver's seat of every AV tested in NYC, plus a $5,000/yr permit and $5M of insurance [P*]. Waymo's NYC test permit (Aug 2025, 8 cars, no paying riders) expired 31 Mar 2026 and there is no commercial pathway [S, via R01/R06/R07], so a NYC robotaxi is a counterfactual.
variables.impact_evidence: [corrected by fact-check: was medium; when on (the NYC legal default) it adds a full driver wage plus shift and fatigue limits to every car-hour] [P*] 34 RCNY 4-17(d)(4); [S] TechCrunch Aug 2025 and West Side Spirit 2026 on the Waymo permit.
variables.applies_to: robotaxi (NYC; most other cities allow driverless service under state rules)
variables.data_source: 34 RCNY 4-17 via https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive [P*]; NYC DOT AV testing permit programme [U]
variables.how_to_model: If on, the robotaxi carries a driver wage plus the shift and fatigue rules from the human sections.

variables.name: Wait, cruise or park
variables.description: After a drop-off, stay put, cruise for street hails, or park at a staging spot to wait for app offers.
variables.values_or_range: Wait in place; cruise a loop; park at a chosen spot.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Buchholz 2022 REStud 89(2): NYC taxis compete by choosing where to search; search frictions leave about 53,000 customers per weekday unserved [uncertain: the 53,000 figure not re-checkable].
variables.data_source: TLC yellow and green trip records (pickup density by zone and hour)
variables.how_to_model: Action on each idle tick; cruising costs fuel and raises the street-hail encounter rate; parking costs time and may risk a ticket.

variables.name: Reposition to a target zone
variables.description: Drive empty to another zone expected to be busier.
variables.values_or_range: Any of 263 taxi zones [P*]; 5-45 min of travel.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Lu, Frazier & Kislev 2018 (ACM EC): seeing the surge heat map changes where drivers go and what they earn; Ashkrof et al. 2022 relocation study.
variables.data_source: HVFHV request_datetime by zone (demand) [P*, field verified]; TLC taxi zone shapefile
variables.how_to_model: Action reposition(zone); travel time from R10; offers can arrive on the way.

variables.name: Accept or decline an offer
variables.description: Take or skip an app trip offer given pickup time, pay, destination and rider rating.
variables.values_or_range: Accept or decline within about 15 s [U]; offer shows pickup ETA, pay and destination (upfront fares).
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Ashkrof et al. 2022: pickup time is the strongest negative factor; surge is valued at $0.50-0.71 per minute of pickup [uncertain: not re-checked]; Uber's 2022 upfront fares show pay and destination before accepting.
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi e-hail, robotaxi dispatch
variables.data_source: HVFHV request-to-pickup gaps (TLC; request_datetime, on_scene_datetime, pickup_datetime [P*])
variables.how_to_model: Offer event with a timeout; a decline passes the offer to the next driver and updates the acceptance rate (R09-040).

variables.name: Cancel after accepting, and no-show wait
variables.description: Cancel an accepted trip, or decide how long to wait for a rider who does not appear.
variables.values_or_range: Wait 2-5+ min before a no-show cancel; fees per R07. Taxi: not serving an accepted e-hail counts as a refusal (35 RCNY 80-20(a)(5)) [P*].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Uber Pro cancellation limit of 4%; Uber JFK page: cancelling several rides loses your queue place; [P*] 35 RCNY 59D-22(c)(3) allows NYC access restriction for excessive cancellation.
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi e-hail, robotaxi
variables.data_source: none found (public TLC files hold no cancellations)
variables.how_to_model: Actions cancel_trip and wait_for_rider(max_min); rider arrival time drawn from R05; no-show fee paid after the threshold.

variables.name: Platform choice and multi-apping
variables.description: Which apps to be online on, and which offer to take when several arrive.
variables.values_or_range: Uber, Lyft, both, or taxi with e-hail apps.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Tyler Technologies on TLC data: a rising share of drivers work for 2-3 platforms [uncertain: not re-checked; R06 uses Gridwise's national panel: about 55% of Lyft drivers also on Uber and 25% of Uber drivers also on Lyft, Q1 2024 (S)]; 2018 press: drivers switch apps to get around one app's hour cap.
variables.data_source: TLC HVFHV (hvfhs_license_num splits Uber HV0003 and Lyft HV0005) [P*, verified in schema]
variables.how_to_model: Agent toggles apps; each platform has its own offer stream, rules and counters; one trip at a time.

variables.name: Airport queue: join, stay or leave
variables.description: Whether to drive to JFK, LGA or EWR and wait in the queue for a long airport fare.
variables.values_or_range: Queue wait 0-3+ h (JFK taxi hold lot historically 2-3 h); Uber runs a virtual FIFO queue in staging lots; lot caps vary by demand; short-trip priority passes. Taxis may not cruise for fares at JFK, LGA or EWR and must use the feed line; a taxi driver taking relief time must park in the holding area and rejoin the end of the line (35 RCNY 80-19(a)(4), (e)(2)) [P*].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Queens DA case and press: JFK taxi hold-lot waits average 2-3 h; Uber JFK driver page: virtual FIFO, and you lose your place if you go offline, leave the zone, or decline or cancel repeatedly; [P*] 35 RCNY 80-19(e).
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, robotaxi fleet
variables.data_source: TLC trip records airport_fee and zones 1 (EWR), 132 (JFK), 138 (LGA) [P*, verified in zone lookup and schema]; Uber JFK driver info https://www.uber.com/global/en/r/airports/jfk/driver-information/ [S]
variables.how_to_model: A queue per airport fed by flight arrivals (R03); the agent sees its position and expected wait (hidden in a hard mode); leaving for a break sends a taxi to the back of the line.

variables.name: Take a break (when, what, where)
variables.description: Choose the timing, type (meal, bathroom, prayer, rest) and place of breaks.
variables.values_or_range: 5-60 min; any zone.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Meal peaks and relief-stand scarcity (R09-010 to R09-014); [design] breaks placed in demand troughs cost little.
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, fleet (stagger breaks across cars)
variables.how_to_model: Action take_break(type, minutes, zone); resets the matching timers.

variables.name: Refuel or charge (when and where)
variables.description: Choose when and where to refuel or charge, trading downtime against range and price.
variables.values_or_range: Gas 5-10 min; EV fast charge 20-45 min; home charging overnight (details R08).
variables.impact_evidence: [S] E-taxi trajectory studies note drivers switch GPS off during breaks such as lunch near chargers; details in R08.
variables.data_source: AFDC stations https://afdc.energy.gov/stations ; EIA fuel prices (R08)
variables.how_to_model: Action refuel_or_charge(station); combining it with a meal break saves time.

variables.name: Go home and use the destination filter
variables.description: Decide when to head home and whether to spend a destination-filter use (app) or go off duty on route home (taxi) to earn on the way.
variables.values_or_range: 0-2 filter uses per day (Uber); start time of the home run; taxi on-route-home pickups (35 RCNY 80-19(a)(5)) [P*].
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Uber allows 2 filter uses per day; drivers report slower matching with the filter on; [P*] taxi garage/home return rule.
variables.applies_to: human app driver, taxi, fleet (each car)
variables.how_to_model: Action set_destination(zone); the matcher restricts offers until home is reached.

variables.name: Route choice
variables.description: Pick the route for a trip or reposition: fastest, shortest, or avoiding tolls and the CBD charge.
variables.values_or_range: App route or 2-3 alternatives; taxis must take the 'shortest reasonable route' unless the passenger asks otherwise (35 RCNY 80-16(a)) [P*], so detours on metered trips are illegal.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] MIT study: metered taxi airport trips about 7.4% longer than optimal; Tang 2018: detours when paid by distance; 2010 TLC case of 1.8 million overcharged trips [corrected by fact-check: that case was meter-rate fraud (drivers set the higher out-of-city rate code), not route detours (U)].
variables.data_source: NYC DOT traffic speeds; OpenStreetMap (R10); 35 RCNY 80-16 [P*]
variables.how_to_model: Offer 2-3 route options with ETA, tolls and distance; detours on metered trips raise the fare but risk complaints, fines and lower ratings.

variables.name: Chase surge or not
variables.description: Drive toward an area showing surge pricing.
variables.values_or_range: Chase or ignore; surges often last under 10 min (2015).
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Chen, Mislove & Wilson 2015 (SF and Manhattan): most surges last under 10 min and often end before drivers arrive; Uber says surge does attract drivers.
variables.how_to_model: Surge map in the observation with a short half-life; arriving after it ends pays normal fares.

variables.name: Street-hail choices and the off-duty light (taxi)
variables.description: Which hailing passengers to stop for and when to switch on the off-duty light, within anti-refusal rules.
variables.values_or_range: Stop or pass; off-duty on or off. To refuse legally a taxi must be ending its shift or going for repairs, logged off with both rear doors locked (35 RCNY 80-20(b)(5)-(6)) [P*]; while returning to the garage or home it may take only riders going directly along its route (80-19(a)(5)) [P*].
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 80-20 and 80-02(e): refusing in-city destinations is illegal (fines $350-1,000, revocation on a third offence within 36 months); [S] enforcement through complaints and secret shoppers.
variables.data_source: 35 RCNY 80-19, 80-20 via https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive [P*]; NYC 311 taxi complaints [U]; yellow and green trip records
variables.how_to_model: Hail encounters while cruising; passing a hailer while on duty may draw a refusal fine with low probability; an on-route-home mode filters hails by direction.

variables.name: Rider interaction and service style
variables.description: How the agent responds to riders: greeting, small talk, help with bags, music, route requests, complaints.
variables.values_or_range: Free-text or menu replies [design].
variables.impact_evidence: [design] tips and ratings depend on service (R05).
variables.applies_to: all (robotaxi through remote support or in-car chat)
variables.how_to_model: Scripted rider messages; replies scored by a rubric that shifts rating and tip draws slightly.

variables.name: Rate or block riders
variables.description: Rate riders and optionally avoid being matched with them again.
variables.values_or_range: 1-5 stars; a low rating blocks future matches [U].
variables.impact_evidence: [U] Uber lets drivers avoid re-matching with riders they rate low; CBS: Uber planned to ban low-rated riders [S].
variables.how_to_model: Optional; matters mostly for repeat riders in long runs.

variables.name: Ride-type opt-ins
variables.description: Opt in or out of shared rides, wheelchair-accessible requests, scheduled rides or larger and premium tiers.
variables.values_or_range: On or off per product; WAV needs an accessible vehicle.
variables.impact_evidence: [P*] HVFHV files carry shared_request_flag, shared_match_flag, wav_request_flag, wav_match_flag and access_a_ride_flag (schema in toddwschneider/nyc-taxi-data; re-verified).
variables.how_to_model: Product filters on the offer stream; opting out lowers the offer rate.

variables.name: Information gathering
variables.description: Whether to spend steps or tool calls checking events, weather, news and traffic before deciding.
variables.values_or_range: None, event calendar, weather forecast, news feed; a tool-call budget.
variables.impact_evidence: [design] team plan to test with and without public event information.
variables.data_source: Event calendars, NOAA forecasts (R03, R04, R12)
variables.how_to_model: Tools that cost simulated minutes or tokens; the harness logs their use.

variables.name: Write and use memory notes
variables.description: What the agent records about hotspots, timing and mistakes for later days.
variables.values_or_range: Notes per day within a size budget.
variables.impact_evidence: [design] 10-day learning protocol; human analogue is learning by driving [S Haggag et al.]. High for the learning evaluation.
variables.how_to_model: write_note tool; notes are injected the next day; measure the gain on day 11.

variables.name: Robotaxi fleet-ops decisions
variables.description: Send a car to the depot, clean it, charge it, take it out of service or hold it in reserve.
variables.values_or_range: Per car, per tick.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Depot operations reporting (Waymo-Lyft Nashville; SF depot).
variables.how_to_model: Fleet actions mapped to depot queues; time out of service earns nothing.

variables.name: Follow or ignore platform nudges
variables.description: Whether to follow app heat maps, 'go here' prompts or demand forecasts.
variables.values_or_range: Follow, ignore, or follow in part.
variables.impact_evidence: [S] Ashkrof et al. 2020: drivers name 'misleading guidance' as a main drawback; Lu et al. 2018: the heat map changes relocation.
variables.how_to_model: Platform nudge in the observation with configurable accuracy and bias (the platform wants supply, not driver profit).

variables.name: Time-dependent link speed profile
variables.description: Typical speed on each road segment for each time bucket of the week; the base layer from which every travel time is computed.
variables.values_or_range: Manhattan south of 60th St 9.1 mph (2010) to 7.1 mph (2017) [S]; 2023 yellow trips within Manhattan below 60th St: weekday 6.8-7.6 mph from 9 AM to 6 PM, 8.5 mph at 8 AM [P*: own analysis of 38.3M TLC 2023 yellow trips]; CBD 8.2 to 9.7 mph after Jan 2025 [uncertain: 8.2 to 9.7 mph is +18%, not the +15% headline, and the mph pair could not be traced to the NBER paper]; overnight local streets ~15-25 mph [corrected by fact-check: TLC trip-average speeds at 0-5 AM are 11.6-13.6 mph within Manhattan below 60th St (yellow 2023) and about 20-25 mph citywide including highways (HVFHV Jan 2023); 15-25 mph fits the outer boroughs, not Manhattan]; expressways 30-50 mph off-peak [U]; 2016 five-minute buckets per week (Valhalla [P]) or 168 hourly buckets
variables.impact_evidence: NYC DOT Mobility Report 2018: speeds south of 60th St fell 9.1 to 7.1 mph 2010-2017; trip time is the denominator of $/hour [S]; TLC 2023 trip speeds reproduce ~7 mph daytime [P*]
variables.data_source: NYC TLC trip records https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page ; NYC DOT Traffic Speeds NBE https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Transportation/DOT-Traffic-Speeds-NBE/i4gi-tjb9 ; MTA Bus Route Segment Speeds https://data.ny.gov/d/58t6-89vi
variables.how_to_model: Per-edge weekly speed profile (Valhalla predicted-speed format) or road-class x zone x hour-of-week multipliers on OSM free-flow speeds, calibrated so zone-pair durations match TLC.

variables.name: Core-versus-periphery speed gradient
variables.description: How much slower the dense core (Midtown, Lower Manhattan) is than the rest of Manhattan and the outer boroughs at the same hour.
variables.values_or_range: Midtown ~4.3-5 mph vs Manhattan south of 60th St ~6.9-7.1 mph (2017-2019) [S]; HVFHV Jan 2023 weekday 9 AM-6 PM trip speeds (both trip ends inside the area): Midtown core (zones 100, 161-164, 186, 230) 5.4-6.0 mph, Manhattan below 60th St 8.2-8.5 mph, citywide 12.3-15.1 mph [P*]; outer-borough arterials ~10-20 mph daytime [U]; core/citywide speed ratio 0.37-0.45 measured, ~0.3-0.6 as a design range [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: Sam Schwartz report from taxi+FHV GPS: Midtown 4.8 mph vs Manhattan below 60th St 6.9 mph [S]
variables.data_source: TLC trip records + taxi zone shapefile; MTA CBD Taxi and FHV Speeds (beginning Oct 2019) https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/mta-central-business-district-vehicle-speeds-beginning-october-2019 [uncertain: dataset title and URL not re-checked]
variables.how_to_model: Zone-level speed multiplier by hour fitted from TLC intra- and inter-zone trip speeds; creates the core trade-off of high demand vs slow trips.

variables.name: Peak-hour slowdown curve
variables.description: Shape of the within-day speed curve (AM peak, midday plateau, PM peak, late-night free flow) applied to travel times.
variables.values_or_range: Midtown to JFK median 38 min (10-11 AM) vs 64 min (4-5 PM) in 2009-2015 [S] [corrected by fact-check: 2023 TLC yellow weekday trips from the Midtown core to JFK took a median 29 min at 3-5 AM, 54 min at 10-11 AM and 75 min at 4-5 PM (P*); the 38-min figure is not reproduced and may reflect an older era or another hour]; CBD worst on weekdays 1-7 PM [S]; core Manhattan 8-9 AM ~9 mph (14.5 km/h) [S; consistent with 8.5-8.8 mph in TLC 2023 data, P*]; overnight ~1.5-3x faster than midday [corrected by fact-check: 1.6-2.2x in TLC 2023 data, e.g. Manhattan below 60th St 13.6 mph at 4 AM vs 6.8 mph at noon, Midtown core 11.8 vs 5.4 mph, P*]
variables.impact_evidence: Schneider analysis of TLC taxi trips 2009-2015: Midtown to JFK median 38 vs 64 min depending on hour [S]; TLC 2023 yellow trips: 29-75 min by hour [P*]
variables.data_source: TLC trip records; NYC DOT Traffic Speeds NBE (i4gi-tjb9)
variables.how_to_model: Hour-of-week multiplier per zone pair or edge class; the calendar that indexes it lives in R02.

variables.name: Day-type and seasonal speed shifts
variables.description: Speed differences between weekdays, weekends, holidays, summer and the December shopping season, including official Gridlock Alert Days.
variables.values_or_range: 20 Gridlock Alert Days in 2025 (UNGA week 22-26 Sep; 19, 20, 25 Nov; 12 days in Dec) [S]; Midtown under 4 mph in UNGA week [S]; weekend mornings and holiday weeks faster [U]; TLC 2023 check: weekday daytime speed within Manhattan below 60th St fell from 8.3 mph (Jan) to 6.5 mph (Sep, Dec), a ~22% seasonal swing, and the slowest weekdays were 18-20 Sep (UNGA week), 21 and 29 Nov and 5-7 Dec [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: NYC DOT 2025 Gridlock Alert Days announcement: Midtown average speeds fell under 4 mph during UNGA [S]
variables.data_source: NYC DOT Gridlock Alert Days https://nyc.gov/gridlockalert ; TLC trip records by date
variables.how_to_model: Day-type factor (weekday / Sat / Sun / holiday / gridlock-alert) multiplying the weekly profile; gridlock days flagged in the scenario calendar.

variables.name: Congestion-pricing speed regime (since 5 Jan 2025)
variables.description: The step change in speeds inside and around the Manhattan Congestion Relief Zone after tolling began, which shifts all calibrated travel times.
variables.values_or_range: CBD speeds +15% vs synthetic control [S] (8.2 to 9.7 mph [uncertain: implies +18%, source not traced]; a later paper version reportedly +11% [uncertain: not re-read]); >20% gains weekday 1-7 PM; trips to/within CBD ~8% faster; 2025 vs 2024 AM-peak crossing times: Holland -36%, Williamsburg -23%, Queensboro -21%, Hugh Carey -16%, Brooklyn Br -13%, Lincoln -10% (some reposts -5%) [uncertain: conflicting secondary figures], Queens-Midtown -4%
variables.impact_evidence: Cook et al. NBER w33584 (Google Maps data, synthetic control vs 5 cities) [S]; NY Governor release 9 Sep 2025 [S]
variables.data_source: NBER w33584 https://www.nber.org/papers/w33584 ; MTA Congestion Relief Zone entries dashboard (data.ny.gov) [uncertain: exact dataset not re-checked]; TLC 2025+ trip records (HVFHV files carry a cbd_congestion_fee column, so post-pricing trips are identifiable [P*])
variables.how_to_model: Calibrate speed profiles on post-Jan-2025 trips for current scenarios; keep a pre-2025 profile as a separate regime for historical or counterfactual scenarios.

variables.name: Weather-to-speed coupling
variables.description: The multiplier by which rain, snow, fog and extreme heat change link speeds and incident rates (the weather itself is R04).
variables.values_or_range: light rain -5 to -10%, heavy rain -10 to -25%, snow -15 to -40% on arterials [U] [uncertain: no NYC source; a fact-check on 2023 data found no daily slowdown: the weekday speed factor within Manhattan below 60th St (vs same month and hour) had a median of 0.99 on dry days, 1.00 on days with 0.25-0.99 in of rain and 1.07 on the eight days with 1 in or more, including the 29 Sep flood at 0.99 (P*); hourly and heavy-snow effects are untested because 2023 had almost no snow]; higher crash rate in rain [U]
variables.impact_evidence: [impact corrected by fact-check: medium to low] FHWA road-weather guidance reports double-digit arterial speed and travel-time penalties in rain and snow [U]; TLC 2023 yellow trips joined to NOAA Central Park daily data show no daily rain slowdown in Manhattan [P*]; weather's main profit effect runs through demand (R04, R05)
variables.data_source: NOAA hourly observations for Central Park (see R04) joined to TLC trip speeds
variables.how_to_model: Regress zone-hour TLC trip speed on NOAA precipitation and snow; apply the fitted multiplier on top of the weekly profile.

variables.name: Endogenous congestion from ride-hail volume
variables.description: Feedback whereby the simulated fleet's own vehicles, and FHV traffic overall, slow the streets they use.
variables.values_or_range: FHVs ~30% of Manhattan-core traffic (2019); SF weekday delay +62% 2010-2016 vs +22% counterfactual without TNCs; a benchmark fleet of 1-500 cars is tiny vs NYC's tens of thousands of FHVs [U]
variables.impact_evidence: Erhardt et al. 2019 Science Advances [S]; TLC 23 Jul 2019 presentation [S]
variables.data_source: none needed for small N; TLC FHV trip volumes for background
variables.how_to_model: Ignore for N up to ~1,000; for stretch scenarios add fleet vehicles to zone-level background volume and apply a BPR-style volume-delay function.

variables.name: Trip-level travel-time noise
variables.description: Random deviation of a realised trip time from its expected time for the same origin, destination and departure time.
variables.values_or_range: multiplicative lognormal with CV ~0.15-0.35 [design] [corrected by fact-check: TLC 2023 weekday zone-pair x hour cells (54k cells, 23M trips) give CV median 0.28 (P10 0.20, P90 0.46) and sd(log) median 0.26; sd(log) is 0.41 for trips under 1.5 mi, 0.29 at 1.5-3 mi, 0.23 at 3-6 mi and 0.21 above 6 mi; these include within-zone address spread, so they are upper bounds on traffic noise (P*)]; Midtown to JFK 4-5 PM P90 84 min vs median 64 (+31%) in 2009-2015 [S]; 2023: P90 94 vs median 75 min (+26%), daytime P90/median 1.26-1.33 [P*]; buffer index 20-60% on unreliable arterials [uncertain: no source given]
variables.impact_evidence: Schneider TLC airport analysis: P90/median about 1.3 [S]; FHWA buffer-index definition (95th pct vs mean) [S]; TLC 2023 dispersion analysis [P*]
variables.data_source: TLC trip records (dispersion of durations per zone pair x hour)
variables.how_to_model: Fit quantiles per zone pair x hour from TLC; realised time = expected x lognormal(0, sigma_zone,hour), seeded identically across models.

variables.name: Day-level and area-level correlated slowdowns
variables.description: Shared shocks that make a whole day or area slower than typical, so errors on consecutive trips are correlated rather than independent.
variables.values_or_range: day factor 0.8-1.25 [design; confirmed by TLC 2023: weekday daily speed factor within Manhattan below 60th St P5-P95 0.82-1.20, P1-P99 0.77-1.23, extremes 0.75 on 6 Dec and 1.40 on 3 Jul (bridge day), P*]; zone-hour factor 0.85-1.2 [design]; extremes on gridlock and storm days (the slowest 2023 weekdays were UNGA week and early December) [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: [design] correlated shocks are what make a learnt 'today is slow' signal valuable; independent noise averages out; TLC 2023 day-level spread [P*]
variables.data_source: TLC trip records (day-to-day variance of zone-hour medians)
variables.how_to_model: Hierarchical noise: realised = typical x day_factor x zone_hour_factor x trip_noise, with AR(1) persistence within the day.

variables.name: Airport-corridor tail risk
variables.description: Heavy right tail of trip times to and from JFK, LGA and EWR via the Van Wyck, Grand Central Parkway, BQE and Hudson crossings.
variables.values_or_range: Midtown to JFK median 38-64 min by hour, P90 up to 84 min (2009-2015) [S] [corrected by fact-check: 2023 weekday Midtown core to JFK median 29-75 min, P90 up to 94 min at 4-5 PM]; LGA ~20-50 min [U] [corrected by fact-check: 2023 Midtown core to LGA median 21 min (3-5 AM) to 44 min (4 PM), P90 up to 60 min; to EWR median 30 min (night) to 54 min (3-7 PM), P90 76 min; all P*]
variables.impact_evidence: Schneider TLC airport analysis [S]; TLC 2023 yellow trips by hour [P*]
variables.data_source: TLC trip records (taxi zones 132 JFK, 138 LGA, 1 EWR)
variables.how_to_model: Separate per-corridor duration distributions with fatter tails (lognormal mixture) fitted on airport zone pairs.

variables.name: Reliability information given to the agent
variables.description: Whether the agent sees only an expected travel time or also a spread (P10-P90) for candidate trips and moves.
variables.values_or_range: none / mean only / mean + P90 / full distribution
variables.impact_evidence: [design] lets the benchmark test risk-aware choices such as late-shift airport runs
variables.data_source: derived from the R10-008 noise model
variables.how_to_model: Harness flag controlling the ETA object returned in observations.

variables.name: Signal delay and cycle length
variables.description: Average waiting time added at signalised intersections, set by cycle length and green split.
variables.values_or_range: Manhattan avenue cycles ~90 s (2008 field note); ~10-40 s mean delay per signal [U]; ~20 short blocks per mile north-south [U]; OSRM's default car profile adds only 2 s per tagged traffic signal [P]
variables.impact_evidence: Blog field note: Manhattan avenues timed in sequence, cycle ~90 s [S]; NACTO cites 60-90 s cycles [S]
variables.data_source: NYC Open Data 'VZV Signal Timing/25MPH Signal Retiming' https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/vzv_signal-timing ; OSM highway=traffic_signals
variables.how_to_model: Implicit in calibrated speeds for v1; optional node penalty = f(cycle, approach class) in a graph engine.

variables.name: Directional progression (avenue green waves vs crosstown)
variables.description: Avenues run coordinated signal progressions while crosstown streets do not, so north-south travel is much faster than east-west in Manhattan.
variables.values_or_range: Avenues historically progressed at ~25-30 mph, retimed to 25 mph under Vision Zero; 3rd Ave 60th-96th St retimed to 15 mph in 2025 (one of 16 green waves citywide) [uncertain: segment and count not re-read]; Midtown crosstown 4.2-4.8 mph (2002)
variables.impact_evidence: NY1 Feb 2025 on 3rd Ave retiming [S]; NYC DOT THRU Streets document: Midtown crosstown 4.8 EB / 4.2 WB mph [S]
variables.data_source: VZV signal timing dataset; TLC trips (compare north-south vs east-west zone pairs)
variables.how_to_model: Direction-dependent speed factor by edge bearing and class (avenue vs street) in Manhattan, calibrated on TLC.

variables.name: Right-on-red ban
variables.description: NYC prohibits right turns on red unless a sign allows it, adding signal wait to right turns.
variables.values_or_range: banned citywide by default: turns on red only where a sign authorises them (34 RCNY 4-03(a)(3)(ii)) [P*]; 336 signed exceptions in 2019 (Manhattan 6, Staten Island 198) [S]
variables.impact_evidence: 34 RCNY 4-03 [P*]; NY1 2019 count of right-on-red locations [S]
variables.how_to_model: Right turns at signals carry red-phase wait (no free right) in a graph engine; NYC-specific since most US cities allow it.

variables.name: One-way grid and turn restrictions
variables.description: One-way streets, left-turn bans, no-U-turn rules and through-movement bans that lengthen paths relative to straight-line distance.
variables.values_or_range: most Manhattan streets one-way; left turns off 14th St banned at all hours [S]; OSRM default turn penalty up to 7.5 s and U-turn 20 s [corrected by fact-check: 7.5 s is the maximum of an angle-based sigmoid, and turns across oncoming traffic add up to 2 s more, P]; U-turns banned in business districts (34 RCNY 4-05(b)) [P*]; network detour factor ~1.2-1.4 vs grid distance [U]
variables.impact_evidence: NYC DOT 14th Street rules [S]; OSRM car.lua defaults [P]
variables.data_source: OpenStreetMap (oneway, restriction relations) via Geofabrik New York extract https://download.geofabrik.de/north-america/us/new-york.html
variables.how_to_model: Edge-based routing graph with turn restrictions and turn costs (native in OSRM and Valhalla).

variables.name: Wrong-side approach and around-the-block loop
variables.description: Extra time when the vehicle arrives on the wrong side or direction of a one-way street for a pickup or drop-off and must circle the block.
variables.values_or_range: 1-6 min in Midtown; under 1 min on two-way outer-borough streets [design]
variables.impact_evidence: [design] follows from the one-way grid and long Midtown blocks; Uber reports opposite-side meetings often fail [S]
variables.data_source: OSM one-way graph; no empirical loop-time data found
variables.how_to_model: Snap pickup to a curb side and route to that side with turn costs; the loop time emerges from graph routing.

variables.name: Busways and through-traffic bans
variables.description: Corridors where cars may only make local trips, such as the 14th Street busway where only buses and trucks may go through from 6 AM to 10 PM.
variables.values_or_range: 14th St 3rd-9th Ave: through trips banned 6 AM-10 PM, must turn at the next right, pickups and drop-offs allowed, camera enforced; open to all 10 PM-6 AM
variables.impact_evidence: NYC DOT 14th Street Busway page [S]; 34 RCNY 4-12(m)(2): in busway hours only buses and Access-A-Ride vehicles may drive in a busway except where signs allow (truck and local access are sign-based) [P*]
variables.how_to_model: Time-conditional edge access that only allows entry when the destination or next right turn is on the corridor; OSRM evaluates conditional restrictions at one timestamp per osrm-customize run (--parse-conditionals-from-now) [P], so time windows need one dataset per bucket or a router with time-aware access such as Valhalla.

variables.name: Car-free and pedestrianised streets
variables.description: Park drives, Open Streets and plazas closed to cars at certain times, which removes links from the network.
variables.values_or_range: Central Park and Prospect Park drives car-free [U]; Open Streets windows vary by block [U]; Open Streets with 'limited local access' still allow pick-up and drop-off, 'full closure' does not (34 RCNY 4-21) [P*]; Broadway plazas closed permanently [U]
variables.impact_evidence: [U] small in network terms but blocks familiar shortcuts
variables.data_source: NYC Open Data Open Streets locations [U]; OSM
variables.how_to_model: Time-conditional edge closures loaded from a closures table.

variables.name: Turning delay from pedestrians
variables.description: Delay to turning vehicles that yield to heavy crosswalk volumes and leading pedestrian intervals, especially in Midtown.
variables.values_or_range: 5-30 s per turn at busy Midtown corners [design]
variables.impact_evidence: [design] a known contributor to Midtown slowness; no public NYC measurement found
variables.how_to_model: Zone-hour turn-penalty multiplier in a graph engine; otherwise implicit in calibrated speeds.

variables.name: River-crossing chokepoint delay
variables.description: Queue delay at bridges and tunnels into Manhattan and between boroughs, which dominates many inter-borough trip times.
variables.values_or_range: Holland Tunnel inbound 12 min 48 s (Jan 2024) vs 4 min 27 s (8 Jan 2025); AM-peak crossing times 4-36% lower in 2025; RPA cites >20 min saved via Lincoln Tunnel
variables.impact_evidence: MTA figures via City & State (Jan 2025) and Governor release (Sep 2025) [S]
variables.data_source: Congestion Pricing Tracker (Google Maps every 15 min, 19 routes); TLC trip records; NYC DOT Traffic Speeds NBE
variables.how_to_model: Dedicated chokepoint edges with hour-of-week delay curves plus stochastic queue shocks.

variables.name: Free vs tolled crossing choice
variables.description: Choice between toll-free East River bridges and tolled tunnels or bridges, trading time for money.
variables.values_or_range: free: Queensboro, Williamsburg, Manhattan, Brooklyn bridges; tolled: Queens-Midtown and Hugh Carey tunnels, RFK, Verrazzano, Hudson crossings [U]; toll amounts in R07
variables.impact_evidence: [U] whether the rider or driver pays the toll decides if avoidance pays; see R07
variables.data_source: MTA Bridges & Tunnels and PANYNJ toll schedules (R07); OSM toll=yes
variables.how_to_model: Route options with generalised cost = time x value of time + toll x payer share; agent picks a route or a preference.

variables.name: Highway versus local-street speed gap
variables.description: Speed difference between expressways (FDR, West Side Hwy, BQE, LIE, Van Wyck, Major Deegan) and surface streets, which drives route choice on longer trips.
variables.values_or_range: expressways ~30-50 mph off-peak, can drop under 15 mph in peaks [U]; Manhattan surface streets 5-10 mph daytime
variables.impact_evidence: NYC DOT real-time speed feed covers mainly highways and major arterials, updated several times a minute [S]
variables.how_to_model: Road-class-specific weekly profiles: expressways from the DOT feed, surface streets from TLC calibration.

variables.name: Robotaxi freeway access and route restrictions
variables.description: Whether the robotaxi may use expressways and which streets or maneuvers its operating domain excludes, which can make trips much longer.
variables.values_or_range: Waymo freeway rides began 12 Nov 2025 in SF, LA, Phoenix for some riders, only when 'meaningfully faster', up to 50% shorter; 2024 LA test: Waymo 33 min 58 s vs 15 min 20 s for Uber/Lyft (~2.2x) [uncertain: a single-trip media test, not a representative ratio]
variables.impact_evidence: TechCrunch and Axios, Nov 2025 [S]; Forbes LA comparison via secondary coverage [S]
variables.data_source: Waymo announcements; none for NYC (Aug 2025 permit was testing only: up to 8 cars, safety driver, no passengers [S]); 34 RCNY 4-17 requires an NYC DOT test permit ($5,000 a year) with a trained test operator in the driver's seat and approved areas and hours [P*]
variables.how_to_model: Per-vehicle-type edge mask (no motorway, excluded zones) and maneuver penalties in the routing profile.

variables.name: Overnight and weekend lane closures
variables.description: Planned construction lane closures that cut capacity at night and on weekends on expressways and crossings.
variables.values_or_range: typically ~10 PM-5 AM weeknights plus some weekend full closures [U]
variables.impact_evidence: [U] 511NY lists construction events statewide
variables.data_source: 511NY developer API (key required, 10 calls per 60 s) https://511ny.org/developers/doc
variables.how_to_model: Replay historical 511NY construction events as capacity reductions on matching edges.

variables.name: Crash incidents and lane-blockage delay
variables.description: Random crashes and breakdowns that block lanes and create queues lasting tens of minutes.
variables.values_or_range: NYPD crash table ~1.7M records Jul 2012-May 2021 [S] (~190k reportable crashes a year [corrected by fact-check: that is the 2012-2021 average; pre-2020 years ran ~200-230k and 2020s years ~100k, U]); expressway blockages 15-60 min [U]; capacity cut 30-70% per blocked lane [U]
variables.impact_evidence: NYPD Motor Vehicle Collisions dataset size [S]
variables.data_source: NYPD Motor Vehicle Collisions - Crashes https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Public-Safety/Motor-Vehicle-Collisions-Crashes/h9gi-nx95 ; 511NY incidents
variables.how_to_model: Poisson incident generator by road class x hour x weather fitted to NYPD crashes; each incident cuts speeds on nearby edges for a lognormal duration.

variables.name: Planned street closures
variables.description: Permitted closures for construction, film shoots and street fairs that remove curb lanes or whole blocks on specific days.
variables.values_or_range: dozens of active closures citywide on a typical day [U]
variables.impact_evidence: [U] mostly local detours; matters more for pickup feasibility than for speed
variables.data_source: NYC Open Data street-closure and film-permit datasets [U]; NYC DOT weekly traffic advisories
variables.how_to_model: Load closures by date as edge or curb closures in the scenario.

variables.name: Event and VIP traffic closures
variables.description: Road closures and spill-over congestion from parades, marathons, UNGA motorcades and presidential visits; the events themselves are R03.
variables.values_or_range: UNGA week Midtown under 4 mph; parade or marathon route closures 6-12 h [U]
variables.impact_evidence: NYC DOT 2025 Gridlock Alert statement on UNGA speeds [S]
variables.data_source: NYC DOT gridlock alerts; NYC event permits (R03)
variables.how_to_model: Event objects carry a closure polygon, a time window and a surrounding speed multiplier.

variables.name: Incident information latency
variables.description: Delay between an incident happening and the agent or its navigation learning about it.
variables.values_or_range: 0-15 min [design]; a robotaxi fleet may learn faster from its own vehicles [design]
variables.impact_evidence: [design] tests reactive re-routing and repositioning
variables.how_to_model: Incident enters observations after a configurable delay; off in the no-live-traffic variant.

variables.name: Default 25 mph speed limit
variables.description: Statutory maximum on most NYC streets, which caps free-flow speeds, mainly at night.
variables.values_or_range: 25 mph default (34 RCNY 4-06(a); Admin Code 19-177(a)) [P*], in force since 7 Nov 2014 [U]; some arterials 30-35 mph [U]; expressways 40-50 mph [U]; school-zone limits 15-20 mph (Admin Code 19-177(e)) and 20 mph neighbourhood slow zones (19-177(d)) [P*]; 2024 'Sammy's Law' lets the city set 20 mph limits more widely [U]
variables.impact_evidence: 34 RCNY 4-06 and Admin Code 19-177 [P*]; NYC Vision Zero '25 mph signal retiming' dataset exists [S]; the limit binds mainly when streets are empty [design]
variables.data_source: NYC Open Data speed-limit layer [U]; OSM maxspeed
variables.how_to_model: Cap edge speed at limit x compliance factor (human 1.0-1.15, robotaxi 1.0).

variables.name: School-zone speed cameras (24/7)
variables.description: Automated speed enforcement that fines the vehicle owner for exceeding the limit by 11 mph or more near schools.
variables.values_or_range: ~2,000 cameras in ~750 school zones, 24/7 since 1 Aug 2022 [S]; $50 owner fine (19 RCNY 39-21) [P*]; violations fell 30% in the first year [uncertain: not re-read]
variables.impact_evidence: CBS New York and 6sqft, 2022-2023 [S]; 19 RCNY 39-21 [P*]
variables.data_source: NYC DOT speed camera program; OSM highway=speed_camera (partial)
variables.how_to_model: If the driving policy exceeds limits, sample fines by camera density along the route; a robotaxi never triggers them.

variables.name: Red-light cameras
variables.description: Automated red-light enforcement at selected intersections.
variables.values_or_range: $50 owner fine, +$25 if unpaid after 30 days (19 RCNY 39-17) [P*]; camera count not verified (state law has authorised up to 150 intersections [U])
variables.impact_evidence: 19 RCNY 39-17 [P*]; relevant only if aggressive driving is modelled [design]
variables.data_source: NYC DOT red light camera program [U]
variables.how_to_model: Fine probability per signal passed when an aggressive-driving mode is on.

variables.name: Bus-lane access rules and camera fines
variables.description: When taxis and FHVs may enter bus lanes (to make a right turn, including a right turn into a street or driveway within 200 ft of entering the lane [corrected by fact-check: the 200-ft exception is for right turns, 34 RCNY 4-12(m)(1)]; briefly to pick up or drop off passengers) and the fines for violations.
variables.values_or_range: camera fines $50 first, then $100 / $150 / $200 / $250 within 12 months, +$25 if unpaid (19 RCNY 39-18) [P*]; ACE cameras on 60+ routes also ticket bus-stop standing over 2.5 min, bus-lane standing over 5 min and double parking [uncertain: route count and dwell thresholds not re-read]
variables.impact_evidence: 34 RCNY 4-12(m) and 19 RCNY 39-18 [P*]; MTA ACE programme coverage [S]
variables.how_to_model: Bus-lane edges closed to through travel in active hours; curb stops on bus-lane blocks carry a fine risk when dwell exceeds limits.

variables.name: Driving-style speed factor (human vs robotaxi)
variables.description: How fast a vehicle drives relative to traffic and limits, from assertive human driving to conservative autonomous driving.
variables.values_or_range: human 1.0-1.1 x traffic speed [design]; robotaxi 0.8-0.95 on surface streets [design]; LA test trip time ratio 2.2x including routing [uncertain: single trip]
variables.impact_evidence: SF Chronicle and Forbes LA tests: Waymo drives slower and takes different routes [S]
variables.how_to_model: Vehicle-type multiplier on realised edge speed plus extra delay at complex intersections.

variables.name: Anti-idling limit
variables.description: NYC limit on running an engine while parked, which constrains how gas vehicles wait.
variables.values_or_range: 3 min (1 min next to a school, or next to or inside a park) (Admin Code 24-163(a), (f)) [P*]; fines $350-$2,000 (Admin Code 24-178 penalty table) [P*] [corrected by fact-check: the '$250+' figure conflicts with the code and was dropped]; citizen idling complaints cover only trucks and buses (24-182(a)) [P*]
variables.impact_evidence: NYC Admin Code 24-163, 24-178, 24-182 [P*]; NYC DEP idling page [S]
variables.how_to_model: Stationary waiting with the engine on beyond the limit carries a small fine probability; EVs effectively exempt (cross-link R08).

variables.name: Pickup dwell time
variables.description: Time from the vehicle reaching the pickup point until the rider is seated and the trip starts.
